items.title: "The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall
items.content_text:
"The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall

Authored by Daniel Lacalle via dlacalle.com,

Decades of bloated government, entitlements, subsidies, and mass migration have destroyed Europe's competitiveness and growth, all paid for with ever-rising taxes and more debt. They have also created enormous social discontent. Taxpayers are exhausted, and the recipients of subsidies are looting and vandalizing the streets. The flames in French cities are the bill that is arriving.

On Saturday 17 October, France burned again. What began as marches against the cost of living and the state of public schools turned into the worst violence the country has seen in decades. According to the French government, 550,000 people took to the streets, 1,200 were arrested, and 150 police officers were injured. In Limoges, rioters set the city hall ablaze; in Marseille, they broke into the city hall; and in Lyon, they torched the tourist office. AFP reporters on the ground described scenes more intense than the 2023 riots and the Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019, six months before a presidential election. Major cities, including Paris, Marseille, and Lille, suffered enormous commercial damage with smashed shopfronts, shattered glass, and ransacked retail spaces. In Bordeaux, Mayor Thomas Cazenave reported that up to 100 stores were looted in his city alone.

The riot images will be explained away as the work of a violent fringe, and it will be said that the mob that loots luxury boutiques and supermarkets certainly does not represent the hundreds of thousands who marched peacefully. However, the anger is real, and it has a cause.

Europe has spent half a century building the largest welfare state in the world on the promise that government could guarantee prosperity, security, and equality for everyone. That model has completely failed, and the people who were promised everything are discovering that the state only delivers stagnation and impoverishment.

France is the clearest example of what "democratic socialism" does to a rich nation. France is the most state-heavy economy in the European Union. French public spending reached 57.2% of GDP in 2025, the second highest in the EU and 7.7 points above the average. Its tax burden is among the highest in the world, at 45.3% of GDP in 2024, behind only Denmark in the EU. Public debt rose to 119% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, and the deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP in 2025. If big government, high taxes, and immigration delivered prosperity and social peace, France would be paradise. Instead, the protesters on the streets of Paris are demanding more of the same medicine that made them sick.

The welfare machine eats the economy.

France is not an extreme or single example. The disease is continental. Government expenditure in the European Union reached 49.5% of GDP in 2025 and 49.8% in the euro area. Half of the economy is directly controlled by the state, and much of the rest is regulated, subsidized, or taxed to the point of exhaustion. Social protection benefits alone reached 4,925 billion euros in 2024, 27.3% of the EU's GDP, after growing 6.9% in a single year while nominal GDP grew only 4.4%.

Add the subsidies. European governments spent 340 billion euros on energy subsidies in 2024 and another 168 billion euros in state aid. Governments first make energy expensive with taxes, regulations, and ideological mandates, then subsidize the very costs they created, and finally borrow to pay for the subsidies. Citizens pay three times, as consumers, as taxpayers, and as the future holders of the debt.

The debt is the inevitable consequence. Greece ended 2025 with public debt at 146.1% of GDP, Italy at 137.1%, France at 115.6%, Belgium at 107.9%, and Spain at 100.7%. And those figures hide the largest liability of all. According to Eurostat, the pension entitlements already accrued in social insurance schemes reach 500% of GDP in Spain, 462% in Austria, 438% in Italy, 397% in France, and 347% in Germany, almost all of them unfunded, according to Eurostat. These are promises that no government can keep without crushing the next generation with taxes or destroying the purchasing power of the currency.

Germany, once the engine of Europe, now transfers 127.4 billion euros from the federal budget to its pension system in 2026, rising to 132 billion in 2027. Spain's Social Security debt has almost quadrupled since 2018, from 34,888 million to 136,176 million euros, and social contributions cover pension payments only until early October. The welfare state now lives on borrowing against the future rather than on what the economy produces.

Competitiveness destroyed

There is no free lunch. Every euro of spending must be paid for by the productive economy, and Europe's productive economy is suffocating. The International Monetary Fund expects the euro area to grow just 1.1% in 2026, compared with 2.3% in the United States, with France at a miserable 0.4% and Italy at 0.8%. Labor productivity per hour worked in the EU stood at only 78.5% of the US level in 2024, and in 2025 it grew just 0.4% compared with 1.6% in the United States.

German industrial production has fallen every year since 2022, and the BDI industry association no longer expects a recovery in 2026, only stagnation. Output in energy-intensive sectors is at its lowest level since the end of 2023. That is what happens when energy is made artificially expensive, labor is taxed at confiscatory rates, regulation multiplies, and capital flees.

Inflation makes the situation even worse. Euro area inflation rose to 3.8% in September 2026, with energy prices up 18.9% year-on-year. Governments that printed and borrowed their way through every crisis now discover that the real wages of their citizens cannot keep up. The cost-of-living crisis that sent hundreds of thousands into French streets has its roots in decades of too much government, not too little.

Mass migration worsens the situation.

Instead of reforming, European governments chose to import the illusion of growth. On January 2025, 46.7 million people living in the EU had been born outside it, 10.4% of the population, and the number of non-EU citizens rose by 1.6 million in a single year to 30.6 million. Immigration may be a powerful engine of prosperity when it is carefully selected for skills and enters flexible labor markets with low taxes and limited welfare. Europe did the opposite. It combined mass migration with rigid labor markets, enormous taxes, and the most excessive welfare benefits on the planet.

The result was predictable. Many immigrants have no incentive to adapt or participate and are trapped in low-wage jobs and welfare dependency. Thus, public services were stretched beyond capacity, housing became unaffordable in the major cities, and integration failed in entire neighborhoods. Governments used headline GDP inflated by population growth to hide stagnant income per person, while workers saw their wages fall in real net terms as inflation and their taxes rise. This is the evidence of a model that promised everything to everyone and delivered disappointment to all.

When you create a state big enough to promise everything, it delivers almost nothing but takes away everything it can.

Angry taxpayers, entitled mobs

Democratic socialism created two angry Europeans. The first is the angry taxpayer, the middle-class worker, the small business owner, and the self-employed professional who pays more every year and receives worse services, longer waiting lists, unaffordable housing, security problems, and a pension system that will not be there when they retire. The second is entitled Europe, a constituency that has been taught for decades that the state owes it everything and responds to inevitable disappointment with rage and violence.

Both are victims of the same lie. Politicians promised that they could raise taxes on the rich, borrow without limit, and expand entitlements forever with no consequences. They told voters that someone else would pay. Now that someone else, the productive economy, is exhausted. Capital is leaving, young talent is emigrating, industry is closing, and the bill is landing on the middle class and on young people who will inherit the debt.

What Europe needs is less state. Another subsidy, another tax on «the rich» or another emergency fund financed with joint debt will only deepen the crisis. The way forward is to cut unproductive spending, reduce the tax burden on labor and investment, end the subsidy culture that keeps the economy zombified, liberalize markets, and abandon the ideological mandates that have made European industry uncompetitive.

Europe needs a migration policy designed for prosperity rather than electoral calculation, selective, linked to employment, and not to welfare entitlement. It needs a gradual transition from unfunded pay-as-you-go pensions to capitalized systems in which workers own their savings, as Sweden and the Netherlands have shown is possible.

Citizens need to realize the truth, which is that the state does not create wealth; it consumes it.

The riots in France are a warning to America. When a society is told for decades that it is entitled to everything and then discovers that the state is broke, the result is not solidarity but violence.

Democratic socialism promised Europe equality and security. It delivered stagnation, inflation, debt, and rage. If America adopts this system, it will follow the same path of misery and desperation. The sooner Europe abandons democratic socialism, the sooner it can recover the prosperity that made it the envy of the world.

items.title: Barclays To Axe 5,000 Jobs As Britain's Youth Employment Crisis Deepens
items.content_text:
Barclays To Axe 5,000 Jobs As Britain's Youth Employment Crisis Deepens

Bloomberg cites a Barclays corporate presentation saying the bank is cutting 5,000 jobs as it pushes ahead with cost-cutting measures and adopts artificial intelligence to improve efficiency.

The reductions would affect about 5% of the bank's workforce. The London-based lender employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025, according to Bloomberg data.

Barclays said it was "structurally reducing" costs to "generate capacity for investment." The presentation also touched on organizational simplification and greater efficiency, supported by AI.

Separately, a Bloomberg report says that technology and finance jobs for young people in the UK have fallen sharply.

Payroll jobs for young people in information and communication have plummeted 30% between the end of 2022 and the end of 2025, according to Boston Consulting Group data. Finance jobs for the same age group fell 10%. Combined, the two sectors - that is, about a decline of 45,000 jobs - left about 163,000 employed. 

Young folks "are being squeezed out of some of the UK's most important sectors," said Raoul Ruparel, senior director at BCG's Center for Growth, as companies grow more reluctant to hire young workers. 

"AI may be playing a part, but it's unlikely to be the whole story," Ruparel said. "Much of the fall happened in 2023 and 2024, before today's more capable AI tools. A post-pandemic tech downturn and remote working, which makes juniors harder to train, are also likely factors."

Layoffhedge, which tracks SEC filings, WARN notices, and verified press reports, has recorded 702,000 job cuts across 541 US companies this year alone. That's about 2,300 job cuts per day.

items.title: Creepy Ad Tells Grandparents To Get Consent Before Hugging Their Own Grandkids
items.content_text:
Creepy Ad Tells Grandparents To Get Consent Before Hugging Their Own Grandkids

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

A publicly funded advert from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's We-Consent campaign shows grandparents arriving at the front door. One grandchild rushes in for a hug. The other winces and recoils as the older couple lean in. The voiceover declares: "Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."

This is not a measured reminder about bodily autonomy. It is a deliberate attempt to plant suspicion inside ordinary homes, cast grandparents as potential abusers, and train the next generation to treat spontaneous family affection as something that requires official clearance.

The same ideological current that wants to erase the words "mother" and "father," rewrite sex education as social engineering, and replace "husband and wife" with sterile inclusive language is now targeting the simple act of a grandmother putting her arms around a grandchild.

?? Ireland is basically telling grandparents that a hug from Nana requires a consent form. The republic has launched a consent campaign ad warning grandparents not to assume their grandchildren want a squeeze. Is the “Irish goodbye” being replaced by the “Irish hello”? Writer: Marie https://t.co/92rg9ifarr

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 21, 2026

The 25-second clip is part of the broader We-Consent programme funded by the Department of Justice and aims, in its own words, to inform and educate the public about "all forms of consent" across every relationship.

In practice it has produced a video that visually distorts the grandparents' approach so they appear threatening.

The indoctrination is getting really weird.

— Paul Joseph Watson (@PrisonPlanet) October 21, 2026

Also, as Graham Linehan pointed out, the makers of the advert even managed to crowbar in a diverse grandchild who looks nothing like the grandparents, just for the sake of it.

Why is one of the kids black? Is this about hugging your grandkids or random strangers?

— Graham Linehan (@Glinner) October 21, 2026

On GB News, Patrick Christys reacted with open disbelief, remarking that you would try telling that to his Greek grandmother.

‘Oh come, sweet asteroid of death… you try telling that to my Greek grandma!’ @PatrickChristys is in disbelief at a video released by the Irish state that warns grandparents over hugging their grandchildren. https://t.co/c3KsOC1dDi

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 21, 2026

The backlash was immediate and cross-party. Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan stated that the video "does not represent the views of the Government," was "both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents," and had been removed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre after officials engaged with them.

He added: "It goes without saying that having loving grandparents in a child's life is an incredibly positive thing to be cherished and not something to be campaigned against."

He further noted that while consent education around sexual relationships is vital, "this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."

Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín called the advert "bonkers" and said it was "planting the seed that a grandparent's hug may be insidious and a suspicious activity," which he described as "really wrong."

He argued that grandparents possess the "emotional intelligence" to know when a child does not want to be hugged, that the state has no business in this space, and that it "owes grandparents an apology."

Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill labelled the piece "a complete waste of resources," "offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," and "a million miles off the mark." He observed that the distorted imagery gave "a distinct impression of threat" and asked: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls... before we can greet family members?"

Councillor Gavin Pepper slammed the government and NGOs for "losing the run of ourselves." He wrote that while children should never be forced into unwanted contact, "we also need a bit of common sense." The grandparent-grandchild bond is "one of the most important bonds in Irish family life," and "a hug from a loving grandparent should not be presented as something strange or suspicious." "Irish culture, family and traditions matter."

None of this is an isolated misstep. It sits inside a wider pattern of institutional hostility toward the nuclear and extended family. The same political and cultural forces that fund these campaigns have pushed to strip "mother" and "father" from official language, treat biological reality as optional, and reframe parental authority as a risk to be managed by the state.

The We-Consent campaign's own materials speak of moving "from a Moment to a Movement" and of changing culture so that consent becomes "an integral part" of every interaction. In the grandparents advert that ambition collapses into the grotesque: ordinary love is reframed as a potential violation requiring prior negotiation.

Families that once operated on shared affection, known character, and instinctive boundaries are now to be tutored by state-funded NGOs in the correct way to greet their own kin.

Public money was spent to produce and circulate this video, and the organisations involved saw no problem with casting Irish grandparents as the face of unwanted physical contact. Real sexual violence is a serious crime. Pathologising a grandmother's hug is not a contribution to preventing it. It is a contribution to the long project of making the family itself feel unsafe, contingent, and in need of external supervision.

Parents and grandparents will continue to hug their children. The state can keep commissioning ads that treat that fact as a problem. The rest of the country has already decided which side of that argument is deranged.

items.title: Italy Makes Parents Pay For Milan Rioters: Meloni Decree Fines Families, Adds Riot Crime Carrying Up To 5 Years
items.content_text:
Italy Makes Parents Pay For Milan Rioters: Meloni Decree Fines Families, Adds Riot Crime Carrying Up To 5 Years

Italy's cabinet approved an emergency decree-law on Oct. 20 in response to the weekend riots in Milan, ANSA reported. The eight-article text creates a new offense of violent participation in demonstrations, extends preventive detention to minors aged 16 and over, and sends 500 more soldiers to Milan through Dec. 31 at a cost of €4.7 million.

Parents of minors who commit violence at demonstrations face fines of €500 to €1,000, and the fine doubles for a repeat. It applies even when the minor is too young to be prosecuted. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that if a minor is responsible for the damage, the parents should pay, and she asked all political forces to side with legality.

The new crime covers anyone who uses sticks or clubs or throws objects at a protest in a way that endangers people. It carries two to five years in prison and a fine of up to €20,000, with a higher penalty for a covered face or damage to public infrastructure or utilities. Anyone who organizes or promotes groups for violent demonstrations, including through online tools, faces four to 12 years.

For minors, those over 14 are presumed capable of understanding their acts and can be charged immediately, a provision carried over from a bill the cabinet approved in July. Meloni said then that anyone who assaults, robs or wrecks must pay "even if he is 15 or 16," and the opposition called it propaganda and an authoritarian drift. The new decree also lets the police chief bar a group of five or more minors from gathering where they behave in an intimidating way. It also makes a minor injury to a police officer prosecutable automatically and adds optional deferred arrest for property damage.

Violence broke out in Milan after a Saturday demonstration over living costs and public services. Reuters reported that hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set fires and looted shops including Decathlon and Vodafone while luxury stores on Via Montenapoleone stripped their windows. Police took 271 young people to the Milan police headquarters; 32 were arrested, 23 of them minors. Similar clashes hit Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin. Euronews counted 14 injured officers and a damage estimate from the Confcommercio business group of over €1 million in Milan alone and at least €1.3 million nationwide.

Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said early findings ruled out structured links to antagonist groups, and no organizer has been identified. He called the youth mobilization spontaneous but said "something certainly happened" and that answers would come soon. Defense Minister Guido Crosetto blamed "hybrid warfare," while Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini rejected the idea of a coordinating hand, Russian involvement included. Ynet reported that assessments suggest many participants simply wanted to break things, though police also identified radical-left activists from social centers who left once force was used.

The package was a political negotiation. After a 90-minute summit at Palazzo Chigi on Oct. 19, Il Sole 24 Ore reported that more than 200 young people had been detained and that 80 percent were under 18. Salvini announced "500 more soldiers to defend Milan. A victory for the League," while Forza Italia claimed credit for the same troops. Crosetto's request to give soldiers judicial police powers did not make it into the text, per ANSA, which also reported that tension with the presidential palace delayed the cabinet meeting by almost an hour. The government denied any blockage.

items.title: A Warning From France
items.content_text:
A Warning From France

Authored by Jeffrey A. Tucker via The Epoch Times,

The chaos in the streets of France has a familiar ring to Americans who watched several cities burn in the summer of 2020. What started as "mostly peaceful" protests were quickly hijacked by chaos actors who whipped up excitable populations into a looting and pillaging frenzy, resulting in police crackdowns in the best cases but utter destruction in the worst cases.

The metaphor of the powder keg is one that is often invoked here. In the U.S. case, we had suffered months of COVID lockdowns that created pent-up energy on the part of an entire generation that had been shut out of schools, spilling into the streets in the name of protesting racism.

Oddly, a media that had been screaming for people to stay home and stay safe flipped on a dime to urge everyone to get out in the streets for purely political protests.

Something similar seems to have happened in France. Rising unemployment, high cost of living, underfunded and failing schools, loss of opportunity, rising crime, and frustration over waves of new immigrant populations have reached a fever pitch. Peaceful protests turned violent with masked and destructive provocateurs lighting fires and pillaging whole commercial sectors in many cities.

It was six years ago that France experimented with some of the toughest lockdowns in Europe. They kept schools open but restricted gatherings of all sorts. Bars, restaurants, and cafés faced particularly long disruptions: closed from mid-March 2020, reopened gradually in June 2020, then closed again from late October 2020 until May and June of 2021. After that, there were long capacity limits. Cultural venues, gyms, and ski resorts were also heavily restricted.

Cities were shut to the unvaccinated. France used the passe sanitaire (health pass: proof of vaccination, recent recovery, or negative test) starting in summer 2021 for restaurants, bars, cinemas, museums, long-distance transport, large events, and shopping centers. From January 2022, this became a passe vaccinal for those over 16 in many of the same places, lasting until suspension on March 2022.

All of this was totalitarian by any standard and it created a fiscal crisis as the state funded the entire mess with huge subsidies and payments to both individuals and businesses. The economy never recovered and business has struggled ever since. In the backdrop of this is one of Europe's most generous and expensive welfare states tangled up with a regulatory apparatus that makes the United States look like a laissez-faire utopia by comparison.

The unemployment problem is particularly poignant for students with advanced degrees as funded by the state. Like the latter years of the Soviet Union, everyone seems to have a high-level credential in something but these pieces of paper are guaranteeing nothing on the real-world job markets.

Then there is the resulting inflation, the worst in 40 years. It was intensified by France's idiotic embrace of net zero policies on energy that have resulted in high prices and rationing. This is the land of austerity, highly controlled, with a ruling class presiding over dramatically declining living standards, a forever rising welfare state, a highly regulated business sector, combined with a disastrous immigration policy that has destabilized demographics.

No French government has balanced its books in 52 years. The parasitic elites have squandered the wealth of the population while closing off opportunities for enterprise and economic growth.

France, more than any other industrialized democracy, has followed the path of Progressive policies in everything. And look where it has gotten them? No one likes the results and absolutely no one trusts the system. French voters keep rejecting establishment politicians but the establishment somehow never leaves. Reform never arrives while frustrations fester.

The 19th-century French economist Frédéric Bastiat long ago nailed the question of the participation in the public life of a nation, explaining why it cannot belong to all but only to those who have the capacity to exercise that right responsibly.

"It is not the voter alone who suffers the consequences of his vote," he wrote, "because each vote touches and affects everyone in the entire community; because the people in the community have a right to demand some safeguards concerning the acts upon which their welfare and existence depend."

Exactly right and this is precisely the problem in which France found itself. It never restricted participation rights even as it flung open the borders and endlessly expanded the welfare state. This is the path to national suicide in any nation.

Is it too late for a political solution? Perhaps but that raises the question of how this chaos will resolve. We could look back to the interwar period in Europe and see one possible path. The inflation and social chaos as fallout from the Great War ended up raising a generation of authoritarian politicians rallying around fascist ideology. We tend to single out Germany but often forget that the same tendencies hit Italy, Spain, and France.

This is the only real modern precedent we have for how this ends. History may not repeat and I've wondered for years if something more dramatic is headed to Europe, something more like 1989 and 1990 in the former Soviet empire. States unraveled in different ways but the result was the same everywhere. An entire establishment and system were washed away in a few short years, discrediting decades of rule.

The states from that period that undertook the biggest reforms - Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Soviet satellites Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia - also happened to be the same states that resisted the push for open borders for several decades. They have avoided the economic sclerosis of Europe along with the social, demographic, and industrial decay. It's possible that the next stage of Europe will involve not just the full-scale unraveling of the European Union but also the abrupt overthrow of whole political establishments.

Let France be a warning to America. The policies that inflicted so many wounds on this country are all the same policies advocated in elite and fashionable circles in the United States, pushed by the heights of academia, and celebrated by establishment media. It's all about more controls, more corporate cartels, more regulations, higher taxes, and more immigration floods without any real standards over what constitutes citizenship.

If the United States goes this way - it very well could happen with enough voter apathy and poor policies such as those being imposed on New York City today - we'll end up right where France is today. We face a choice. We can choose chaos or choose to return to the ideals of a constitutional republic that our Founders envisioned. This is not only a fork in the road for France. It points to a coming fork for the United States too.

Views expressed in this article are opinions of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of The Epoch Times or ZeroHedge.

items.title: "High Likelihood Of Error": Judge Halts DHS Voter-Fraud Door-Knocks In Nine States
items.content_text:
"High Likelihood Of Error": Judge Halts DHS Voter-Fraud Door-Knocks In Nine States

The Trump administration wanted an AI dragnet for weeding out illegals trying to vote - however a federal judge says it's catching legal citizens in the process and has put a stop to it. 

Late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California, a Biden appointee, issued a preliminary injunction barring the Department of Homeland Security from election-related field operations in nine states when the targets are people agents "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens." The ruling lands in a week full of voter-roll news. This morning we reported that the LA County registrar admitted it has no way to check the citizenship of 20,000 voters flagged by DOJ, which came on the heels of the Trump admin's lawsuit against the state.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín's core finding on Wednesday, however, was that there was a "high likelihood of error" (California Nurses Association v. Mullin, No. 4:26-cv-10680):

"Even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents."

In other words, DHS cannot reliably tell who is a citizen.

Below we walk through how the target lists were built, what the judge actually blocked (it is narrower than the headlines suggest), the administration's case, and why the real deadline is 5pm Friday.

DHS focused their searches on California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The raw material was 48.2 million records received "through independent sources" the judge deemed to have "questionable provenance," plus 50.6 million records from DOJ. Those came from state voter rolls or, where states refused to share, "unreliable commercial versions." DHS then "enriches" the data through a system called iLab, "using unknown artificial intelligence tools." USCIS staff then had to whittle the list down:

"...a minimum of 40 suspected subject reviews, which requires officers to take no more than twelve minutes to eliminate a person from the target list using the commercial databases."

That said, the ruling doesn't mean DHS can't investigate voter fraud.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections."

The order runs until 8:00pm on Nov 3 or when polls close.

items.title: Netanyahu To IDF: 'Overthrow The Iranian Regime'
items.content_text:
Netanyahu To IDF: 'Overthrow The Iranian Regime'

Authored by Dave DeCamp via AntiWar.com

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that his directive to the Israeli military is to "overthrow the regime in Iran" as he continues to ramp up his rhetoric in the days before the October 27 Israeli elections.

"My directive to the IDF, the Mossad, and the defense establishment… is to overthrow the regime in Iran," Netanyahu told a group of graduating IDF officers, according to The Jerusalem Post.

The Israeli leader went on to claim that Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, is pursuing nuclear weapons, a claim he’s been making about the Islamic Republic for decades.

"The Iranian regime still has not learned its lesson. Mojtaba Khamenei decided to follow in his father’s footsteps and has released the safety catch, and Iran is once again trying to develop weapons of death," he said. "Iran is once again attempting to develop a nuclear bomb."

While both Netanyahu and President Trump continue to frame the conflict as being about preventing a nuclear-armed Iran, there was no evidence either before the June 2025 war or the current war that Tehran had decided to pursue nuclear weapons, and that was the consensus of the US intelligence agencies.

Netanyahu also referenced Trump’s suggestion that the US and Israel will "finish the job" against Iran, something the US president said when endorsing Netanyahu for Israel’s elections.

"And so, as long as they are here, as long as they are willing to join a threatening and terrible weapon, the State of Israel is in existential danger. And our role, the role of all of us, is to save the nation. My good friend, President Trump, also believes that this is the only way," Netanyahu said.

"He said a few days ago, ‘We are ready to finish the job, to finish the job, he said. We are ready to finish the job, but we will do it only with you, the State of Israel.’ And this is exactly what we will do," he added.

The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that Netanyahu wanted to resume bombing Iran earlier this month and that the IDF was ready to start the strikes on October 10, but that Trump decided not to restart the conflict before the November 3 US midterm elections.

Meanwhile, an Iranian response to Trump recently touting the MOAB/nicknamed Mother of all Bombs, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb:

Iran says it is preparing to unveil a weapon called the “father of all bombs”, amid reports Trump has ordered plans for strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure using the “mother of all bombs”, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. LIVE updates: https://t.co/AfJieCwffH https://t.co/Z1vzPKS5sM

The report said that the strikes would have targeted Iran’s nuclear facilities, government sites, and civilian infrastructure, and that if Trump had given the green light, the attacks would have been heavier than the ones launched when the war began on February 28.

items.title: "Wicker" Movie A Feminist Anti-Patriarchy Fantasy About Sex With Monsters
items.content_text:
"Wicker" Movie A Feminist Anti-Patriarchy Fantasy About Sex With Monsters

If you want to know the deepest and darkest dreams of the feminist cult, you don't have to look very hard.  All you have to do is watch their movies and read their books, which put their mental illness and hypocrisy on full display for the world to see.  

A now infamous example of this is a romance novel called "Morning Glory Milking Farm", a feminist inspired sex fantasy book about a broke woman trying to pay off her student loans who takes on the job of "milking" a Minotaur to collect sperm to be used for pharmaceutical products.  In other words, she's a whore working for Big Pharma in a world where monsters exist at the same time as student loans. 

But her favorite Minotaur respects her agency and treats her like a queen, so they fall in love.

Yes, this sounds like writing for retards, and it is.  Yet, this book became a viral best seller in 2026 and hit Amazon's top ten list.  The "monster sex fantasy" genre has skyrocketed in popularity among women in recent years, moving beyond the typical vampire love story into the realm of the truly disturbing and bizarre.  For the most part, these books are "feminist coded" and they are filled with woke propaganda. 

In other words, the publishing industry has been hijacked by liberal women and most books are now designed to cater to their degenerate fetishes.  Furthermore, it's interesting that these novels have been leaning more and more into romantic encounters with animals, monsters and demonic creatures:  This is because feminism has made expressions of female passion (and submission) with normal men impossible. 

Hollywood has only made minor efforts to tap into this market of feminist fetishism, but they are definitely making an attempt with the movie "Wicker", described as a "feisty feminist fable" set in a Medieval village where traditional gender roles and patriarchy dominate. 

An unattractive and smelly fishmonger woman has boldly rejected the standards of the village, and as a result, she has become a middle-aged spinster with no husband, no children and no prospects.  Rather that accepting her fate as a consequence of her choices, she employs a magical basket weaver to "make her a husband."  He does exactly that, and of course, her new wicker partner turns out to be the "perfect man", at least in the minds of feminists.

He acts as a sex toy and house slave who fixes everything, helps her with chores and basically agrees to everything she says (we'll just skip past all the jokes about splinters).  He can't lie and he makes her erratic emotions the center of his attention.  This of course, leads to all the other women in the village becoming jealous, questioning their own marriages and demanding more equality from the patriarchy. 

Obviously, in Medieval times, these women would be worried about survival rather than having their egos stroked and their emotions catered to at every waking moment, but since this is supposed to be a fairytale we can set aside the fact that "patriarchy" kept the human species alive all the way up to the 1970s before modern women decided they no longer needed men.  

The thing about Wicker, though, and all the fictional feminist media like it, is that it acts as an inadvertent admission from modern women that they do, in fact, need men.  They refuse to say it out loud, but their fantasies betray their desires.  The wicker husband does all the things that men normally do, from heavy labor and house repairs to keeping a woman's urges regulated.  

What he doesn't do, though, is take charge and lead the way.  This is the trade-off that feminists refuse to accept.  They want all the benefits of a strong and capable man, but they don't want to give up anything in return.  They even feel guilty about sexual desire for a man.  

Women are no longer allowed to swoon over Fabio, or the cowboy on the white horse, or even the shirtless "noble savage" who saves them from danger.  Most feminists desperately want to live out their fantasies of a white knight (or a bad boy) coming to save them from harm, or poverty, or boredom, but they will never admit they need something from a man.  So, feminist fiction has turned to inhuman monster figures as symbols for male virility and dominance. 

It's the only way for authors to avoid being cancelled. Let's not forget, only a decade ago one of the best selling books in the US for women readers was "50 Shades Of Grey", a story about a female college student who works in a hardware store and ends up in a relationship with a corporate mogul who engages her in a BDMS contract.  These women are freaks, and feminism is making them freakier. 

Will "Wicker" succeed at the box office in the same way that romance monster porn is succeeding in bookstores? Probably not.  Reading is a solitary activity.  Women are less inclined to go to movies on their own and there is little chance that men will want to pay good money to watch something like Wicker on date night.  It's most likely a box office bomb in the making, but at the very least, the makers of the film know exactly who their audience is. 

Woke films that do end up making their money back usually market specifically to women instead of trying to market to everyone.  Wicker will end up becoming yet another case study of the twisted minds of feminists searching for that perfect woke world that will never exist.  That world without patriarchy in which men serve only as utilities for them to exploit, or as emotional tampons that they can hold hostage. 

Wicker also reveals the crushing terror many of these women feel as they approach "the wall" and cat lady status.  The real fantasy on display here is the idea that a woman can reject the laws of nature and still get all the benefits of a feminine life, including a doting husband, long after her viability on the sexual marketplace has expired.

items.title: 梵高名画《The Starry Night》可能描绘的是真实的夜空
items.content_text: 梵高于 1889 年创作的名画《The Starry Night》可能描绘的是 1889 年 7 月 22 日法国真实的夜空。《The Starry Night》被普遍认为风格化地呈现了梵高在法国普罗旺斯圣雷米的窗外看到的景象。争议在于这片夜空究竟是这位后印象派画家自己的幻想，即象征性表达，还是真实的天文观察结果。此外这幅画的具体创作日期也无法确定。为解决这一问题，韩国庆熙大学的研究人员开发了一个框架，将天文学模拟结果与星象位置测量数据、历史天气记录，以及梵高的信件结合起来。研究人员根据描绘这片景色的早期素描重建了画中的窄视场。他们发现，下蛾眉月、金星，以及金牛座的毕星团或许肉眼可见于 1889 年 7 月 22 日的黎明前后，并且其构型与画中的排列大体相符。历史气象记录显示，1889 年 7月 22 日前后的夜空清澈到足以看见这一天文排列。此外梵高信件中频繁提及的蝉表明当时气候炎热，这也更贴近 1889 年 7 月的历史温度。

items.title: 希腊通过法案禁止 15 岁以下儿童使用社媒
items.content_text: 希腊议会周五通过了一项法案，禁止 15 岁以下的儿童使用社媒平台。此举旨在回应公众对社交媒体会对未成年人的健康与安全产生负面影响之日益增长的担忧。禁令将于 2027 年 1 月 1 日生效。澳大利亚是首个通过立法限制未成年人使用社媒的国家。法国也曾通过类似法律，但于 8 月被宪法委员会裁定无效。希腊总理基 Kyriakos Mitsotakis 表示，社媒平台有 2 个半月的时间制定方案，核实用户年龄并保护其隐私。希腊政府表示，将支持家长共同遏制“无限滚动”现象——这种行为会导致儿童睡眠不足、注意力难以集中，挤占与朋友相处的时间。

items.title: 宫本茂成为首位获得日本文化勋章的游戏从业者
items.content_text: 日本文部科学省公布了 2026 年度文化勋章获得者名单，任天堂首席游戏设计师及代表董事宫本茂位列其中， 成为首位获得文化勋章的游戏从业者。文化勋章旨在表彰在文化发展方面做出特别显著贡献的人士，自 1937 年设立以来，获得者包括了画家横山大观、诺贝尔物理学奖得主汤川秀树、棒球明星王贞治和长岛茂雄等。宫本茂在记者会上表示：“游戏并非由我一人独自完成，而是与众多伙伴共同创造的成果。我是怀着代表大家的心情来接受这份荣誉的。”

items.title: 联合国警告厄尔尼诺可能导致数千万人粮食短缺
items.content_text: 今年的厄尔尼诺事件强度可能前所未有。它将于 2026 年底前后达到峰值，但其影响在此之后仍将持续很长时间。热带太平洋（厄尔尼诺的中心区域）的海面温度在 2026 年 11 月至 2027 年 1 月期间可能比平均值高出 3.8°C。 一次非常强的厄尔尼诺会扰乱许多地区的正常温度和降水格局。它可能给一些地区带来严重干旱，给另一些地区带来强降雨和洪水，并导致世界大片地区温度升高。极端天气事件可能会成倍增多，并发生级联效应。 联合国人道主义事务协调厅（OCHA）厅长弗莱彻警告称，全球可能有多达 5000 万人面临严重的粮食短缺。他呼吁各国政府做好充分准备。厄尔尼诺可能会给非洲、中南美和东南亚等地带来巨大破坏。

items.title: mRNA 癌症疫苗将死亡复发风险减少 42%
items.content_text: 制药公司 Merck 和 Moderna 宣布，在 III 期黑色素瘤临床试验中，基于 mRNA 技术的个性化癌症疫苗相比标准治疗，将死亡或复发风险减少 42%。黑色素瘤是最致命的皮肤癌。两家公司正与监管机构接洽争取该疫苗早日获批。有 1,137 名患者参加了 III 期临床试验，他们此前均患有 IIB-IV 期黑色素瘤，已通过手术切除肿瘤。患者被以 2:1 的比例随机分配至两组：一组接受个性化 mRNA 疫苗联合标准治疗，另一组仅接受标准治疗。标准治疗采用 Merck 已上市的单克隆抗体抗癌药物 Keytruda。定制 mRNA 疫苗名为 intismeran 或 mRNA-4157，编码了癌症特有的突变，帮助免疫反应精准识别和对癌细胞进行攻击。Intismeran 和 Keytruda 治疗组两年后有 82% 的患者存活且未出现复发，Keytruda 和安慰剂组中这一比例为 70%。

items.title: 浏览器 Arc 将于 12 月关闭
items.content_text: The Browser Company 宣布其浏览器 Arc 将于 12 月 22 日关闭，用户将无法再能启动应用。Arc 基于 Chromium，于 2023 年释出了 1.0 版本，但 2024 年就停止了开发，2025 年 5 月宣布它正在开发 AI 驱动的浏览器 Dia。Arc 从 10 月 22 日起无法创建新的 Arc 账号，11 月 23 日起停用部分功能，12 月 22 日无法启动应用，Arc 账户将被停用，个人数据会在 30 天内被删除。The Browser Company 表示 Arc 用户可通过数据导出功能无缝使用其全力开发的新浏览器 Dia，声称用户在 Arc 中使用的浏览器功能在 Dia 中均可免费使用，而 AI 功能则是可选使用的。

items.title: Switch 2 越狱能运行自制程序
items.content_text: 研究员 Sammy Hajhamid 利用软件漏洞在 Switch 2 上实现越狱，而且能运行自制程序。越狱利用了一个专门运行在任天堂硬件上的编程环境和解释器 SmileBasic 4。Hajhamid 使用 OpenAI 的 Codex 对 SmileBasic 的语言解释器进行探测，花了两周时间发现了一个 32 位整数溢出漏洞，利用该漏洞能对部分系统内存进行读写操作。他在此基础上从 Switch 2 内部找到了其它漏洞，提权获得任意读写权限。他之后演示了在越狱的游戏机上运行自制程序。SmileBasic 4 已从任天堂的 Switch eShop 中下架，漏洞可能会在后续的固件更新中修复。

items.title: KeePassXC 2.8.0 释出
items.content_text: 开源密码管理器项目 KeePassXC 释出了 v2.8.0。KeePassXC 代表 KeePass Cross-Platform Community Edition，是 KeePassX 的一个分支，而 KeePassX 则是基于 Qt 构建的 KeePass 克隆版本，但已停止维护。KeePassXC 2.8.0 带来了用户期待的新功能，大量 bug 修复和安全修正。主要特性包括：Qt 的版本从 Qt5 升级到 Qt6，Wayland(Linux) 下支持 Auto-Type，可自定义快捷键，使用外部工具实现远程数据库同步，macOS 支持密码快速解锁，Linux 下支持通过 Polkit 快速解锁，Windows 下提供了支持 ARM64 架构的原生版本，等等。

items.title: eMudhra 退出全球 CA 业务
items.content_text: 在曝出惊人丑闻之后，印度公司 eMudhra  宣布退出全球 CA 业务，将专注于核心企业解决方案和信任服务而非 SSL/TLS 相关业务。它是印度唯一一个被主流浏览器信任的 Root CA 机构。截至 2026 年，公司已发行逾 6000 万张证书。此前 eMudhra 的八个中间证书的私钥泄漏，而这些私钥被发现是极其简单的数字如 4。该公司在声明中称这些简单密钥是“多重人为错误”导致的。相关密钥是在 2025 年  4 月 30 日生成，它使用专门的硬件安全模块生成了一组密钥，但软件脚本的一个缺陷导致其生成了另一组较弱的密钥，由于两组密钥名称相似，结果其员工选择了弱密钥组。

items.title: 趋势科技在公开的内核邮件列表上披露内核漏洞
items.content_text: 趋势科技的安全团队 Zero Day Initiative 向人人可访问的内核邮件列表上递交了一系列新发现的内核漏洞。按照惯例，漏洞应该递交到不对外公开的安全邮件列表。递交的部分漏洞没有补丁，部分漏洞已有补丁在测试，这些漏洞的 CVSS 风险评分最高为 9.0。稳定版内核维护者 Greg Kroah-Hartman 批评安全研究人员将漏洞报告递交到公共的邮件列表。而在 AI 辅助漏洞发现时代，此类的漏洞报告越来越多。

items.title: 科学家揭示低温延缓衰老的机制
items.content_text: 适度低温已被证明能有效延长动物寿命，延缓与衰老相关的机能衰退。但低温延缓衰老的分子机制是什么？研究人员利用秀丽隐杆线虫（Caenorhabditis elegans ）发现，低温会触发代谢物 dihydrobiopterin (BH2)的大量产生，其中肌肉充当了中央工厂的作用，负责合成 BH2，BH2 随后输送至身体其它组织，诱导氨基酸酪氨酸（tyrosine）的合成，它有助于维持蛋白质稳态，在衰老过程中促进组织健康。论文发表在《自然》期刊上。研究还发现，同时补充 BH2 和酪氨酸能在秀丽隐杆线虫及细胞培养物上再现低温的部分有益效应，即便在标准温度或更高温度下也能显著延长寿命。研究人员强调，就目前研究而言，开发出一种能重现低温长寿效应的药丸还为时过早。

items.title: 逾半数美国人认为 AI 对社会有害
items.content_text: 根据 ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos 的调查，57%的美国人认为 AI 对社会有害，42%的人认为它对社会有益。仅有 2% 的人认为它对社会极其有益，17% 的人认为它对社会极其有害。与年长者相比，年轻的美国人更有可能认为 AI 对社会有害：在 30 岁以下的美国人中，65% 的人持此观点；在 30-39 岁的群体中，这一比例为 59%。而在 40 岁及以上的美国人中，认为 AI 对社会有害的比例相对较低，但也超过半数（53%）。在民主党人（63%）和独立人士（58%）中，多数人认为 AI 对社会有害；共和党人认为有益有害的比例差不多，51% 的人认为  AI 对社会有益，47% 的人认为它对社会有害。当谈及 AI 对个人自身的影响时，50% 的人认为 AI 对自己有益，49% 的人认为对自己有害。持负面态度的人群立场更为强烈——认为 AI 对自己极其有害的人数（15%）是认为其极其有益人数（3%）的五倍。多数共和党人（57%）认为 AI 对自己个人有益，而多数民主党人（55%）则认为 AI 对自己个人有害。无党派人士对于 AI 对自己个人而言究竟是好（50%）还是坏（49%）比例差不多。

items.title: 研究识别出第一位企业心理病态者
items.content_text: 一项新研究指出，有毒企业领导人身上所见的性格特征可追溯到一位 400 年前的荷兰东印度公司的企业官员。该公司的商户部经理 Jeronimus Cornelisz 可能是最早有文献记录的企业心理病态者。研究发现，他表现出了与企业心理病态者相关的全部 10 项核心特征。这些特征包括：利用个人魅力博取信任；在身边聚集忠诚的追随者；清除潜在的挑战者；在竞争对手之间制造分裂；营造恐惧氛围；出问题时推卸责任；将追求权力、金钱和控制权置于一切之上。荷兰东印度公司是世界上第一家跨国股份制企业；1602 年该公司在阿姆斯特丹开设了世界最早的证券交易所之一。研究认为，Cornelisz 的案例表明，早在资本主义萌芽时期，受权力、财富和个人晋升欲望驱动的人，就已被商业性企业所吸引。研究聚焦于 1629 年发生在西澳大利亚海岸外岛屿上的 Batavia 沉船惨案。沉船事故后，约 200 名幸存者被困在几座孤岛上。由于高管已乘船前往今天的雅加达寻求救援，身为经理的 Cornelisz 便成了幸存者中职位最高的企业代表。在他的领导下，约有 100 名男女老少遭到杀害，部分女性还遭受了性暴力。Cornelisz 将这些杀戮辩解为节省食物和水资源的一种手段，而这些谋杀同时也铲除了他眼中的竞争对手。

items.title: 毅力号行使距离超机遇号刷新历史记录
items.content_text: 毅力号火星车创下新的世界纪录——它在地外天体表面的行驶里程，超过了此前所有探测器。10月11日，它的里程表读数达到28.10英里（45.22公里），超越了此前由机遇号保持的28.06英里（45.16公里）纪录。机遇号于2004至2018年间在火星开展探测。机遇号耗费近15年才跑完该里程，而毅力号仅用时5年半。这一里程碑事件发生在它的第2006个火星日。毅力号能长途行进，一大核心原因是搭载了先进的自主行驶系统。这套系统名为 AutoNav。依靠它火星车大多时候不需要等待地球发来详细行驶指令，就能自主在火星地表认路。行进过程中，毅力号持续拍摄周边影像，绘制包含障碍物信息的三维地图，在地面操控人员选定的目的地之间自行规划安全路线。该系统可以让火星车以接近最高速度行驶，单个火星日最多可前进1351英尺（412米）。毅力号超过90%的行驶里程都依靠AutoNav自主评估地形。与之对比，机遇号及其孪生探测器勇气号早期自主导航系统，仅能自主评估约5%的行驶路段。

items.title: 因加州考虑征收亿万富翁税扎克伯格有意离开
items.content_text: Meta 周三警告，如果加州通过亿万富翁税，公司 CEO 扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）可能会离开加州迁往他处。扎克伯格已向公司特别委员会告知了这一可能性。据 Meta 在监管文件中披露的计划，为了让扎克伯格未来八年继续留在加州领导公司，公司将设立一类新股票，允许他出售在 Meta 中最多一半的经济权益，同时保留投票控制权。亿万富翁税提案已列入加州 11 月的选票，提议对亿万富翁的资产一次性征收 5% 的税款。Google 联合创始人Sergey Brin 已投入超过 1 亿美元反对该提案。英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋则是少数表示不介意缴纳税款的加州亿万富翁。

items.title: 美光桃园厂员工罢工一天
items.content_text: 美光在台有两座工厂，其中桃园厂工会与资方就员工利润分红未能达成共识，星期四（10月22日）发动24小时罢工；台中厂工会于周三签署劳资协议，但未公布具体内容。桃园厂工会星期四上午9时起，在厂区门口展开为期24小时的罢工行动，预计持续至星期五（23日）上午9时。美光桃园厂约有3000名员工，其中约2400人为工会会员；台中厂则有约1万2300名员工，工会会员约1万1000人。桃园厂工会的主要诉求是，要求建立以公司营业利润15%为基础的长期员工分红制度，并将奖金发放方式由每年改为每季，以改善过往绩效奖金（IPP）不透明、分配不对称的问题。

items.title: EA 关闭 BioWare 工作室，取消《质量效应》新作开发
items.content_text: EA 裁员约 400 人，关闭 BioWare 工作室，取消《质量效应》新作开发。BioWare 工作室成立于 1995 年，创始人是医生，2007 年出售给 EA，创始人在 2012 年左右退出。该工作室的游戏包括了《博德之门》、《无冬之夜》、《星战旧共和国武士》、《翡翠帝国》、《龙腾世纪》和《质量效应》系列，以及《圣歌》。其中旨在获得持续收入的服务型游戏《圣歌》饱受批评，游戏于 2021 年停止开发，服务器于 2026 年 1 月关闭。BioWare 的最后一款游戏是 2024 年发布的 《龙腾世纪：影障守护者》，该作品的销量未达预期，工作室在 2025 年大规模裁员，只剩下约 50 人从事《质量效应》新作的早期开发。BioWare 在官网发表了一封告别信，简要回顾了工作室的历史。前 BioWare 员工之后泄漏了《质量效应》新作《宇宙》的预告片。

items.title: 坏苹果效应：人们会效仿他人的违规行为
items.content_text: 俗话说，一颗烂苹果，能毁掉一整桶好苹果。发表在《Proceedings of the Royal Society B》期刊上的一项研究再次为坏苹果效应提供了证据。这项研究旨在探讨个人如何在社会情境中做出是否违规的决策。研究人员说，很多人可能以为自己的决策是完全自主做出的，但事实上在很多情况下，我们的行为深受他人的影响。研究人员在美国招募了 750 名参与者进行了一项在线实验，共和党人和民主党人的比例大致相当。研究结果显示了他人的选择如何产生影响：看到别人遵守规则会略微降低个人违规，看到别人略微违规则会略微增加自己的违规，看到他人明显违规则会明显增加自己的违规。而当违规者与自己属于同一阵营，坏苹果效应则会更显著，表明政治立场一致的人更容易相互影响。研究期间有三分之一的参与者始终遵守规则，尽管这么做并不能获得最大收益。

items.title: 鸟类是地球最重要的养分搬运者之一
items.content_text: 鸟类在塑造地球化学环境上的作用被低估了，它们是地球最重要的养分搬运者之一。研究人员揭示了鸟类如何通过自身的排泄物和身躯，将养分在陆地、湖泊和海洋之间搬运。这一过程深深影响着从土壤和水体的化学性质，到动植物的生长。飞行能力让鸟类能跨越广阔的距离，甚至逾越海洋和山脉等天然屏障。鸟类在处理和循环养分上也极其高效。鸟类的食物摄入率比体型相当的哺乳动物高出约 30%。因此鸟类始终处于进食状态——它们大量摄取富含氮和磷的种子、昆虫、无脊椎动物及果实——并以极高的速率释放出养分。鸟类会将高浓度的养分集中在小片区域内，为当地的植物及其它生物提供关键资源。研究团队发现，饮食的季节性变化会导致鸟类的排泄物成分发生显著改变。春季鸟类摄入较多昆虫，其排泄物氮含量更高；秋季鸟类摄入较多果实和种子，其排泄物碳含量相对更高。根据《State of the World’s Birds》报告，全球 45% 的候鸟物种数量正在下降，可能会导致许多生态系统的肥力下降，进而降低其生产力。

items.title: Peer Review will never be the same.
items.content_text:
We show that AI-generated [academic journal] reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts. No matter how we look at the data, AI wins. It wins in 100% of the pairs overall when judged by another AI model...and 87% overall when judged by human journal editors... [H]umans agreed as much or more with AI's judgment than they did with other humans.

In this paper, we provide head-to-head experiments, using an unusually high quality set of human reviews, and show that AI now dominates human peer reviews at their best — according to blind judgments by other AI models in every area and by (human) former editors of major scholarly journals. Given prior research on earlier AI models, we had expected AI to win some in some areas, some of the time, but we found that the latest AI wins in them all, by every criterion we measured, by wide margins, with no fabricated sources, and with about a third the rate of incorrect claims of the human reviews. Some Bsky commentary.

items.title: Why Talarico Still Might Lose: Can He Nail Down the Black Vote?
items.content_text:
When James Talarico, the 37-year-old Texas representative and Presbyterian seminarian, won the Democratic Party’s Senate nomination seven months ago, few believed he would win the general election in November. For one thing, Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office in nearly 30 years. There was also little to suggest that Talarico’s progressive Christian beliefs championing working-class folks against mega-billionaires and corrupt corporations would make a dent in Texas, a MAGA stronghold with 88 billionaires, including Elon Musk, and more Fortune 500 company headquarters than any other state.  

And, importantly, there was one more factor, internal to Democratic politics, that rendered Talarico a long shot: He didn’t have the Black vote.         

Black Democratic voters overwhelmingly supported Talarico’s opponent in the Democratic primary in March, Representative Jasmine Crockett, nationally known for her vivid rhetoric and punchy comebacks on Capitol Hill. A popular figure in her Dallas district, Crockett enjoyed the support of Black political and religious leaders and rank-and-file voters. She received approximately 61 percent of the Black vote in the primary. Perhaps not surprisingly, hard feelings cropped up between the two camps during and after the campaign.  

At a post-primary town hall when Talarico backers raged against Crockett, the nominee took up her defense. “I felt, just at a personal level, offended,” he told TheGrio, a website focusing on African Americans. “If we were really serious about winning this race,” he said, “if people who claim to be my supporters or who claim to be part of this movement we’re building, if they’re sincere in their support, then they should be trying to heal divisions, not deepen divisions.”

Crockett endorsed him after her loss but has not campaigned with him, turning her attention to candidates in downballot races. But one of the state’s Black leaders, Rodney Ellis, a Harris County commissioner and former state senator from Houston, was among the first to speak out for Talarico. “I was for Jasmine Crockett in the primary,” he said on a video. “But there is too much at stake in this race to be petty. I like Talarico’s message. It’s grounded in faith.… I think he’s going to have a tremendous amount of support in the African American community.”  

Talarico has since been moving on several fronts to win Black support. His campaign engaged Black political operatives and Black communications firms. It laid out the largest Black voter outreach plan of its kind in modern Texas history, and gave priority to Black media, podcasts, radio, television, newspapers, and other outlets.  

Talarico may have one more huge factor in his favor. His name is Ken Paxton. The state’s scandal-scarred attorney general has plenty of PAC money and dark money. The New York Times reported on October 16 that Elon Musk alone has given Paxton $158 million. Overall, outside Republican groups have poured around $250 million into backing Paxton, which is more than five times what Democratic groups have given Talarico. Talarico has raised more than $130 million so far, which is far more than Paxton, but Paxton’s dark money gives him an overall advantage.

In mid-September, a Texas Southern University survey showed Black voters backing Talarico 87 percent to 10 percent. Around that time, Talarico won the crucial endorsement of the Congressional Black Caucus’s political wing, a powerhouse in Congress.

Recently, Cal Jillian, a professor of political science at Southern Methodist University, told me that the Black vote in Texas usually runs 80 percent to 85 percent in favor of most Democratic candidates, but to win the U.S. Senate seat, Talarico needs no less than 90 percent.

Is that anywhere near possible?


From the start, “there were questions about the Talarico campaign and whether Black voters would be there for him,” Kardal Coleman, the chair of the Dallas County Democratic Party, told me.  

The friction between the two camps broke out in the final stretch of the Crockett-Talarico primary race when a social media post claimed that in a private conversation in January, Talarico referred to the former Congressman Colin Allred as “a mediocre Black man,” according to The Texas Tribune. Allred lost the Senate race against Senator Ted Cruz in 2024, and he was Talarico’s early rival in 2025 until Crockett declared her candidacy for the Senate. (Allred now is running for the congressional seat in the Dallas-area 33rd congressional district.)  

In response, Talarico said it was a “mischaracterization of a private conversation,” the Tribune reported. He said he had described Allred’s “method of campaigning” as “mediocre,” not Allred himself. But the damage was done.

The rancor lingered through the primary and through the early months of Talarico’s campaign against Paxton. The campaign intensified the drive to win over Blacks. Talarico engaged with pastors and congregations in numerous Black churches, notably Friendship-West Baptist Church in Dallas, which has 13,000 congregants, including Crockett, and is led by a prominent pastor, the Reverend Dr. Frederick D. Haynes III, now running for Congress in the 30th district-seat Crockett vacated to seek the Senate seat. Talarico dropped by Black restaurants like Smokey Joe’s in south Dallas and Mikki’s Soul Food in Houston. He toured HBCU campuses, attending the Prairie View A&M game against Grambling State University, where he received a standing ovation. And back in May, he had a highly publicized lunch with President Barack Obama at Taco Joint in Austin.  

Along the way, he launched a $25 million project to build Black voter turnout across Texas, addressed the maternal mortality crisis affecting Black women, released statewide digital and radio ads, and built a multimillion-dollar campaign chest mostly with state and out-of-state donations. He became something of a celebrity, showing up on national TV and creating a stir when his scheduled interview on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert was banned by CBS attorneys citing equal-time Federal Communications Commission rules. Colbert then posted the full segment on his YouTube Channel, and it went viral with millions of viewers.


“Talarico is fortunate in his opponent,” professor Jillian said during our conversation.

Paxton, 63, who has refused to debate Talarico, has been a target of numerous federal and local investigations and was impeached in 2022 by the Republican-led state House and acquitted by the state Senate. His wife, Angela Paxton, 63, a Republican state senator, has filed for divorce “on biblical grounds,” meaning adultery. Such imbroglios, accusations of abuses of power, allegations of corruption—and several recently leaked audio recordings of Paxton that damaged mostly himself—have come to define him and his campaign, and Trump’s three rallies in Texas haven’t helped. (Trump is so unpopular, even in Texas, that Governor Greg Abbott, in an unexpectedly close race with State Representative Gina Hinojosa, didn’t show up for the president’s San Antonio rally.)   

Paxton doesn’t actively court the Black vote, though more Blacks live in Texas, 4.5 million, than in any other state, making up approximately 13 percent of the state’s population of 32 million.

“Republicans are openly hostile to Blacks,” said Matt Angle, director of the Lone Star Project, a Democratic political action committee and strategic communications organization based in Texas. “You can see it in the way they have redrawn districts to eliminate the Black vote.”

Angle met Talarico in 2017, when Talarico was 29 years old. “Young-looking, earnest, talented, an extraordinary talent,” Angle recalled. “He’s good with the Black community. He goes to Black churches, takes tough questions, takes criticism, and listens.”  

In his appearances, Talarico speaks often of his faith, cites Bible passages of compassion and humility, and takes issue with the racist, white Christian nationalism of many in the Republican right wing.  

No dirty trick seems too low for Paxton. When Talarico left the campaign trail for nine days in late September to stay home in Austin with the flu, Paxton supporters peddled a rumor on the internet that Talarico had been taken to a mental health facility in Ohio for tests. Paxton gleefully egged them on, and the post went viral. Finally, the health facility responded: James Talarico was not then nor had ever been at that facility. Talarico reappeared in public on October 9, at a Kacey Musgraves concert in Austin and was swamped with fans.   


“Talarico’s campaign is finally in stride,” Kardal Coleman said. “To his credit, he has shown up to answer questions everywhere, and he goes on Black media and has shown himself to be an advocate of Blacks here in Texas. His message is resonating, meeting people where they are.… His campaign has finally caught fire. He will likely get 90 percent of the Black vote.”

It’s an opinion I heard from another Black leader, State Representative Rhetta Bowers, who called Talarico her state House classmate because they joined the legislature at the same time, in 2018.

“I’ve seen numbers recently that reach 90 percent,” she said. “Talarico’s Christian message helps with Blacks. It speaks volumes for him. It resonates with Black people.”

Senator Royce West, who has served in the state legislature more than 30 years, sees strong signals from the Black community for a high turnout. “Talarico is doing all the necessary things to get the Black vote. But Trump is doing an even better job turning the Black vote to Talarico, with all Trump has done in this Second Reconstruction period. People are fed up with what’s going on in D.C., and the economy and gas prices, the affordability issue, the central issues.”

West, too, supported Crockett in the primary. “Many of us thought Jasmine was going to be the candidate,” he said. “There were some hard feelings, but Talarico is better than Paxton. Paxton’s record weighs him down. Also, there’s something else. Talarico may have coattails and help downballot races and Gina Hinojosa in her campaign for governor.”  

That Talarico could pull off a historic Democratic victory doesn’t surprise Matt Angle. “He may not be the male Texas stereotype, tough-talking macho, but he’s the tough guy in the race,” Angle said. “Two things about him appeal to Blacks. One is his Christian faith, and the other is that he was brought up by a hardworking single mother.”

Chairman Coleman was optimistic but cautious. “I want to stress how important this race is for Texas, this being once in a generation. But this time I think the Democrats are in the driver’s seat. We’ve got great candidate selection. A perfect storm.”

A perfect storm is what it’s going to take for a Democrat to win a statewide election in Texas. And that storm will have to include Talarico hitting that 90 percent mark among Black voters.

items.title: NAZA Confronts Israel’s High-Tech Killing Machine
items.content_text:
I didn’t cry until the very end of NAZA. The new documentary, by Academy Award–winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is all about Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza. But it’s only in the film’s final minutes that we get a direct view of the suffering on the ground there—a bombed building, a screaming crowd, and then a close-up of a man searching desperately through the debris. He’s shouting over and over, “Sa’id, my love, it’s Daddy. Sa’id, my love, it’s Daddy,” until he collapses, sobbing in the rubble that buried his child. 

Sa’id was a “NAZA,” the Israel Defense Forces’ acronym for collateral damage: the number of civilian deaths—adults and children—that Israel deemed acceptable for every Hamas operative it eliminated (“Hamas operative” meaning anyone Israel’s AI targeting systems identify as being in some way connected to Hamas). After 80 minutes listening to Israeli officers describe strikes with 15 approved NAZA, 20, 100, even an instance of a 500-NAZA strike, to be confronted with the desperate, hopeless agony that is one single NAZA—that is the murder of this man’s beloved child—is as big a cinematic gut punch as any I’ve experienced.

The searing emotion of this finale is a sharp tonal break from NAZA’s preceding scenes, which are composed of nighttime interviews with 24 Israeli intelligence officers. The core of each interview is an often quite clinical description of the systems these soldiers used—and may be still using—to target and kill Palestinians. Though of course the Israeli government has gone on offense to label NAZA “distorted, misleading, and disingenuous”—with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatening to revoke the directors’ Israeli citizenship—the film is remarkably straight in its presentation. Abraham, who conducts each interview, is shown on-screen; we hear his questions and how he sometimes pushes back on his interviewees’ answers. We also see how an interview was interrupted by an air raid siren, a regular fixture of life for Israelis. Though the cinematography is effective, there is no filmmaking magic or trickery here, no moments that a reasonable person could describe as propaganda. Just 24 Israelis explaining from their own firsthand experience how they helped kill thousands of unarmed men, women, and children in Gaza.

Much of NAZA’s run time focuses on descriptions of two related AI surveillance and targeting systems used by many of the interviewees. The first, named Lavender, identifies Hamas operatives—or, more accurately, the phones of Hamas operatives—through their behavior. So if someone calls another person whom the system has identified as related to Hamas, they’re awarded a certain number of points; if they go to a location the system has identified as related to Hamas, they get more points. Once the person has enough points, they’re automatically added to Israel’s kill list. “It’s a perfect job for machine learning,” noted one officer who helped develop the program. “Looking at characteristics, making a determination. Is it a cat or a dog?” Lavender allowed Israel to unleash “targeted” attacks at scale. “Efficiently, like in a factory,” said an interviewee—attacks directed not just against senior Hamas officials but people “so junior we didn’t know who they were.” It was, said another officer, about “quantity, not quality.” Of course, as anyone who’s encountered a large language model hallucination knows, AI regularly makes mistakes. And this was factored in too. As one officer explained, Israel operated with an understanding that its Lavender kill list had a 10 percent–15 percent error rate. 

The second system, nicknamed  “Where’s Daddy?” identifies the right time to bomb a target. The right location is already decided—Israel’s protocol, the officers explain, is to strike targets in their homes. To determine whether the person is actually at their home, Where’s Daddy? monitors their family (again through their cell phones), searching in particular for children asking their mothers when their fathers would be home—hence the program’s name. One officer described monitoring a 12-year-old girl and then calling in a strike, saying, “You hack her phone and then you kill her.” Another remembered hearing a baby crying in the background before he signaled for an attack. In a third conversation, an officer described looking through the photographs saved on a target’s phone to help identify the best angle of attack on the man’s apartment. He recounted seeing a picture of the target with his young daughter, then listening in real time to the family’s screams as the girl was burned alive. 

One officer described monitoring a 12-year-old girl and then calling in a strike, saying, “You hack her phone and then you kill her.”

How many times have we heard defenders of Israel try to pin the blame for the disproportionate carnage in Gaza on Hamas’s use of human shields? You can’t blame Israel for killing so many civilians when Hamas hides its military targets behind civilian infrastructure, the line goes. And all the while, the Israeli military has been making a conscious decision to attack its targets at night, after they return to their crowded residential apartment blocks. As one interviewee said, “There are only so many military sites in Gaza. But there are lots of private homes.” The human shields argument never actually relieved Israel of culpability for its slaughter of tens of thousands of Palestinians. But it certainly tried. Like so many other defenses of the indefensible, it was, from the very beginning, a willfully immoral delusion.

Israel can utilize killing systems like Lavender and Where’s Daddy? because it controls all telecommunications in Gaza. An officer described being able to listen in through any cell phone’s microphone or look out through any cell phone’s camera. “You feel like God,” he said. What the subjects of NAZA are describing is a new era of warfare, based on mass surveillance and AI decision-making, that should never have been allowed to escape the realm of dystopian sci-fi. Now that this computerized barbarity has seeped out into our real world, we’d be fools to think the contagion won’t spread.

This is where, as grounded as NAZA is in Israel and Gaza, the lessons of the film extend out far beyond the specific atrocities it chronicles. Palestine has always been a testing ground for the West’s newest security systems. Some of Israel’s strongest American supporters are quite explicit about this—in a recent debate, Republican Congressman David Valadao defended his support for military aid for Israel, saying, “The fact that those weapons are used there and tested there, we are able to learn from that and use that experience to develop our weapons systems to help us.” When you add together Flock, Palantir, NSA surveillance, and the development of a class of oligarchs who, like the Israeli officer peering into a victim’s phone, “feel like God,” as they control our government and invest in luxury bunkers and talk openly of Armageddon, it is not hard to see NAZA as prefigurative: a warning of what the entire world can become—will become—if we don’t take action now to stamp out this nightmare vision.

Of course, for the Palestinians who remain trapped in Gaza, this isn’t a possible dystopian future—it’s their lived reality today. These people are the victims of this nightmare. 


Still, the nightmare is leaving deep marks on the Israelis executing and implementing it too—effects we see laid bare in this documentary. Watching NAZA as a Jew, it is hard not to grieve over the ways that nationalism, fear, and hate have shaped the attitudes of too many in our community. How else to describe some of these quotes by NAZA interviewees—some describing their own feelings and some describing the broader views of their society—which I jotted down as best as I could in the movie theater:

There are no innocent people in Gaza.

Whatever we do to them, they deserve it.

I’d carry out strikes and then go out with my friends.

Dogs would eat the bodies. I didn’t like to watch. But people around me would watch the dogs eat the bodies.

It’s so insanely fun. Like a video game. You enjoy completing your mission.

There was talk of bringing in psychologists to see us, but there was no need. Not one person raised any doubts.

Some of the officers were themselves grieving what they had become: 

Yes, it’s a genocide. Completely. Even if you say it’s NAZA, it’s intentional. We intended to kill those children.

I never understood how the Germans could do it. Today, I understand it. I still see those Nazis as evil. But what does that make me?

This is the ultimate question underlying NAZA. The Holocaust and Israel’s genocide in Gaza are different in many ways—scale, context, rationale, historical era. But the systems creating these atrocities, and the mindsets that allow them, share obvious similarities. No one in NAZA ever actually says the words, “I was just following orders.” But many equivalent justifications—“I was a small cog”; “If I hadn’t done it, someone else would have”; “It’s not my role to say something”—can be heard throughout. 

Ultimately, whatever historical comparisons one might draw, the most salient fact about the destruction of Gaza is that it is ongoing to this day. The survivors in Gaza, in addition to experiencing hell on earth—as Israel continues restricting aid and squeezing them into an increasingly small and dangerously overcrowded area—are still being killed every single day. At least 30 men, women, and children were murdered just this past week, and over the last year, Israel has injured more than 5,000 Gazans and killed nearly 1,500, including more than 300 children—all during an ostensible ceasefire. Just last Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike hit a family’s apartment in Gaza City, killing a 33-year-old-mother; video footage from inside the apartment shows her young daughter watching as her mother was consumed by flames. 

There are people—many people—who still deny this reality. NAZA won’t change their minds. After justifying apartheid, famine, and genocide, it seems simple enough to write off a documentary—even one made by Israeli filmmakers, featuring Israeli military officers—as nothing more than anti-Israel or even antisemitic lies. But hopefully there are some previously quiet people out there whom NAZA can influence—people who can be inspired to begin speaking out against these crimes. Israelis who, like Abraham and Szor, feel nauseated by what their government and military have been doing. Americans who don’t want to keep paying for these atrocities with their taxes. Jews who are sick and tired of seeing children killed in their name. In some ways, we have all served as small cogs in this nightmare system. Likewise, we all have a role to play in dismantling it.

items.title: Silicosis Kills Workers. Ashley Moody Just Worries About the Lawsuits.
items.content_text:
In the summer of 2021, Wade Hanicker felt a pain under his shoulder blade. He took ibuprofen, thinking it was a muscle knot that would go away with massage and time. One day at work in a Tampa-area stone fabrication shop, the pain started creeping around to his chest. He was having trouble breathing. His wife insisted they go to the emergency room when he got home. After a misdiagnosis and a series of biopsies, Hanicker was eventually diagnosed with silicosis—a progressive and potentially fatal lung disease now ripping through people who cut, grind, and polish artificial stone.

Hanicker’s diagnosis came just after he found out that his wife was pregnant with their second child. He had to shut down his countertop servicing business and estimates that he’s lost about half his income—and strength. The kinds of household projects he once zipped through now take “20 times longer,” he told me. “As a father you want to be able to play with your kids and teach them how to ride bikes.” His kids—now three and five—“might get five or 10 minutes of actually good play time before I’m winded and have to go sit down.... That has become the hardest part.”

Hanicker has spent the last few years cycling between doctors and medications to manage a hellish array of symptoms. His lungs, irritated and scarred by replicable crystalline silica, or RCS, have become dotted with fibrous nodules as the tissue hardens. But the silicosis also triggered an autoimmune condition. Doctors prescribed him a corticosteroid to deal with the ensuing inflammation. The side effects from that drug—especially after longer-term usage—can include bone and muscle degradation. When we spoke, Hanicker, 39, was still recovering from a double hip replacement. Tired of experimenting with medications, he’s cut his treatment down to just two pills and semiannual injections of the chemotherapy drug Rituxin at a local cancer center. This regimen keeps him relatively comfortable and able to function day to day, as doctors try to preserve and improve his lung capacity. “That’s all they can do for me until my lungs are bad enough for transplant.”

After his second biopsy, Hanicker got a medical bill for roughly $100,000. That’s when, somewhat reluctantly, he opted to join the hundreds of workers nationwide who are suing the manufacturers of the products—crystalline silica-based countertops, or artificial stone—they hold responsible for their disease. They aren’t alone. 

Since California’s Department of Public Health began tracking what it calls engineered stone silicosis in 2019, it has recorded 668 confirmed cases and 35 deaths; the Department expects to tally 3,000 new cases by 2030. The Golden State’s Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board is now poised to ban engineered or artificial stone—names manufacturers dispute—by way of emergency regulation. In doing so, they’ll follow in the footsteps of Australia, which banned “quartz” countertops in 2024 after recording hundreds of cases of silicosis among engineered stone countertop workers since 2015. 

As lawsuits like Hanicker’s mount, one of his Senators—Republican Ashley Moody, who’s up for reelection next month—has sponsored legislation that would put an end to workers suing for damages. The proposed bill, “Protection of Lawful Commerce in Stone Slab Products Act of 2026,” would grant stone slab manufacturers immunity from civil actions parallel only to that enjoyed by gun and vaccine manufacturers. A companion bill in the House, which was first introduced last September, made it out of the House Judiciary Committee early this June. 

Moody’s sponsorship of the Senate version doesn’t seem to have come out of nowhere. Last October 30, her campaign and the Ashley Moody Victory Fund accepted a total of $38,000 from the family of Marty Davis, a prominent Trump donor and CEO of the United States’s largest manufacturer of engineered quartz, Cambria. According to Federal Election Commission filings, Davis and someone who appears to be his son Daniel—also listed as an employee at Cambria—made six separate gifts that day. A day after the bill was introduced, Moody also received a donation from one of the lobbyists that Cambria and three other engineered stone sellers hired to make the case for it to Congress.

Although unlikely to move forward in the next few months, Moody’s bill may give some voters pause. Hanicker, at least, who is a Republican and a steadfast Trump supporter, said he’s now “up in the air” about whether he’ll vote for for her given her support for stopping lawsuits against stone slab manufacturers. “I don’t support her on how she’s supporting this bill,” he said. “She was the main sponsor on that. I can’t stand that. There are certain aspects where I want the Democrats to win here,” he told me of Florida, “for everyone that’s being affected in this industry.”

Whether or not Moody’s backing of engineered stone companies moves the needle for other Floridians, a rare window has seemingly opened for Democrats in the state, as in other typically Republican strongholds across the country. Polling shows Moody with a shrinking lead over three-term Democratic state legislator Angie Nixon, who scored an upset primary victory running on a platform that includes Medicare for All, a federal rent freeze, and free childcare. Moody’s Republican bonafides are meanwhile airtight. Having previously served as Florida’s Attorney General, Moody was tapped by Governor Ron DeSantis to fill Marco Rubio’s seat after he joined the Trump administration in early 2025. She won her Republican primary in August to keep that seat in this year’s special Senate election. 

Compared to DeSantis and Rubio, Moody has kept a relatively low profile during her short time in the Senate. Even in the context of an understated legislative record, her sponsorship of S.4792 has flown under the radar. Her Senate office doesn’t appear to have issued a press release announcing its introduction; her campaign’s website doesn’t mention it, either. Neither have responded to detailed requests for comment on her sponsorship of the bill or Davis’s donations to her campaign.


Moody may have good reason for wanting to stay quiet on the issue. A recent Bloomberg investigation revealed that Cambria’s own air sampling had “dozens of times” found respirable crystalline silica exposures “above the threshold that the company insists it’s staying below,” in some cases exceeding levels OSHA established as permissible in 2016. In six cases, Cambria “documented RCS levels that were also above the permissible exposure limit,” Bloomberg’s Joshua Eidelson reported earlier this month.

Like its companion in the House, Moody’s bill asserts that the countertop materials now subject to lawsuits and national bans are “not inherently dangerous,” and “do not pose an inherent risk of injury to human beings.” As Hanicker points out, the giant stone slabs made by Cambria and other companies need to be cut in order to be sold on to customers. 

Understanding how countertops could pose such a grave threat to the people who make them requires understanding how they’re made. Unlike natural stone countertops, engineered versions rely on bonding mined and pulverized quartz together with resins, dyes, and metal. Those composites—typically made of at least 90 percent crystalline silica—are then poured into molds, dried, and baked. While larger firms like Cambria do some in-house fabrication, manufacturers most often ship giant stone slabs on to fabrication shops that shape, polish, and grind them based on their customers’ specifications. When customers receive the finished product, the contractors they hire to install them might make additional adjustments to fit them more precisely around sinks and appliances.

Cambria has consistently argued that the problem is “the process, not the product,” blaming silicosis injuries and deaths on fabrication shops they accuse of using unsafe methods that put their own workers at risk. Hanicker argues, however, that even shops trying to keep their workers safe would struggle to eliminate any human contact with crystalline silica dust. Among the most commonly used methods to mitigate exposure are so-called “wet shops,” using wet saws, floors and vacuums to keep nanoparticles out of the air. “Even wet cutting is still dangerous,” Hanicker pointed out. “Once the slurry dries there’s still dust. Even if it gets sucked into a vacuum, somebody still has to clean that filter out. There’s going to be human interaction with the dust regardless of the form of the dust.”
