items.title: Data Center Alley Goes Dark: Amazon Abandons Data Centers In Loudoun County
items.content_text:
Data Center Alley Goes Dark: Amazon Abandons Data Centers In Loudoun County

Finishing a data center in America has become a logistical nightmare. Now just starting one is turning into a problem too, even in the one county that was supposed to say yes to everything.

Back in April, when we reported that "Half Of US Data Centers Scheduled To Start In 2026, Will Be Canceled Or Delayed," the blame was spread across the usual suspects: power, transformers, permitting and a vague, growing sense that the locals were getting restless. Two months later, Blackstone sold its stake in three Northern Virginia data centers amid grassroot outrage, cashing out of a bet it made less than three years earlier, in the heart of what is known, with zero irony, as "Data Center Alley."

And now the restless locals have claimed their biggest scalp yet.

According to the Washington Post, Amazon has scrapped a plan to build data centers on the site of George Washington University's former campus in Ashburn, Northern Virginia, after reaching an agreement with local officials amid widespread opposition from residents. Under the deal announced Tuesday by Loudoun County Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis J. Randall, Amazon will repurpose the majority of the 122-acre campus for mixed-use and residential development, and commit to never building data centers on the land. It will also donate 25 acres to the county for a community arts center and recreational facility, and hand $5 million to the county's housing fund.

"By choosing dialogue over reflexive disagreement, Loudoun County and Amazon created an opportunity for the County," Randall said in a statement. "This agreement provides new places for our Loudoun residents to gather, create, and play. And, most importantly to me, we will provide more attainable homes for working families."

Some context on just how big a reversal this is: Amazon paid GWU $427 million for the campus earlier this year, roughly four times its assessed value, according to Supervisor Juli Briskman, because the zoning made data centers "a reasonable expectation." It filed a site plan in late July for "Bridgefield Tech Center": four two-story data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet. Briskman promptly vowed to fight it "every step of the way," and by September Randall was meeting with Amazon because a "likely disagreement" was emerging over what the land could legally be used for, per Bisnow. Amazon's take was that it read the site's legal potential differently than the county, but chose a "shared vision" over costly litigation. Translation: Amazon also agreed not to sue.

So instead of 800,000 square feet of servers, Loudoun gets an arts center, an indoor sports facility, housing, and roughly $70 million in land and cash (the 25 acres carry a stated fair market value of about $65 million). The rezoning alone is expected to take about a year, even on a fast-track schedule. Amazon, for its part, is left holding a very expensive future apartment complex.

Now for the punchline: according to Fortune, Loudoun's ~233 data center buildings generated about $1.2 billion in property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, roughly 39% of the county's entire budget. Amazon alone says it has invested more than $63 billion in the county since 2011. In other words, the county that arguably needs data centers more than any other in America just accepted a check to make sure one never gets built. If "Data Center Alley" is saying no to data centers, well, who exactly is left to say yes?

The timing was impeccable too. One day later, President Trump took to Truth Social to urge data center developers to "pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend'" to win local support, adding "MAKE DEALS, and get them built!" Amazon did pay a dividend, and it did make a deal. It just forgot the "get them built" part.

Data Center Alley, Unplugged

Amazon's U-turn is the latest in a remarkable string of reversals in what was, until recently, the most data-center-friendly real estate on the planet. Regular readers will recall that the trouble started in Prince William County, next door, where the 2,100-acre "Digital Gateway" (up to 37 buildings, ~5GW of capacity and roughly $100 billion of planned spending) was hit by a court ruling that voided its rezoning. In April, Brookfield-backed Compass pulled out after spending "tens of millions" and years chasing approvals. Then came Blackstone's sale on June 29... and two days later, we flagged the other shoe dropping:

*BLACKSTONE’S QTS ABANDONS MASSIVE DATA CENTER IN VIRGINIA

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 2, 2026

Then, last month, Loudoun's board voted 7-1-1 to draft an up-to-12-month pause on new data center applications, which Randall insisted was "not a moratorium" (a 12-month pause being "the maximum allowed by Virginia law"). The final vote was due this week; instead, on the same day as the Amazon deal, it was pushed to November 17. Here is how 2026 has gone in Data Center Alley so far:

Note that none of this involves a sputtering hyperscaler running out of money: Amazon spent $427 million to buy the land and is now spending another $70 million to walk away from what it bought it for. The capital is there. The permission is not.

The 6% Problem

The most striking thing here is how fast "community opposition" went from footnote to deal-breaker. As recently as July, when Data Center Dynamics surveyed 88 industry respondents about their biggest delivery constraints over the next 12 months (a survey Bernstein highlighted in its modular-builds deep dive [MARKETDESK LINK]), "community opposition/political risk" ranked second to last, at just 6%, behind equipment lead times (24%), power and interconnection (23%), permitting (17%) and supply chains (17%).

Three months later, that 6% just killed an 800,000-square-foot Amazon campus in the friendliest zip code in America. Maybe the respondents should get out more: the Heatmap/Embold poll that tracks Americans' views on a data center "being built near where you live" shows the share strongly opposed going from 24% in August 2025 to 61% in August 2026, while total support collapsed from 43% to below 20%.

And the backlash has gone institutional. In September, Wells Fargo flagged a fourfold jump in active local moratoriums, to 374 by the end of summer from 92 in June, with the average one lasting nearly a year. Its utilities analyst Shahriar Pourreza summed it up: "DCs are unpopular across the political spectrum." Just how bipartisan? In Ohio, one of the top data center states, both leading candidates for governor are running on restricting the industry:

Ohio is one of the top data center states: AWS, META, GOOGL, MSFT and SB Energy are all building here. Both leading governor candidates, Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, said they want new restrictions on the industry. Acton said she supports what she’s calling a “conditional moratorium” on new data center construction. Developers must cover 100% of their own utility costs, build exclusively with union labor, operate with full transparency and meet Ohio’s existing air and water quality standards Ramaswamy also laid out his data center policy, which he calls his "Ohioans-First Data Center Pledge." His campaign describes the plan as resting on three “non-negotiable” requirements: nearby residents must receive free electricity from data center developers, new facilities must pay their full property taxes with no abatements, with that revenue used to fund property tax rebates for homeowners, and developers must meet strict air and water quality standards while prioritizing brownfield sites over farmland. “If a project fails to meet any one of these three requirements, it will not be built. Period,” Ramaswamy’s campaign states.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 23, 2026

Morgan Stanley's map of the November races that could tighten the screws further (from its "Following AI's $1.6 trillion Money Trail" report shows 50.8GW of capacity, including 10.6GW already under construction, sitting in states where the elections "could lead to more restrictions on data center construction." Texas alone accounts for 24GW, and its governor has already ordered a halt to new data centers pending an audit of 250-300 projects. Midterms are 11 days away.

To be fair, not everyone thinks the pitchforks matter. Last week SemiAnalysis did a project-by-project audit and concluded that of the ~21GW of capacity sitting in moratorium areas, only about 2.3GW (three projects) is likely to be delayed, which The Economist's Archie Hall described as "much more bark than bite."

Perhaps. But here is the thing: the Amazon campus was never under a moratorium. Loudoun's pause hasn't even been enacted. What killed it was a zoning fight, a threat of litigation and a negotiated "dividend," none of which shows up in a moratorium tracker. Which is probably why Hall himself sees the bigger risk in deterrence: the projects that quietly never get proposed, or get "re-envisioned" into townhouses before anyone counts them.

Goldman's Outlook Is "Largely Intact"... Assuming Half Of It Never Shows Up

What does Goldman make of all this? In its latest Power Tracker (available to pro subs) Goldman's commodity team argues that "despite rising political push back against US data centers," its capacity estimates "show the 2027 growth outlook is largely unchanged, with moderate revisions." The bank raised its year-end 2026 US data center capacity forecast by 5GW to 64GW, while cutting its year-end 2027 forecast by 5GW to 90GW, and still sees US data center power demand growing 38% in both 2026 (+12GW) and 2027 (+17GW).

So far so bullish. But read the fine print under the chart:

Our GS data center capacity forecast assumes only 60/50% of currently scheduled additions are realized, which is derived from the historical relationship between scheduled and activated capacity.

In other words, Goldman's "largely intact" outlook already assumes that 40% to 50% of what's on the schedule never gets switched on. Which, if we recall, is precisely the "half" we wrote about in April (when Sightline Climate warned that 30-50% of the ~16GW slated for 2026 would be delayed, with only ~5GW actually under construction), and which SemiAnalysis spent an entire June post telling everyone to "stop saying." Goldman, it turns out, never stopped saying it; it just put it in a footnote. And note which way the revision went: the near term got pulled forward, while 2027, the year the hyperscalers are spending like there is no tomorrow for, got cut.

Goldman also notes that "effective peak spare capacity tightened YoY across nearly every key region" this summer. That matters, because even the projects that do survive the zoning board walk straight into the next wall.

Break Ground, Then Wait For The Grid

Because getting permission is merely step one. Step two is getting power, and that is where the timelines go from awkward to absurd. Per Berkeley Lab data compiled by Bernstein, the median time from interconnection request to commercial operation in the US has stretched to over five years, more than triple the 1.5 years it took in 2005.

Hence the scramble for "speed to power." Goldman's Carbonomics team (in its report on "Behind-the-meter power solutions for data centers," which we covered in detail last month) lays out the mismatch neatly: a data center takes 2-3 years to develop, while a heavy-duty gas turbine takes 5-7 years to show up. GE Vernova, recall, is now taking reservations for 2031 delivery.

Then there are the transformers, switchgear and generators that topped the Bernstein survey: Apollo's Torsten Slok (who took his number from our June report) pegs transformer lead times at up to 26 months in his latest note, while Bloomberg reported earlier this year that delivery times for the large units data centers need had stretched to as much as five years. Throw in a chronic shortage of electricians (there is a reason why we told readers to learn to be one back in January) and you get a pipeline where every link must arrive on time for any of it to matter.... which will never happen. As one TechRadar headline put it, "if one piece of your supply chain is delayed then your whole project can't deliver." Correct.

Add it all up and Morgan Stanley's verdict is grim. Even after counting every "time to power" fix available (spare grid capacity, nuclear, announced turbines and engines, Bloom fuel cells), the bank projects that US data center developers face a 32GW power shortfall through 2028, a result of "intensifying challenges with respect to People, Power and Politics." That is down from the 44GW shortfall MS warned about last November, which says more about how hard everyone is scrambling for turbines and fuel cells than about any improvement in the grid.

And, as a reminder, the "Politics" part of that triad just got a lot worse in Virginia, a lot worse in Ohio, and possibly a lot worse in Texas on November 3. Which is why we keep saying the only real solution is to make "behind the meter" mandatory: if the community won't give you its grid, bring your own power plant... and then hope the zoning board lets you build that too.

Who Wins When Nothing Gets Built

So who benefits from a buildout that keeps getting pushed out? Torsten Slok had a timely answer this week in "Winners and Losers if the Data Center Buildout Is Delayed." The winners are owners of operating data centers ("capacity that is already online can raise rents and fill every megawatt"), holders of powered land and grid access, long-lead equipment makers and on-site power producers. The losers: hyperscalers whose "revenue is capped by supply rather than demand, and committed capex keeps accruing while capacity sits idle," developers and construction-stage investors whose "cash flows start later while interest and carrying costs continue," and equity investors in the AI trade, whose "valuations that assume on-time delivery are exposed to earnings revisions and multiple compression."

Slok draws a crucial distinction between delay and cancellation:

A delay hurts returns by pushing cash flows out, but the asset remains and may become more valuable. The real risk is that scarcity unwinds, for example, if supply catches up in a rush or demand softens, which would erode the premium on existing capacity.

Which, come to think of it, is a pretty good description of what Blackstone did in June: sell fully leased, already operating Virginia capacity to Digital Realty at a scarcity premium, while it lasts. Amazon's Loudoun campus, meanwhile, falls squarely in the "cancellation" bucket, and joins a fast-growing list. Here is the latest update of our AI data center Casualty List, which also includes last week's Nextdc collapse after protesters stalled power to its Melbourne campus:

If Loudoun Says No, Who Says Yes?

The bulls will say this is one 800,000-square-foot campus in a county that already has 233 data center buildings, and that SemiAnalysis still sees 38GW of US capacity coming online in 2027 (good luck with that). Maybe. But the bull case has always rested on the assumption that the binding constraints were physical (chips, power, transformers) and that money could eventually buy its way through all of them. Loudoun just showed that money can't buy permission. Amazon brought $427 million, a $70 million "dividend" and the threat of a lawsuit, and the best it could get was the right to build townhouses.

Despite all this, Goldman says the outlook is "largely intact." We'd note that it is intact precisely because Goldman already assumes that half of it won't happen, and that the one revision it did make cut 2027. Between Loudoun's pause vote on November 17, the midterms two weeks before that, and turbine slots booked into the next decade, we suspect that haircut is the floor... and that the next revision (undoubtedly lower) won't be confined to a footnote.

Then again, Amazon can always try again somewhere else in Loudoun... in 12 months, "the maximum allowed by Virginia law."

Much more in the full Goldman Power Tracker, the Morgan Stanley "Following AI's $1.6 trillion Money Trail" report and Goldman's Carbonomics "Behind-the-meter power solutions for data centers" note, all available to pro subs.

items.title: "We Should Not Have Done It": Thiel Breaks With Trump Over Iran War, Warns America May Not "Have The Hard Power"
items.content_text:
"We Should Not Have Done It": Thiel Breaks With Trump Over Iran War, Warns America May Not "Have The Hard Power"

One day after we reported that Donald Trump Jr. has privately broken with his father over the Iran war, Peter Thiel, the PayPal and Palantir (PLTR) co-founder who was the first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016 and the biggest funder of super PACs behind JD Vance's 2022 Senate run, has also drawn a line in the sand over Trump's defining foreign-policy gamble.

In audio from an Oct. 12 private lecture in Nashville obtained by Decoded by POLITICO (Calder McHugh), Thiel told the room:

"I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made."

"Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war."

In other words, one of the architects of the MAGA-tech alliance now thinks the war was a mistake and that America may not be strong enough to finish it. The scoop crossed overnight:

🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Peter Thiel, one of Trump's most influential billionaire backers, says the Iran war was a MISTAKE

"I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made."

Thiel made the comments last week during a private lecture in Nashville.

He also raised... pic.twitter.com/FkTnpb91sm

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 22, 2026

Thiel on the Iran war: "I think we should not have done it" https://t.co/0JG5vUcY0r

— Alex Burns (@alexanderburns) October 22, 2026

Below we walk through what Thiel said, the even stranger parts of the lecture, and why it lands at exactly the wrong moment for the White House.

"The Sword Of Damocles"

Per Politico, Thiel spent much of the lecture on what he called the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on Rumsfeld and Cheney, and then said this:

"I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late... And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran."

("Persecute" is the word in Politico's transcript. We assume he meant "prosecute," though at this point in the war, who knows.) Translation: the president's most cerebral backer is publicly speculating that Trump officials face war-crimes exposure. Very reassuring.

Thiel also recounted a meeting with Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after Oct. 7, in which he asked about Israel's plans for Gaza. According to Thiel, Netanyahu replied: "I can't just Dresdenize it," a reference to the Allied firebombing that killed roughly 25,000 people.

Still On Team Trump (Sort Of)

To be fair, Thiel didn't defect. Politico says he "highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president," and framed his critique as opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars rather than to Trump personally. That's the Vance-wing argument, and Politico reported back in March that Vance himself was "skeptical" of striking Iran before the war began. Neither Thiel's representatives nor the White House responded to Politico. Put differently, this is the restrainer wing of the coalition saying in private what it can't say from the podium, and the audio got out 12 days before the Nov. 3 midterms.

* * *

items.title: California Man Said ICE Stole His Wife; Police Now Say He Murdered Her...
items.content_text:
California Man Said ICE Stole His Wife; Police Now Say He Murdered Her...

Authored by Catherine Salgado via PJ Media,

A man who accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) of taking his wife is now in custody under suspicion of murdering her.

There have been some creative excuses to cover up murder, but this might be a first. Gurinder Gill - immigration status currently undisclosed - first told investigators that his wife went missing after September 30 because ICE detained her. Detectives subsequently uncovered inconsistencies in his story and dug deeper, coming to the conclusion that she was actually dead, and her husband is the likely guilty party. Jasmine and Gurinder were in a divorce dispute at the time she went missing.

The biggest tell that his story was bunk, as Fox News notes below, is that there had not actually been any ICE activity at the Gills' home.

A Sacramento man allegedly told detectives ICE agents arrested his missing wife when she went to get the mail. Authorities contacted ICE, which confirmed no enforcement activity had occurred at the residence. Days before Gurinder Gill even made that claim, investigators in neighboring El Dorado County had already discovered burned and buried remains about 70 miles from the couple's home. Those remains were later confirmed to belong to his wife, 30-year-old Jasmine Gill, an India-born registered nurse and mother of their 8-month-old child. Gill, 28, is now charged with murder. The couple had been going through a divorce and child custody dispute when Jasmine vanished on Sept. 30. Her cousin reported her missing on Oct. 4. Deputies arrested Gurinder on Oct. 14 and executed search warrants at two homes associated with him. He is ineligible for bail. Full story here https://t.co/jm72AA8H5u

— Fox News US (@FoxUSNews) October 20, 2026

As Fox also reported, investigators found burned and buried remains, which they have since confirmed as Jasmine Gill - what Gurinder allegedly left of her. Apparently, he tried to destroy her corpse about 70 miles from their home. Jasmine was born in India, but was a registered nurse in California and the mother of Gurinder's 8-month-old baby. Part of the couple's struggles was a child custody dispute. As usual, the child will end up suffering most from the craziness of the parent.

Jasmine's family started a GoFundMe to deal with the financial aftermath of her death and help her baby. It describes her as "A Daughter, a Sister, a Nurse, and a Mother Who Deserved So Much More." Apparently, the family needs money to send Jasmine's body back to India, where her mother still lives. Fox News did not state whether Jasmine is a legal immigrant or not.

SFGate, which obtained the criminal complaint from the Sacramento County District Attorney's Office, also mentioned that Gurinder claimed ICE arrested his wife while she was getting her mail outside, but that the agency confirmed it had not been to the residence. Apparently, Gurinder forgot to put out the fire he was using to try to burn his wife's corpse, because authorities discovered her remains after spotting smoke and having to put out a minor forest fire. Jasmine's jewelry was also in the burned area.

SFGate also reported:

Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Gurinder Gill, who was taken into custody Oct. 14. Investigators also executed search warrants at two residences associated with him, although authorities have not disclosed what evidence, if any, was recovered. The criminal complaint, filed Oct. 16 in Sacramento County Superior Court, alleges that Gill killed his wife "with malice aforethought" on or about Sept. 30. He faces one felony count of murder.

Gurinder Gill is not only evil but also stupid. He seems to have expected that California authorities would just take him at his word if he accused ICE of kidnapping. He also apparently set his wife's body on fire and then left without bothering to see what would happen. The whole situation would be humorous if a young mother were not dead.

items.title: "I Am F**king Getting You!" Unhinged Mayor Lunges At Resident During Chaotic Meeting
items.content_text:
"I Am F**king Getting You!" Unhinged Mayor Lunges At Resident During Chaotic Meeting

A New Jersey mayor erupted in a profanity-laced tirade during a chaotic public meeting Wednesday night, charging toward a resident and threatening him before several people rushed to restrain the furious politician.

Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini, a Republican, was caught on camera lunging toward Michael Sawka, a frequent critic of his policies, as an already contentious council meeting descended into pandemonium.

"I'm fucking getting you," Bianchini shouted as others scrambled to prevent a physical confrontation.

The wild incident unfolded while recently fired township official Ken Gerber, a retired police chief, was addressing council members about his dismissal, which supporters have characterized as politically motivated.

Video captured Sawka gesturing toward the back of the room before making an obscene gesture toward the mayor. Bianchini suddenly sprang from his seat and rushed toward him.

Councilman Perry Doyle Jr., a retired police officer, helped restrain the mayor before escorting him away. Police subsequently arrived to restore order.

In an interview with WPVI-TV afterward, Bianchini conceded to losing control.

"I just basically snapped," the mayor admitted. "I hate to put it this way, but it's a long time coming."

"Was it wrong? Absolutely. Was it justified? Absolutely. And I would do it again if I had to," he added.

Sawka disputed the mayor's account, insisting he never left his seat, Fox News reports.

"I'm just sitting there. I never got up. I sat there the whole time. I was calm the whole time," Sawka said.

Sawka has filed a municipal court complaint seeking assault and terroristic threats charges against Bianchini. Police have not announced any charges against the mayor.

items.title: Watch: Arizona Governor-Aligned Canvassers Caught Willing To Allow Noncitizens To Vote
items.content_text:
Watch: Arizona Governor-Aligned Canvassers Caught Willing To Allow Noncitizens To Vote

Submitted by Muckraker, 

Canvassers registering voters for groups backing Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs's re-election told undercover Muckraker journalists posing as a non-citizen and as a felon on probation that they could go ahead and register to vote, hidden-camera footage shows.

With the midterm elections weeks away, Muckraker visited voter registration drives run by three Democrat-aligned organizations: Stand Indivisible Arizona, Worker Power, and the Democratic National Committee's When We Count program. At each, a Muckraker journalist told the canvasser they were not eligible to vote. Muckraker also attended an AFL-CIO phone bank mobilizing voters for Hobbs, where a journalist volunteering to make calls asked whether voters' citizenship mattered.

Muckraker stopped every exercise before any voter registration form was submitted.

BREAKING: Katie Hobbs-Aligned Canvassers Caught Willing to Allow Non-Citizens and a Felon to Vote Muckraker went undercover in Arizona to investigate the groups working to re-elect Gov. Katie Hobbs @katiehobbs and other Democrats. Here’s what we found: Stand Indivisible Arizona (endorsed Gov. Hobbs in their 2026 ballot guide) — Our journalist posed as a Canadian citizen and asked to register to vote. The canvasser not only agreed to help the alleged non-citizen register, but when asked whether other Canadians could register too, she said, “Tell them to do it online.” Worker Power (working to re-elect Gov. Hobbs) — Our journalist told a canvasser they were not a U.S. citizen. Despite this, at our journalist’s request, the canvasser marked “yes” on the citizenship question of the voter registration form. When We Count (the DNC’s own registration program) — Our journalist posed as a felon on probation and asked to register to vote. The canvassers looked up the law and saw that a felon on probation is ineligible. Even so, they encouraged our journalist to register: “You should just do it.” AFL-CIO (phone bank mobilizing voters for Gov. Hobbs) — Our undercover journalist asked a phone bank trainer whether to ask the people being called if they're citizens. The trainer’s answer: “We don’t care.” Our journalists stopped every exercise before any voter registration form was submitted. We also asked Gov. Katie Hobbs about these findings. Watch this report and share it with the world.

— Muckraker (@realmuckraker) October 22, 2026

Stand Indivisible Arizona: "Take this and tell them to do it online"

Stand Indivisible Arizona, a nonprofit that has endorsed Hobbs and other Democrats running in 2026, was running a voter registration drive at Paradise Valley Community College. A Muckraker journalist, posing as a Canadian student in the U.S. on an F-1 visa, approached a canvasser.

When the canvasser was told that the journalist was a Canadian on a student visa, she first said, "We can't do it." But when the journalist asked, "Can I just fill it out, submit it with you, and then forget it?" she answered: "Yeah, I guess. The other thing you could do is you could go online, but I'd rather do it with you."

Asked whether the journalist's Canadian friends could register to vote too, she said: "Take this [a business card with a QR code linking to an online voter registration form] and tell them to do it online."

When Muckraker's Anthony Rubin returned to ask about the exchange, she said, "I told you, I can't stop you from putting it online," and declined further comment.

Worker Power: "Okay, if you want to"

Worker Power is a Phoenix-based nonprofit that raised nearly $10 million in the 2024 election cycle and says it runs the largest electoral field program in Arizona. This year it is working to re-elect Hobbs and other Democrats. Muckraker found a canvasser registering voters at the Phoenix Public Library and again posed as a non-citizen.

"Are you a USA citizen?" the canvasser asked.

"Not yet," the journalist said.

"You have to be a USA citizen to vote," she replied. The journalist said they were a resident and asked to "just send it." She asked, "Are you sure you want to try it?" then said, "Okay, if you want to," and marked "yes" for U.S. citizenship on the Arizona voter registration form.

"Yes, and then you need to sign there," she said.

Approached afterward, she declined to say how often non-citizens are registered.

When We Count: "You should just do it"

When We Count is the DNC's own voter registration program, the largest in the party's history. It launched in Arizona in 2026 and pays young fellows to register new Democratic voters. Muckraker found its canvassers at Mesa Community College, where journalist Anthony Rubin posed as a felon on probation.

Under Arizona law, a felony conviction suspends the right to vote (A.R.S. § 13-904). The canvassers looked it up. "You're restored to vote when probation has been completed," one said.

Asked whether they cared if the journalist registered anyway, one said, "You should just do it. Just do it."

When Rubin returned to ask how often the group helps ineligible people register, the canvassers declined to comment and left.

AFL-CIO phone bank: "Not our business"

Muckraker also attended an AFL-CIO phone bank at a union hall in central Phoenix, where volunteers were phone banking to mobilize voters to support Katie Hobbs.

A Muckraker journalist asked the phone bank trainer whether to ask the people being called if they were citizens. "No, we don't get into any of that," the trainer said. "We don't care."

"If he's not a U.S. citizen, why should I proceed?" the journalist asked. "Not our business," the trainer said.

Gov. Hobbs: no comment

Katie Hobbs later spoke in the same building as the AFL-CIO phone bank at an event hosted by AFSCME, one of the unions endorsing her re-election. Anthony Rubin asked her about non-citizens being registered to vote and about the groups working for her re-election. She did not respond

What the law says

No Arizona law requires voter registration drives to verify citizenship; county recorders check eligibility after forms are submitted. But Arizona law makes it a class 6 felony for anyone who "knowingly causes or procures another person to be registered" while "knowing that such other person is not entitled to such registration" (A.R.S. § 16-182).

If you work inside an organization involved in the electoral process and have information that should be reported, contact Muckraker at support@muckraker.com or muckraker.com/contact.

items.title: Ex-FBI "Shadow Government" Official Among Two Charged With Lying To Congress Over Hunter Biden Laptop
items.content_text:
Ex-FBI "Shadow Government" Official Among Two Charged With Lying To Congress Over Hunter Biden Laptop

Two former senior FBI officials who ran the bureau's now-defunct Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

Nikki Cole Floris, 46, and Bradley Benavides, 56, each face one count of lying to Congress in a criminal complaint, D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced in a post on X. Both surrendered Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington, according to the AP.

Floris led the task force as a deputy assistant director from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides was its section chief through the 2020 election, FBI Director Kash Patel said. Both testified that the FITF was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations. "Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony," Patel wrote, crediting the bureau's Kansas City field office alongside the Justice Department and Pirro.

Two former senior FBI officials, Nikki Cole Floris and Bradley Benavides, were taken into custody today on charges of allegedly lying to Congress about their involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden. The charges stem from an ongoing investigation into the since-dissolved FBI Foreign Influence Task Force. Floris led the FITF as a Deputy Assistant Director from mid-2019 through mid-2022. Benavides was the FITF Section Chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election. Both testified that the FITF was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations. Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony. Floris is also on record privately claiming to be "running a shadow government" during the 2020 election in her role on the FITF. Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law. The FBI has already dismantled the corrupt CR-15 squad that engaged in political weaponization targeting their opponents, including President Trump. Thanks to @TheJusticeDept @FBIKansasCity and @USAttyPirro . -DKP

— FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 23, 2026

Benavides told Congress he learned about the laptop story from Wikipedia, but the Justice Department says it has evidence he discussed it with others inside the FBI, Fox News reports. Prosecutors also say Floris discussed Hunter Biden with members of the task force despite testifying otherwise. Pirro said the evidence showed "their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election."

Floris' lawyers called her "a patriot" who served as an FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years and said the Justice Department accused her "on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts." "It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they said in a statement. Benavides has not publicly commented.

The case lands less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, the latest in a series of politically charged Justice Department actions in the run-up to the vote, the AP noted.

What The Task Force Knew

Christopher Wray set up the task force in 2017 to counter foreign influence operations, and it served as the bureau's line to social media companies ahead of the 2020 election. The task force knew the laptop was real when the New York Post began publishing its contents in October 2020, Laura Dehmlow, then the FITF's section chief, told House Judiciary investigators in July 2023, the Free Beacon reported.

The FBI nonetheless refused to answer social media companies' questions about the laptop, including from a Twitter employee who asked task force representatives about its authenticity at a previously scheduled meeting the day the Post story ran, according to the committee.

Benavides also crossed paths with the two Republican senators then digging into the Biden family's foreign money. On Aug. 6, 2020, he briefed Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson in a session that, according to a June 2023 letter from House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, hampered their investigation into Hunter Biden's financial connections. Grassley called the briefing "unnecessary and completely irrelevant to the substance of our investigation." Jordan's letter asked Benavides, by then a senior risk manager at Amazon, to sit for a transcribed interview.

The Shadow Government Line

Patel's post also invoked a private message Floris sent during an unrelated episode. Floris wrote she was "basically running a shadow government" in September 2020, as the bureau recalled a report alleging Chinese election interference, according to FBI messages declassified in July and reported by the Washington Examiner.

Wray named Floris in 2022 to run the Washington Field Office's intelligence division, and Patel forced her out of the FBI in May 2025, the Examiner reported. Attorney General Pam Bondi had already disbanded the task force in February 2025, one of her first acts in office.

The CR-15 squad Patel cited at the end of his post was a Washington Field Office public corruption unit that worked Arctic Frost, the probe that fed into Jack Smith's election case against Trump. Patel abolished it last October after disclosures that Arctic Frost had tracked Republican senators' phone records.

The alleged lies date to 2023, according to Patel, which keeps them inside the five-year statute of limitations that generally governs federal false-statement charges until 2028. Anything the pair did during the 2020 campaign itself fell outside that window last fall.

items.title: Melania Trump 'Brokers' Oleshky Ceasefire - But The White House And Russia Give Different Start Dates
items.content_text:
Melania Trump 'Brokers' Oleshky Ceasefire - But The White House And Russia Give Different Start Dates

The White House said Friday that First Lady Melania Trump brokered a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in Ukraine's Kherson region, to let aid in and civilians out. The White House says it starts October 29, but Gen. Valery Gerasimov said Russian forces would stop firing October 27.

In its statement, the White House said "both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." Melania Trump called Oleshky "a front-line war city on the brink of disaster" and said she anticipates "some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Civilian leaders from both countries are to visit residents in their homes, and an "impartial American media organization" will document the work. Reuters reported that Newsmax said its cameras would get "exclusive access to document the effort."

Moscow's account is looser. Gerasimov said fire would cease on the Kherson axis at 4 a.m. Moscow time on Tuesday, and that Russia would first carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and secure a humanitarian convoy's route into the city, AP reported. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the sides were still working out a ceasefire so residents could leave, according to the Kyiv Independent. Peskov did not say whether evacuees would go to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory, and said the evacuation would likely take several days.

The talks themselves ran through human rights officials. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman, said he led negotiations for Ukraine and that Russia's rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, led them for Russia. Lubinets said the operation would be gradual and "extremely challenging to implement." The White House release casts Melania Trump as "Exclusive Intermediary" who "initiated discussions with both nations," but what she did in the room is not spelled out. The Daily Beast noted this week that her role in the Oleshky crisis was unclear. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters Putin asked envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg to pass on his "gratitude," and Peskov said the matter came up in a recent Putin-Trump call.

Oleshky sits on the Dnipro across from Kherson. About 24,000 people lived there before the war; the White House puts the remaining population at 1,700 to 2,000, mostly elderly, with about 50 children. AP described a city with no electricity, heat or running water, scarce food and medicine for months, and mined roads out. The Kyiv Independent adds that the roads would need demining before buses could reach it. Russian forces took the city on the first day of the 2022 invasion, and the June 2023 Kakhovka Dam collapse, which an AP investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military, flooded it and killed hundreds.

Pressure had been building for weeks. The Kyiv Independent says the blockade drew appeals from Pope Leo XIV, and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia thanked both the pope and Melania Trump. Ukraine has repeatedly asked for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations; as the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to see that civilians under its control have what they need to survive, AP noted.

Local truces in this war have often been poorly implemented, the Kyiv Independent notes, and the last one Washington announced is a warning. When Trump declared an energy ceasefire on Truth Social earlier this month, Zelensky said it was "news to me." Zelensky said Russia hit at least six energy targets overnight after the announcement, and Trump then said both sides had violated the deal and that they agreed "because I said: 'you agree.'"

The announcement lands amid strain between Washington and Kyiv. Trump recently waived new Russian sanctions and agreed with Russia to import diesel, AP reported, while Kyiv faces restrictions on its use of Starshield satellite internet. Zelensky, speaking at the Hudson Institute, did not mention Oleshky; he said U.S. Patriot interceptors were still on hold. Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo before traveling to see Putin.

Melania Trump has made children caught in the war her signature issue. Last October she said she and Putin had an open channel of communication on the subject, after the president hand-delivered her letter to Putin in Alaska. Her top aide, Marc Beckman, has claimed she facilitated the reunification of 34 children with their parents, the Daily Beast reported.

Skeptics are not waiting for the paperwork. Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator at the NGO Humanity, told the Kyiv Independent he worried about "provocations, blackmail, a route through the Russian Federation." "I have little faith," he said. Russia's October 27 date arrives Tuesday; the White House's is two days after that.

items.title: Rare Earth Stocks Hit 52-Week Low As William Blair Says China Supply Optimism Is "Incorrect"
items.content_text:
Rare Earth Stocks Hit 52-Week Low As William Blair Says China Supply Optimism Is "Incorrect"

Our "Great Rare Earth Disconnect" note earlier this week highlighted the widening gap between elevated rare earth prices and tumbling junior miners and producers. William Blair rare-earths analyst Neal Dingmann has also weighed in on the forces driving the selloff.

"Revived rate-hike fears, hot CPI, and other macro concerns along with rare earth headline and company-specific concerns have notably hurt the largely high-beta rare earth group in recent weeks," Dingmann wrote.

The VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX) has lost more than half its value since peaking in May, even as commodity prices remain strong and demand for conflict-free Chinese supplies continues. That divergence raises one key question: how much of the selloff reflects deteriorating fundamentals, and how much reflects misplaced expectations of easing supply constraints?

Dingmann wrote that investors may be overestimating the relief a thaw in US-China relations would bring.

"Specifically, many investors anticipate (incorrectly, in our opinion) cooling rare earth supply-scarcity with improved U.S./China relations ahead of the next Trump/Xi meetings in November (in China) and December (G20 in Florida)," he said. 

He continued: 

Further, investors appear to have increased liquidity concerns given heavy spending requirements against minimal near-term revenue and milestone-based government funding that for many companies has yet to be collected. 

While we continue to point to strong REE prices and potential long-term volumes, many companies are not yet benefiting from the high levels given limited current output at the mine or processing, alloy, and magnet facilities. 

While we continue to believe the insatiable demand for REE provides a strong long-term backdrop for much of the group, driving many of our Outperform ratings, we remain cautious in the near term over much of the group given the large stock price declines in many REE companies, as it adds to near-term liquidity concerns. 

We continue to favor MP Materials and Lynas Rare Earths most in the near term given the former's attractive offtake agreements and price floors along with the latter's limited funding needs and long-term track record. 

The firm's basket of seven miner stocks (MP, LYSDY, AREC, IPX, NB, UAMY, and TMCR) has tumbled about 30% on average over the previous month at the time of the report. He said interest rate concerns, inflation pressures and expectations of improving US-China relations have compounded worries about spending requirements and delayed government funding. 

Lower share prices are fueling another major concern for these miners: equity financing is more costly for companies building capital-intensive mines, processing plants and magnet facilities. He warned that some of these miners could hit a "debt wall," substantial shareholder dilution or material project delays.

What changed with investors? 

Investors appear to continue to shift their focus from upside driven by government support and strategic value toward actual production and cash flow, causing growing concerns about how capital-intensive projects will be funded at lower equity values. 

With equity prices significantly lower, raising the capital needed to fund these projects becomes increasingly dilutive, leaving companies that still require significant external funding with fewer options. 

From here, we could see a rebound if Chinese restrictions are renewed, government funding, or company-specific production milestones restore urgency to the ex-China buildout. On the flip side, another trade extension, company project delays, or funding delays could keep valuations under pressure and further increase funding risk, dilution risk, and overall company finance risk

Canaccord's critical minerals team, led by Reg Spencer, also questioned the scale of the selloff, highlighting the disconnect between elevated rare earth prices and sharp declines across junior miner and established producer stocks.

Potential catalysts for renewed investor interest across the space include tighter Chinese export restrictions, government funding commitments and production milestones that demonstrate commercial progress. Until then, balance-sheet strength and execution remain key differentiators. Producers with operating assets and robust liquidity to fund their growth plans appear better positioned to weather the shakeout and participate in a recovery once bears are down and dragging the space down.

items.title: Measles Surge In Pennsylvania Prompts New Warning
items.content_text:
Measles Surge In Pennsylvania Prompts New Warning

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

As the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania grows larger, state officials have issued a warning regarding the impact of measles during pregnancy.

"Measles in pregnancy can lead to serious adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and highly effective," the Pennsylvania Department of Health said in an Oct. 19 health alert. "Getting vaccinated BEFORE pregnancy is the best way to prevent measles and congenital measles."

More cases of measles have been recorded recently during pregnancy, and there are "rising concerns" about congenital measles, or measles transmitted to infants from pregnant mothers, the department said.

Women and teenagers in outbreak areas should receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, separated by 28 days, according to the department. Other women should be offered one dose.

Women should take care not to become pregnant for at least 28 days after receiving a shot.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that pregnant women should not receive the MMR vaccine. Pennsylvania's guidance says the vaccine should not be administered during pregnancy.

Infants born to women who had measles are at risk for symptomatic and transmissible measles infection, Pennsylvania officials said. Infants should be isolated, monitored, and provided with immune globulin, which could prevent measles or reduce symptoms.

Infants showing symptoms within 10 days of birth, such as rash, should be tested, and treatment should include vitamin A, since vitamin A deficiency has been linked with poorer outcomes from measles, they said.

Cases Jump in State

After the alert, Pennsylvania officials said the outbreak's case count rose to 1,317.

Thirty-one of those cases were new, according to the Oct. 21 update.

All but four of those individuals had not received a vaccine, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

Five people who contracted measles have died. That includes at least one death that a coroner deemed unrelated to measles.

A one-year-old is held by his mother while he receives a measles vaccine at a clinic in Lubbock, Texas, on March 1, 2025. Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images

The CDC lists three of the deaths on its website. The CDC said the number may change as it reviews information it has received.

The CDC is also working with a group of epidemiologists to develop a case definition for deaths due to measles.

Nationwide, there have been 4,410 measles cases this year, 96 percent of which have occurred in people who are unvaccinated or have unknown vaccination status. Ten percent of the patients have been hospitalized.

Vaccination Effort

About 300 state workers are teaming up with community organizations and health care providers to combat the outbreak by providing factual information and access to the MMR vaccine, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said.

State workers have administered more than 6,300 shots across hundreds of pop-up clinics since the outbreak started in April. They've administered more than 3,700 shots in other venues this year.

Healthcare workers are reporting increased interest in the vaccine.

They usually administered about 25,000 doses a month. In September, more than 56,000 doses were injected, and through the first three weeks of October, 39,000 doses have been administered.

The vaccine is estimated to provide 97 percent protection after two doses. Side effects include fever and rash.

items.title: Trump Admin Asks Supreme Court To Allow Border Wall Construction In Texas
items.content_text:
Trump Admin Asks Supreme Court To Allow Border Wall Construction In Texas

Authored by Troy Myers via The Epoch Times,

The Trump administration has petitioned the Supreme Court to allow border wall construction to resume in the Big Bend area of Texas.

In an emergency application filed with the high court on Oct. 21, lawyers for the federal government asked the justices to lift a lower court order halting construction of President Donald Trump's key project that began during his first term in office.

In the Oct. 3 order, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone sided with environmental groups who claimed the work was unconstitutional, breached the separation of powers, and took land from residents.

"This case involves a baseless injunction that halts a major portion of the construction of the border wall," U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the emergency application. "Leaving a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses would act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit as other routes close off."

The Trump administration argued that continuing construction was crucial because the Big Bend region encompasses nearly one-quarter of the U.S. - Mexico border.

Between fiscal years 2021 and 2025, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) apprehended more than 89,000 foreign nationals attempting to enter through the Big Bend sector, according to the emergency application, "and those are just the aliens who were detected."

According to CBP data, there were 11,823 apprehensions in the region during 2023 and 3,096 in 2025.

CBP has seized increasing amounts of illegal narcotics across the southwest border, and the Sinaloa and Juarez cartels, which operate south of the Big Bend area, continuously seek to exploit any vulnerabilities in the U.S. border to further drug, human, and weapons trafficking, Sauer stated.

He argued that Cardone's order, if allowed to remain in place, would lead to a number of harms for the federal government, including a disruption of its ability to secure a large portion of the southern border against cartel incursions and activity in addition to irreversible delays, costs, and operational harms from halting already-begun construction.

Sauer accused Cardone of misbalancing the equities and harms in her ruling.

The judge had conceded the federal government "will experience at least some degree of irreparable harm" because of her block. Nonetheless, Cardone "illogically concluded" the environmentalist groups' harms outweighed the government's, Sauer said.

"The notion that respondents' interest in 'escaping from modern life' in the 'wild spaces in the Big Bend Sector' and preserving 'the spiritual, recreational, and aesthetic value of the area,' surpasses the United States' paramount interest in preventing a quarter of the border from becoming a magnet for cartel exploitation defies credulity," the solicitor general wrote.

Plans for border construction in the Big Bend region were announced in January, with administration officials waiving environmental laws to speed up the building.

The plaintiffs, the Center for Biological Diversity, nonprofit Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and Rio Grande river guide and landowner in the Big Bend area Danny William Miller, filed suit in April over the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) waiving of regulations.

Zeynep Graves, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, told The Epoch Times via email that she and the groups are confident the Supreme Court will hand down a favorable decision.

"We're deeply disappointed that the Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court for a green light to bulldoze one of America's wildest, most extraordinary landscapes," Graves said. "Once Big Bend's canyons, cultural treasures and wild ecosystems are destroyed, they'll be lost forever."

By early October, Cardone had sided with the groups.

But Sauer argued in the emergency application that she never had jurisdiction to issue such a ruling.

He cited a section of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996.

Through that legislation, Congress granted authority to the attorney general and secretary of DHS to construct border security measures while making it "harder for federal judges to block those critical national security endeavors."

Congress also allowed the DHS secretary to waive legal requirements he deemed necessary to ensure speedy construction of roadways and barriers.

To further guard against delays of border wall construction, Sauer said, Congress "stripped federal courts of jurisdiction to hear any non-constitutional challenges to" a DHS secretary's waiver decisions.

Under that authority, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued two waivers in 2026 to expedite construction on border walls and roadways in Big Bend.

"The President received a mandate from the American people to build a wall, defeat the cartels, and stop the flow of illegal aliens and dangerous drugs like fentanyl into our country," DHS General Counsel James Percival wrote in a post on X. "[Cardone's] order is as unprecedented as it is flawed, and we look forward to the Supreme Court's expeditious consideration of this important question."

However, Graves told The Epoch Times she believed that the lower court does have authority to resolve the groups' claims, and "only Congress can authorize something as consequential as walling off the entire U.S. - Mexico border."

CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said he expects the border wall to be completed by the end of 2027.

items.title: Hegseth Barred Trans Troops - Yet Navy And Marine Boards Are Voting To Keep Them
items.content_text:
Hegseth Barred Trans Troops - Yet Navy And Marine Boards Are Voting To Keep Them

Military boards set up to push transgender troops out of the service are instead voting to keep many of them, the New York Times reported Friday, in a quiet break with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's ban.

Nine of the 12 service members who have come before the boards have been approved to stay, according to the Times. Boards at Marine Corps Base Quantico, assigned to carry out the removals, "were doing the opposite," the paper said, and Navy boards given strict instructions to force out sailors were "voting to let them stay." A Marine staff sergeant who appeared in August thought his career was over, and the panel approved him.

The Air Force is the exception. The Times found no similar pattern there, where transgender airmen are being discharged quickly. The Pentagon has not said how many hearings have been held or how many people have been removed, and the proceedings are closed, even to spouses.

Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer now at Southwestern Law School, told the Times the boards "are being told to do something that they know is wrong."

The boards are the last step in a removal campaign that began with a January 2025 executive order. In a September 2025 speech at Quantico, Hegseth told troops, "No more identity months, DEI offices, dudes in dresses." The Supreme Court let the ban take effect on May 6, 2025, and Hegseth's May 8 memo gave active-duty troops until June 6 and reservists until July 7 to leave voluntarily before involuntary separation began. Pentagon data from December 2024 counted about 4,240 service members with a gender dysphoria diagnosis.

The boards were designed to reach one result. Priya Rashid, a military attorney who represents transgender service members, told NPR in February that the outcome is "generally predetermined" and put the cost of assembling each board at $22,000.

An October 2025 Pentagon memo lets commanders overturn a board's decision to let a transgender service member stay. The memo, from Undersecretary Anthony Tata and obtained by AP, breaks with longstanding policy that boards act independently. It also requires transgender troops to appear in uniforms matching their birth sex, and a hearing proceeds without them if they refuse.

items.title: Supreme Court Allows New Hampshire To Bar Student IDs At Polls For Midterms
items.content_text:
Supreme Court Allows New Hampshire To Bar Student IDs At Polls For Midterms

Authored by Matthew Vadum via The Epoch Times,

The Supreme Court sided with New Hampshire Republicans, allowing officials to stop accepting student ID cards as valid proof of identity for voting.

The high court cited the Purcell principle, which guards against changes to election rules close to Election Day.

The court's decision took the form of an unsigned opinion issued late on Oct. 22.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

The Supreme Court here applied the so-called Purcell principle against last-minute judicially ordered changes to election rules.

A state law known as HB 323 forbids the use of student IDs as valid proof of identity when voting. New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance directing election clerks not to accept student IDs as a backup form of identification.

A group called the Coalition for Open Democracy challenged both the state law and the directive in federal court. The group's attorneys argued that the law ran afoul of both the U.S. and New Hampshire constitutions and discriminated against young voters on the basis of age. They also argued Scanlan exceeded his lawful powers as secretary of state.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante denied the group's request to bar enforcement of HB 323, but temporarily blocked Scanlan from advising election clerks that student IDs were never acceptable. Days later, the judge extended his order to cover public statements to that effect made by Scanlan. Together, the two orders meant clerks had to keep treating a student ID card as possible backup proof.

In its emergency application to the Supreme Court, the state argued that the district court's order came a mere 32 days before the general election, and that this goes against the Supreme Court's rulings, which have repeatedly held that lower federal courts should not "intervene in state election procedures in the lead up to an election."

The justices stayed Laplante's orders.

"This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election," the justices wrote, citing a 2020 precedent. "Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle."

In her dissent, Jackson said Laplante had determined that it was necessary to correct Scanlan's "publicized misstatement about what New Hampshire's election rules require."

The injunction issued by the district court, Jackson said, "was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law."

"An injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem," she said. "I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State's electoral processes."

New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella hailed the Supreme Court's ruling.

"New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written," he said in a statement.

"The Supreme Court's decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials."

The Coalition for Open Democracy criticized the high court's new ruling, calling it "wrong" and a misinterpretation of the Purcell principle.

"We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell," the group said in a statement.

"We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire."

The Supreme Court's order remains in effect through the Nov. 3 general election, while the case continues on appeal in the lower courts.

items.title: 梵高名画《The Starry Night》可能描绘的是真实的夜空
items.content_text: 梵高于 1889 年创作的名画《The Starry Night》可能描绘的是 1889 年 7 月 22 日法国真实的夜空。《The Starry Night》被普遍认为风格化地呈现了梵高在法国普罗旺斯圣雷米的窗外看到的景象。争议在于这片夜空究竟是这位后印象派画家自己的幻想，即象征性表达，还是真实的天文观察结果。此外这幅画的具体创作日期也无法确定。为解决这一问题，韩国庆熙大学的研究人员开发了一个框架，将天文学模拟结果与星象位置测量数据、历史天气记录，以及梵高的信件结合起来。研究人员根据描绘这片景色的早期素描重建了画中的窄视场。他们发现，下蛾眉月、金星，以及金牛座的毕星团或许肉眼可见于 1889 年 7 月 22 日的黎明前后，并且其构型与画中的排列大体相符。历史气象记录显示，1889 年 7月 22 日前后的夜空清澈到足以看见这一天文排列。此外梵高信件中频繁提及的蝉表明当时气候炎热，这也更贴近 1889 年 7 月的历史温度。

items.title: 希腊通过法案禁止 15 岁以下儿童使用社媒
items.content_text: 希腊议会周五通过了一项法案，禁止 15 岁以下的儿童使用社媒平台。此举旨在回应公众对社交媒体会对未成年人的健康与安全产生负面影响之日益增长的担忧。禁令将于 2027 年 1 月 1 日生效。澳大利亚是首个通过立法限制未成年人使用社媒的国家。法国也曾通过类似法律，但于 8 月被宪法委员会裁定无效。希腊总理基 Kyriakos Mitsotakis 表示，社媒平台有 2 个半月的时间制定方案，核实用户年龄并保护其隐私。希腊政府表示，将支持家长共同遏制“无限滚动”现象——这种行为会导致儿童睡眠不足、注意力难以集中，挤占与朋友相处的时间。

items.title: 宫本茂成为首位获得日本文化勋章的游戏从业者
items.content_text: 日本文部科学省公布了 2026 年度文化勋章获得者名单，任天堂首席游戏设计师及代表董事宫本茂位列其中， 成为首位获得文化勋章的游戏从业者。文化勋章旨在表彰在文化发展方面做出特别显著贡献的人士，自 1937 年设立以来，获得者包括了画家横山大观、诺贝尔物理学奖得主汤川秀树、棒球明星王贞治和长岛茂雄等。宫本茂在记者会上表示：“游戏并非由我一人独自完成，而是与众多伙伴共同创造的成果。我是怀着代表大家的心情来接受这份荣誉的。”

items.title: 联合国警告厄尔尼诺可能导致数千万人粮食短缺
items.content_text: 今年的厄尔尼诺事件强度可能前所未有。它将于 2026 年底前后达到峰值，但其影响在此之后仍将持续很长时间。热带太平洋（厄尔尼诺的中心区域）的海面温度在 2026 年 11 月至 2027 年 1 月期间可能比平均值高出 3.8°C。 一次非常强的厄尔尼诺会扰乱许多地区的正常温度和降水格局。它可能给一些地区带来严重干旱，给另一些地区带来强降雨和洪水，并导致世界大片地区温度升高。极端天气事件可能会成倍增多，并发生级联效应。 联合国人道主义事务协调厅（OCHA）厅长弗莱彻警告称，全球可能有多达 5000 万人面临严重的粮食短缺。他呼吁各国政府做好充分准备。厄尔尼诺可能会给非洲、中南美和东南亚等地带来巨大破坏。

items.title: mRNA 癌症疫苗将死亡复发风险减少 42%
items.content_text: 制药公司 Merck 和 Moderna 宣布，在 III 期黑色素瘤临床试验中，基于 mRNA 技术的个性化癌症疫苗相比标准治疗，将死亡或复发风险减少 42%。黑色素瘤是最致命的皮肤癌。两家公司正与监管机构接洽争取该疫苗早日获批。有 1,137 名患者参加了 III 期临床试验，他们此前均患有 IIB-IV 期黑色素瘤，已通过手术切除肿瘤。患者被以 2:1 的比例随机分配至两组：一组接受个性化 mRNA 疫苗联合标准治疗，另一组仅接受标准治疗。标准治疗采用 Merck 已上市的单克隆抗体抗癌药物 Keytruda。定制 mRNA 疫苗名为 intismeran 或 mRNA-4157，编码了癌症特有的突变，帮助免疫反应精准识别和对癌细胞进行攻击。Intismeran 和 Keytruda 治疗组两年后有 82% 的患者存活且未出现复发，Keytruda 和安慰剂组中这一比例为 70%。

items.title: 浏览器 Arc 将于 12 月关闭
items.content_text: The Browser Company 宣布其浏览器 Arc 将于 12 月 22 日关闭，用户将无法再能启动应用。Arc 基于 Chromium，于 2023 年释出了 1.0 版本，但 2024 年就停止了开发，2025 年 5 月宣布它正在开发 AI 驱动的浏览器 Dia。Arc 从 10 月 22 日起无法创建新的 Arc 账号，11 月 23 日起停用部分功能，12 月 22 日无法启动应用，Arc 账户将被停用，个人数据会在 30 天内被删除。The Browser Company 表示 Arc 用户可通过数据导出功能无缝使用其全力开发的新浏览器 Dia，声称用户在 Arc 中使用的浏览器功能在 Dia 中均可免费使用，而 AI 功能则是可选使用的。

items.title: Switch 2 越狱能运行自制程序
items.content_text: 研究员 Sammy Hajhamid 利用软件漏洞在 Switch 2 上实现越狱，而且能运行自制程序。越狱利用了一个专门运行在任天堂硬件上的编程环境和解释器 SmileBasic 4。Hajhamid 使用 OpenAI 的 Codex 对 SmileBasic 的语言解释器进行探测，花了两周时间发现了一个 32 位整数溢出漏洞，利用该漏洞能对部分系统内存进行读写操作。他在此基础上从 Switch 2 内部找到了其它漏洞，提权获得任意读写权限。他之后演示了在越狱的游戏机上运行自制程序。SmileBasic 4 已从任天堂的 Switch eShop 中下架，漏洞可能会在后续的固件更新中修复。

items.title: KeePassXC 2.8.0 释出
items.content_text: 开源密码管理器项目 KeePassXC 释出了 v2.8.0。KeePassXC 代表 KeePass Cross-Platform Community Edition，是 KeePassX 的一个分支，而 KeePassX 则是基于 Qt 构建的 KeePass 克隆版本，但已停止维护。KeePassXC 2.8.0 带来了用户期待的新功能，大量 bug 修复和安全修正。主要特性包括：Qt 的版本从 Qt5 升级到 Qt6，Wayland(Linux) 下支持 Auto-Type，可自定义快捷键，使用外部工具实现远程数据库同步，macOS 支持密码快速解锁，Linux 下支持通过 Polkit 快速解锁，Windows 下提供了支持 ARM64 架构的原生版本，等等。

items.title: eMudhra 退出全球 CA 业务
items.content_text: 在曝出惊人丑闻之后，印度公司 eMudhra  宣布退出全球 CA 业务，将专注于核心企业解决方案和信任服务而非 SSL/TLS 相关业务。它是印度唯一一个被主流浏览器信任的 Root CA 机构。截至 2026 年，公司已发行逾 6000 万张证书。此前 eMudhra 的八个中间证书的私钥泄漏，而这些私钥被发现是极其简单的数字如 4。该公司在声明中称这些简单密钥是“多重人为错误”导致的。相关密钥是在 2025 年  4 月 30 日生成，它使用专门的硬件安全模块生成了一组密钥，但软件脚本的一个缺陷导致其生成了另一组较弱的密钥，由于两组密钥名称相似，结果其员工选择了弱密钥组。

items.title: 趋势科技在公开的内核邮件列表上披露内核漏洞
items.content_text: 趋势科技的安全团队 Zero Day Initiative 向人人可访问的内核邮件列表上递交了一系列新发现的内核漏洞。按照惯例，漏洞应该递交到不对外公开的安全邮件列表。递交的部分漏洞没有补丁，部分漏洞已有补丁在测试，这些漏洞的 CVSS 风险评分最高为 9.0。稳定版内核维护者 Greg Kroah-Hartman 批评安全研究人员将漏洞报告递交到公共的邮件列表。而在 AI 辅助漏洞发现时代，此类的漏洞报告越来越多。

items.title: 科学家揭示低温延缓衰老的机制
items.content_text: 适度低温已被证明能有效延长动物寿命，延缓与衰老相关的机能衰退。但低温延缓衰老的分子机制是什么？研究人员利用秀丽隐杆线虫（Caenorhabditis elegans ）发现，低温会触发代谢物 dihydrobiopterin (BH2)的大量产生，其中肌肉充当了中央工厂的作用，负责合成 BH2，BH2 随后输送至身体其它组织，诱导氨基酸酪氨酸（tyrosine）的合成，它有助于维持蛋白质稳态，在衰老过程中促进组织健康。论文发表在《自然》期刊上。研究还发现，同时补充 BH2 和酪氨酸能在秀丽隐杆线虫及细胞培养物上再现低温的部分有益效应，即便在标准温度或更高温度下也能显著延长寿命。研究人员强调，就目前研究而言，开发出一种能重现低温长寿效应的药丸还为时过早。

items.title: 逾半数美国人认为 AI 对社会有害
items.content_text: 根据 ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos 的调查，57%的美国人认为 AI 对社会有害，42%的人认为它对社会有益。仅有 2% 的人认为它对社会极其有益，17% 的人认为它对社会极其有害。与年长者相比，年轻的美国人更有可能认为 AI 对社会有害：在 30 岁以下的美国人中，65% 的人持此观点；在 30-39 岁的群体中，这一比例为 59%。而在 40 岁及以上的美国人中，认为 AI 对社会有害的比例相对较低，但也超过半数（53%）。在民主党人（63%）和独立人士（58%）中，多数人认为 AI 对社会有害；共和党人认为有益有害的比例差不多，51% 的人认为  AI 对社会有益，47% 的人认为它对社会有害。当谈及 AI 对个人自身的影响时，50% 的人认为 AI 对自己有益，49% 的人认为对自己有害。持负面态度的人群立场更为强烈——认为 AI 对自己极其有害的人数（15%）是认为其极其有益人数（3%）的五倍。多数共和党人（57%）认为 AI 对自己个人有益，而多数民主党人（55%）则认为 AI 对自己个人有害。无党派人士对于 AI 对自己个人而言究竟是好（50%）还是坏（49%）比例差不多。

items.title: 研究识别出第一位企业心理病态者
items.content_text: 一项新研究指出，有毒企业领导人身上所见的性格特征可追溯到一位 400 年前的荷兰东印度公司的企业官员。该公司的商户部经理 Jeronimus Cornelisz 可能是最早有文献记录的企业心理病态者。研究发现，他表现出了与企业心理病态者相关的全部 10 项核心特征。这些特征包括：利用个人魅力博取信任；在身边聚集忠诚的追随者；清除潜在的挑战者；在竞争对手之间制造分裂；营造恐惧氛围；出问题时推卸责任；将追求权力、金钱和控制权置于一切之上。荷兰东印度公司是世界上第一家跨国股份制企业；1602 年该公司在阿姆斯特丹开设了世界最早的证券交易所之一。研究认为，Cornelisz 的案例表明，早在资本主义萌芽时期，受权力、财富和个人晋升欲望驱动的人，就已被商业性企业所吸引。研究聚焦于 1629 年发生在西澳大利亚海岸外岛屿上的 Batavia 沉船惨案。沉船事故后，约 200 名幸存者被困在几座孤岛上。由于高管已乘船前往今天的雅加达寻求救援，身为经理的 Cornelisz 便成了幸存者中职位最高的企业代表。在他的领导下，约有 100 名男女老少遭到杀害，部分女性还遭受了性暴力。Cornelisz 将这些杀戮辩解为节省食物和水资源的一种手段，而这些谋杀同时也铲除了他眼中的竞争对手。

items.title: 毅力号行使距离超机遇号刷新历史记录
items.content_text: 毅力号火星车创下新的世界纪录——它在地外天体表面的行驶里程，超过了此前所有探测器。10月11日，它的里程表读数达到28.10英里（45.22公里），超越了此前由机遇号保持的28.06英里（45.16公里）纪录。机遇号于2004至2018年间在火星开展探测。机遇号耗费近15年才跑完该里程，而毅力号仅用时5年半。这一里程碑事件发生在它的第2006个火星日。毅力号能长途行进，一大核心原因是搭载了先进的自主行驶系统。这套系统名为 AutoNav。依靠它火星车大多时候不需要等待地球发来详细行驶指令，就能自主在火星地表认路。行进过程中，毅力号持续拍摄周边影像，绘制包含障碍物信息的三维地图，在地面操控人员选定的目的地之间自行规划安全路线。该系统可以让火星车以接近最高速度行驶，单个火星日最多可前进1351英尺（412米）。毅力号超过90%的行驶里程都依靠AutoNav自主评估地形。与之对比，机遇号及其孪生探测器勇气号早期自主导航系统，仅能自主评估约5%的行驶路段。

items.title: 因加州考虑征收亿万富翁税扎克伯格有意离开
items.content_text: Meta 周三警告，如果加州通过亿万富翁税，公司 CEO 扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）可能会离开加州迁往他处。扎克伯格已向公司特别委员会告知了这一可能性。据 Meta 在监管文件中披露的计划，为了让扎克伯格未来八年继续留在加州领导公司，公司将设立一类新股票，允许他出售在 Meta 中最多一半的经济权益，同时保留投票控制权。亿万富翁税提案已列入加州 11 月的选票，提议对亿万富翁的资产一次性征收 5% 的税款。Google 联合创始人Sergey Brin 已投入超过 1 亿美元反对该提案。英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋则是少数表示不介意缴纳税款的加州亿万富翁。

items.title: OpenClaw 作者称他上个月花掉了千万美元的 Tokens
items.content_text: 周三旧金山举行的 Cloudflare Connect 2026 大会上，OpenAI 技术部成员、OpenClaw 作者 Peter Steinberger 在与 Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht 对话时透露，上个月运行 AI 工作负载消耗了价值约 1000 万美元的 Token。当然这笔支出不用他自己掏钱，他花的是投资人的钱。Steinberger 称自己拥有几乎无限的 Token 预算。Steinberger 认为，未来每个人都会拥有某种智能体——它们能持续运行、进行思考，在全天候为你提供帮助，甚至能预判你未来可能需要什么，这样你或许无需提问就能直接获得答案。

items.title: 美光桃园厂员工罢工一天
items.content_text: 美光在台有两座工厂，其中桃园厂工会与资方就员工利润分红未能达成共识，星期四（10月22日）发动24小时罢工；台中厂工会于周三签署劳资协议，但未公布具体内容。桃园厂工会星期四上午9时起，在厂区门口展开为期24小时的罢工行动，预计持续至星期五（23日）上午9时。美光桃园厂约有3000名员工，其中约2400人为工会会员；台中厂则有约1万2300名员工，工会会员约1万1000人。桃园厂工会的主要诉求是，要求建立以公司营业利润15%为基础的长期员工分红制度，并将奖金发放方式由每年改为每季，以改善过往绩效奖金（IPP）不透明、分配不对称的问题。

items.title: EA 关闭 BioWare 工作室，取消《质量效应》新作开发
items.content_text: EA 裁员约 400 人，关闭 BioWare 工作室，取消《质量效应》新作开发。BioWare 工作室成立于 1995 年，创始人是医生，2007 年出售给 EA，创始人在 2012 年左右退出。该工作室的游戏包括了《博德之门》、《无冬之夜》、《星战旧共和国武士》、《翡翠帝国》、《龙腾世纪》和《质量效应》系列，以及《圣歌》。其中旨在获得持续收入的服务型游戏《圣歌》饱受批评，游戏于 2021 年停止开发，服务器于 2026 年 1 月关闭。BioWare 的最后一款游戏是 2024 年发布的 《龙腾世纪：影障守护者》，该作品的销量未达预期，工作室在 2025 年大规模裁员，只剩下约 50 人从事《质量效应》新作的早期开发。BioWare 在官网发表了一封告别信，简要回顾了工作室的历史。前 BioWare 员工之后泄漏了《质量效应》新作《宇宙》的预告片。

items.title: 坏苹果效应：人们会效仿他人的违规行为
items.content_text: 俗话说，一颗烂苹果，能毁掉一整桶好苹果。发表在《Proceedings of the Royal Society B》期刊上的一项研究再次为坏苹果效应提供了证据。这项研究旨在探讨个人如何在社会情境中做出是否违规的决策。研究人员说，很多人可能以为自己的决策是完全自主做出的，但事实上在很多情况下，我们的行为深受他人的影响。研究人员在美国招募了 750 名参与者进行了一项在线实验，共和党人和民主党人的比例大致相当。研究结果显示了他人的选择如何产生影响：看到别人遵守规则会略微降低个人违规，看到别人略微违规则会略微增加自己的违规，看到他人明显违规则会明显增加自己的违规。而当违规者与自己属于同一阵营，坏苹果效应则会更显著，表明政治立场一致的人更容易相互影响。研究期间有三分之一的参与者始终遵守规则，尽管这么做并不能获得最大收益。

items.title: 鸟类是地球最重要的养分搬运者之一
items.content_text: 鸟类在塑造地球化学环境上的作用被低估了，它们是地球最重要的养分搬运者之一。研究人员揭示了鸟类如何通过自身的排泄物和身躯，将养分在陆地、湖泊和海洋之间搬运。这一过程深深影响着从土壤和水体的化学性质，到动植物的生长。飞行能力让鸟类能跨越广阔的距离，甚至逾越海洋和山脉等天然屏障。鸟类在处理和循环养分上也极其高效。鸟类的食物摄入率比体型相当的哺乳动物高出约 30%。因此鸟类始终处于进食状态——它们大量摄取富含氮和磷的种子、昆虫、无脊椎动物及果实——并以极高的速率释放出养分。鸟类会将高浓度的养分集中在小片区域内，为当地的植物及其它生物提供关键资源。研究团队发现，饮食的季节性变化会导致鸟类的排泄物成分发生显著改变。春季鸟类摄入较多昆虫，其排泄物氮含量更高；秋季鸟类摄入较多果实和种子，其排泄物碳含量相对更高。根据《State of the World’s Birds》报告，全球 45% 的候鸟物种数量正在下降，可能会导致许多生态系统的肥力下降，进而降低其生产力。

items.title: 早报｜微信初步适配iPhone Duo，仍不能平板登录/全球PC出货下降21%/何刚出任华为董事

Earlier this week, the immigration resource/news site Documented released an investigative report by data journalist Sam Rabiyah that is damning, enraging, and probably unsurprising hereabouts: a look at fake immigration lawyer TikTok accounts, how AI is enabling scammers to prey more efficiently on immigrants, and how AI fuels TikTok's outrage machines with lurid stories of immigrant crime. Today he followed up with a guide allowing others to duplicate this work & help detect false, misleading, & AI-generated content.

Documented spent six months analyzing a sample of 10,000 TikTok posts to understand what risks lie in the ways videos are created and shared by those looking for help on the platform. [...] Through our findings, we uncovered dozens of copycat accounts ripping off legitimate immigration attorneys, some actively scamming immigrants into sending them money, as well as a band of news influencers circulating tropes about immigrants committing crimes to garner popularity. [...] In the process, we realized this technology could be useful to anyone trying to analyze content being shared on TikTok, and so we chose to share our work directly with the public. 
The three related Documented reports: TikTok Lawyers Face Their AI Clones (the original report, side-by-side videos better viewed on big screen) News Influencers Cash In on the "Criminal Immigrant" Narrative Follow the Bots: A Technical Guide

items.title: Peer Review will never be the same.
items.content_text:
We show that AI-generated [academic journal] reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts. No matter how we look at the data, AI wins. It wins in 100% of the pairs overall when judged by another AI model...and 87% overall when judged by human journal editors... [H]umans agreed as much or more with AI's judgment than they did with other humans.

In this paper, we provide head-to-head experiments, using an unusually high quality set of human reviews, and show that AI now dominates human peer reviews at their best — according to blind judgments by other AI models in every area and by (human) former editors of major scholarly journals. Given prior research on earlier AI models, we had expected AI to win some in some areas, some of the time, but we found that the latest AI wins in them all, by every criterion we measured, by wide margins, with no fabricated sources, and with about a third the rate of incorrect claims of the human reviews. Some Bsky commentary.

items.title: Ken Paxton’s Ties to Convicted Fraudster Exposed via Blind Trust
items.content_text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and his wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, invested $600,000 into a business run by a man convicted of fraud.

The Texas Tribune reports that the Paxtons gave the cash to a construction materials business run by Scott Sherman, a home builder who pleaded guilty to mortgage fraud in 2014, through what was presented to the public as a blind trust. In reality, the Paxtons’ business activities were not shielded, as should be the case in a blind trust.

According to the Tribune, which cited previously unreleased records from Ken Paxton’s 2023 impeachment investigation, Sherman’s companies sent the Paxtons thousands of dollars while they were facing mounting tax debts. Ken Paxton was investigated by the Texas state legislature and was eventually acquitted. Now he’s Texas’s Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in a tight race with Democratic challenger James Talarico.

Paxton’s business dealings fly in the face of his public statements. He said in a news release last year that “in Texas, we fight fraud head-on and will not rest until every last corrupt actor is brought to justice.” Ethics experts told the Tribune that his activities undermine his position as Texas’s top law enforcement official.

Richard Painter, a former chief ethics lawyer to President George W. Bush, said he thought Paxton would be smarter than this. Referring to people like Sherman, Painter said, “They’ll pay out their friends while they’re not paying their taxes, run up debt. But the question is, why is the attorney general of Texas dealing with those kinds of people?”

Painter added that he thought “the attorney general of Texas would have the good sense not to be dealing with a convicted felon.”

Angela Paxton filed for divorce from Ken last year on “biblical grounds,” referring to her husband’s infidelity. Ken Paxton has continued to deal with shady characters since his investment in Sherman, spending New Year’s Eve 2024 partying with his mistress and two campaign donors who both fled the U.S. from health care fraud charges.

items.title: 45-Year-Old Republican Candidate Sued by His Own Parents
items.content_text:
A 45-year-old Republican candidate in Iowa is being sued by his parents for $275,000 in unpaid rent. 

The Des Moines Register reported that the parents of lieutenant governor nominee Derek Wulf allege that he stopped paying rent two years ago on the farmland he rented out from them. A court petition filed Tuesday demands repayment and also accuses him of lying about his assets in financial documents to a lender.

While Wulf has yet to comment, his Trump–endorsed running mate, gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn, denied that Wulf owes his parents any money at all—and insinuated that the conflict was spurred by the poor health of Wulf’s father. Wulf’s parents rejected that, calling the claim “categorically false.” 

Duane and Jackie Wulf, 83 and 82 years old respectively, join a long list of creditors demanding repayment from the Republican candidate. Eight people and companies have sued Wulf and his company, Shallow Creek Land & Livestock, since 2023 for payments owed to them. All but one of the lawsuits have been settled. That one is from the WCF Financial Bank, which claims that Wulf is over a year behind on credit payments. 

Wulf is a 45-year-old man with a wife and two children running for lieutenant governor. These financial issues are not only embarrassing but raise alarming questions about how he might abuse a position in office. Hopefully, Iowa will never have to find out. Polls show that he and Lahn are currently trailing Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand by about 11 points—in a state Trump won by 13 points two years ago.

items.title: Federal Judges Rule ICE Can Keep Detaining People Indefinitely
items.content_text:
A federal appeals court on Friday stripped due process rights from hundreds of immigrants held by Immigration and Custom Enforcement.

In a 10–7 en banc decision, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that ICE detainees with pending immigration hearings are not entitled to receive a bond hearing, where a judge could assess their dangerousness and flight risk, regardless of how long they have been in detention.

The decision blocks efforts by federal judges who have been ordering the release of hundreds of immigrants—many of whom have no criminal record and have deep ties to the United States—held without bond by ICE’s mass deportation policy.

After the Fifth Circuit upheld ICE’s policy in February, other federal judges discovered that they were able to argue that detention violated immigrants’ constitutional due process rights. In the past year, judges have ruled against detentions without bond more than 21,150 times. The Fifth Circuit has now choked off that legal argument.

The case will likely head to the Supreme Court, which is set to decide on a number of immigration reform cases in the coming term.

items.title: “Nonsense”: Trump DOJ Charges Former FBI Officials Over Hunter Biden
items.content_text:
