Her vision for Ohio stands in stark contrast with her opponent, billionaire scam artist Vivek Ramaswamy, who has spent his campaign spewing repulsive lies from the seat of the private jet he insists on taking everywhere.”

Contrary to the impression given by headlines from this race, there are plenty of policy issues that Ohioans care about this year. As in Ohio’s Senate race, data centers have become a standout issue forcing Republicans to play defense. Acton has called for a “conditional moratorium” under which data centers must use union labor, cover their own utility costs, and follow environmental standards. Ramaswamy, who used to speak positively about data centers, has backtracked somewhat and now says that they should only be built on abandoned industrial sites, must comply with environmental rules, and should provide free electricity for the closest 100,000 residential homes.

All evidence suggests that voters care even more about affordability. Acton’s campaign has put out a detailed affordability plan that includes proposals for working-class family tax cuts and lowering energy bills, among other things. Ramaswamy, meanwhile, has called for cutting property taxes and phasing out state income tax—moves that some experts say could decimate municipal services like police, firefighters, and libraries.

Education is another critical issue in the state. In 1997, the state’s Supreme Court ruled that Ohio’s method for funding public education was unconstitutional. Since then, politicians have tried and failed to reform the education system. The state spent more than $1 billion on voucher programs in the 2026 fiscal year. Acton opposes the voucher programs, and Ramaswamy would like to see them expanded.

The new attack ad against Acton, and the fallout from it, may not change the race, which has already been marked by negativity and personal attacks. Early voting has already started, and voters have been inundated with ads for months. But there’s always a chance that it could make a last-minute difference. “The common thought in Ohio politics is that the state tends to break towards Republicans in the final weeks of the campaign,” Jackson said. “Ramaswamy may have given up that built-in advantage in the last couple weeks here with this backlash.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

Protesters, community leaders, family members, and local news reporters in Senatobia, Mississippi, have been trying for months to get answers and keep the spotlight on the horrifying case of one-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was killed by police in June. Now, the story may finally be gaining national traction. On Monday, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced her department’s finding that “use of force was justified” when police shot the one-year-old in his mother’s arms during a confrontation in a Walmart parking lot over a report of diaper shoplifting.

Outrage over the finding is growing now that body cam and surveillance footage published by Darkhorse Press, and subsequently verified by The New York Times, has shown police officers running and pulling their guns en masse at a car that, at the time, was traveling in reverse, away from them. You can read the Times’s analysis of the video, which then shows the sedan moving forward and at least one officer firing into it, here. In July, Mississippi Today reported that the officer involved had previously been accused of “exaggerating the risks that a vehicle posed to officers during another parking lot confrontation that escalated into violence in 2019.” (He has also been named in one other misconduct complaint and has been accused of racist speech toward a co-worker.)

Fitch, a Republican, is running for governor in 2027. The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus (MLBC) on Tuesday, prior to the new video emerging, condemned Fitch’s finding and called for the release of evidence and an independent review. “Kohen Wiley was a baby. He posed no threat,” MLBC Chairman and Mississippi Representative Kabir Karriem, a Democrat, said. On Tuesday, Mississippi’s Democratic Party leadership also issued a statement calling for a release of evidence, an independent review, “direct, respectful communication with Kohen’s family” (who reportedly first heard about Fitch’s finding via Facebook), and “strong safeguards governing the use of gunfire against moving vehicles.” The Intercept noted this week that Senatobia police in the past two years have “[jailed] a 10-year-old boy for public urination,” forcefully arrested two teenage sisters while the then-police chief told them to “get your Black ass out of the road,” and “on Mother’s Day 2025 — in the same Walmart parking lot where Kohen Wiley would be shot dead … forced a woman out of her car in front of her young children for sitting in a handicapped parking space.”

Elsewhere:

  • The Bush family increasingly seems to be backing James Talarico against Ken Paxton in Texas’s Senate race. Hot on the heels of last week’s news that Barbara Bush donated to Talarico’s super PAC, George W. Bush’s brother Neil Bush announced on Tuesday that he voted for Talarico, praising the candidate’s character. “I have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas Attorney General,” he wrote, adding “I believe Donald Trump and those who have enabled him have done enormous damage to the Republican Party.” Last week, Trump called Texas GOP pillars John Cornyn and Karl Rove “WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks” for refusing to back Paxton, so… start your clocks.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

As the lawsuit against Cornell University and seven fraternity members over a gang rape continues to make headlines, Data for Progress releases a new survey that found that a majority of voters don’t trust “college administrations, elected officials, or fraternities and sororities to appropriately respond to sexual assault claims,” and they think fraternities and sororities are bad for campus life.

On Thursday at 4 p.m., University of Massachusetts Amherst’s Political Economy Research Institute, in conjunction with Third Act and the Better Futures Project, will host an online conversation between Bill McKibben, Michael Ash, James K. Boyce, and Joel Tickner on “Environmental Policies that Work for Working Americans.” It’s part of “an eight-week series this fall, highlighting policy proposals developed by more than 40 experts on the [university’s] Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America, team.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Here’s Why That’s B.S.

The Trump administration is escalating its “investigation” into Representative Ilhan Omar over whether the age that her now-deceased father put on her immigration application more than 25 years ago was accurate. Watch TNR’s Edie Olmsted make the case that this is really about the midterms.


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

With Rob Sand apparently poised to win Iowa’s gubernatorial race: When did the Hawkeye State last elect a Democratic governor?

(Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Trump Spends Entire Rally Speech Just Making Weird Noises
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump went post-verbal Wednesday at his rally in South Carolina.

After holding 20 campaign rallies in the span of just two months, the evidently exhausted 80-year-old president has started to insert wild sound effects into his already incoherent rants.

At one point, Trump appeared to short-circuit in the middle of a sentence. Instead of saying former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley’s name, the president produced a gagging sound.

“I’d say 90 percent of the reason I took the governor—EUHH,” Trump said. “I took the governor, I put her over at the United Nations, because I wanted this guy to be, I wanted the guy to become governor.”

Trump has repeatedly misspelled or misstated Haley’s name. Recently, Trump has appeared to forget the names of candidates he’s shown up to support.

Later, Trump described the unlawful military strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats using one of his favorite sound effects. “We brought the flow of deadly drugs coming in by ocean and sea down by 97—pew, pew, pew. Ninety-seven,” he said. Trump has been repeating this number for months, but the Pentagon’s own statements don’t support this claim.

It then appeared that Trump has given up on pretending that the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz has been restored. He’s also given up on trying to say it.

“Oh, and when Iran ends. POW,” Trump said, miming a downward flow. “The oil,” he clarified.

Trump’s nearly eight-month “six-week war” against Iran has caused a sustained spike in energy prices, creating a quagmire for Republicans in the coming midterm elections. The president’s pathetic deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil hasn’t helped. Trump continues to promise that an end is near, but indirect negotiations are still ongoing.

It’s hard not to view this latest rally as one humiliating moment after another. Speaking in front of thousands of people, Trump ranted about wanting to change the name of the Atlantic Ocean to “Trump Ocean,” insisted that he should’ve won the Pulitzer Prize for writing (after confusing it for his much-coveted Nobel Peace Prize), cheered on a rallygoer who assaulted a heckler, and leered at Senator Tim Scott, of all people.

items.title: JD Vance Totally Humiliated as NFL Team Ignores Him
items.content_text:
JD Vance was ghosted by practically every player on the Cincinnati Bengals football team during what he apparently believed would be a spontaneous meet and greet Wednesday evening.

The vice president waited outside the locker room. Just about every team member looked at Vance and decided not to interact with him—save for tight end Drew Sample, who gave Vance’s son a fist bump. Sample then gave Vance a handshake.

The entire situation—and its terrible optics—echoed a similar locker room visit by FBI Director Kash Patel, who unexpectedly appeared in videos with the U.S. men’s hockey team after their Olympic gold medal win earlier this year.

At the time, Patel was caught on tape chugging beers inside the locker room in Milan, spurring nationwide backlash as the American public questioned if the conspiracy podcaster turned intelligence chief had utilized taxpayer funds for the excursion. But at least Patel made it inside.

Despite occupying the number two office in America, Vance quietly waited for attention in the Bengals’ hallway. When it became clear that a meet and greet wasn’t going to happen, Vance wandered off with his entourage.

It was not immediately clear why the team snubbed Vance, but either way, the vice president should have bigger things on his plate. Earlier Wednesday, Vance sparked statewide backlash across Ohio for defending a disturbing advertisement by Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that featured the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s opponent, Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton.

The advert had Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, claim that “Amy has a serious problem.” Acton has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, ABC News reported. Arthur abandoned her two children to skip town with her husband, Acton’s stepfather, who was indicted for sexually abusing the Democratic candidate as a young girl.

“Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” Vance said on Wednesday.

items.title: “I Loved That”: Trump Celebrates as MAGA Fans Beat Protester
items.content_text:
President Trump celebrated violence at his rally in South Carolina Thursday night.

At least nine protesters interrupted his speech at Clemson University, according to a pool report. In one instance, a heckler was punched by a Trump supporter in the crowd, and the president loved it.

“Wow. Man, I love that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was, that was unbelievable. Is everybody OK? Who’s the guy that threw that punch?

“You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” Trump added, referring to the champion boxer in attendance.

“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally. He got whacked.”

In another instance, a MAGA fan followed a protester as security escorted him out, and hit him on the head.

Trump has a history of celebrating violence in his rallies going back to the start of his political career. In February 2016, Trump wished aloud at a rally in Las Vegas that he would have liked to punch a protester in the face. The next month, he told a rally crowd in Iowa, “So if you see somebody getting ready to throw a tomato, knock the crap out of ’em, would you? I promise you, I will pay for the legal fees. I promise. I promise.”

As the president’s dwindling popularity keeps setting records, more and more people are showing up to his pre-midterm election rallies to heckle and protest him. The economy continues to grow worse thanks to his failed economic policies and disastrous war in Iran, increasing dissatisfaction even in areas that voted for him by wide margins.

However, Trump still retains a core group of die-hard supporters, who are perfectly willing to engage in violence to demonstrate their loyalty, whether it’s storming the Capitol building or beating up protesters. To Trump, however, nothing can go too far.

items.title: Sheriffs Say Greg Abbott Is Lying About Their Endorsements
items.content_text:
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott publicized the endorsements of 11 Democratic sheriffs. Three of them denied ever endorsing him.

Zapata County Sheriff Ramon Montes, Val Verde County Sheriff Joe Frank Martinez, and Webb County Sheriff Marin Cuellar all publicly announced that they were not endorsing Abbot after he posted them on his endorsement list on Monday. While Cuellar has been removed from the list, Montes and Martinez are still on it.

“Please remove my name from this for the Governor Abbott. This is Sheriff Martin Cuellar. The governor endorsed Tano my brother’s opponent,” Cuellar wrote in a text screenshot he posted on Facebook. Cuellar is the brother of Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar, who is currently running for Texas’s 28th House district.

“I want to make it unequivocally clear that I have not issued a political endorsement of Governor Greg Abbott, and I did not authorize anyone to use my name as an endorsement,” Martinez wrote in his own official statement. “I made it clear to the Sheriff who submitted the endorsement that I could not endorse Governor Abbott. I also made it clear that no one from the Governor’s office ever contacted me regarding an endorsement, and that I do not need anyone speaking on my behalf.”

Sheriff Montes’s office told Border Report that he “is not endorsing anyone at this time.”

Recent polling has Abbott sitting just three points ahead of his Democratic challenger, former state Representative Gina Hinosoja.

items.title: Top Democratic Leader in Redistricting Fight Arrested
items.content_text:
Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas, the Democratic leader behind the state’s redistricting effort, was arrested Thursday in connection with an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme.

In a 45-page indictment filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, Lucas and six co-defendants were charged with conspiring to distribute and possess marijuana, conspiring to launder money, laundering money, and committing bribery by distributing large quantities of illegal marijuana under the auspices of her legal medical cannabis business.

Lucas, an 82-year-old great-grandmother, has served in the Virginia Senate since 1992. She faces five of the eight charges included in the indictment. These charges arrive five months after the FBI raided Lucas’s office in Portsmouth, Virginia, and the neighboring cannabis dispensary she co-owns.

Speaking at a press conference, FBI Director Kash Patel claimed that Lucas had accumulated nearly $5 million in ill-gotten gains over the past five years.

Lucas has been a frequent critic of Republicans and President Donald Trump, and is an ally to Virginia’s Democratic Governor Abigail Spanberger. The state senator was a central figure in mounting her party’s redistricting efforts earlier this year, which were ultimately blocked by the Virginia Supreme Court.

Also listed in the indictment were Lucas’s daughters Theresa Lucas-Lamb and Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is currently running for Portsmouth City Council. The DOJ manual prohibits federal prosecutors from timing any action for the purpose of undermining a candidate in an upcoming election.

But speaking at the press conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche insisted that the government’s actions were proper and “consistent with past practices.” When asked whether the investigation was political payback, Blanche said: “We don’t do political paybacks,” and claimed the probe had begun years before Trump reentered office. The  attorney general couldn’t offer a good explanation, however, for why he and the FBI director had bothered to give an official press conference for charges related to a declassified drug.

The indictment contains wiretap transcripts illustrating Lucas’s involvement in an alleged illegal moneymaking scheme. In a phone call in February 2026, Lucas discussed the language surrounding the state’s pending recreational marijuana legislation with an unindicted co-conspirator, according to the charging document. Lucas spoke about the possibility of the co-conspirator receiving a license, and sharing the proceeds with her because “this is our last chance at generational wealth.”

“I’ve got too old to not be greedy,” Lucas said, according to the indictment.

In another phone call a month later, Lucas said she hoped that the cannabis legislation would pass in order to make what she’d done legal, because “when I did it, it was obviously illegal.”

In a statement, Lucas indicated she intended to fight the allegations in the indictment.

“Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great grandmother,” she wrote.

“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now. I’m not new to this. I’m true to this,” she wrote. “I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”

This story has been updated.

items.title: Trump Bars Reporters From Press Pool Despite CNN’s Renewed Threat
items.content_text:
The president is tacking on to his White House media ban.

The White House stripped media access from CNN and The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg on Wednesday, despite the fact that both were scheduled to provide pool coverage.

“Today is CNN’s turn to fulfill both in-town and out-of-town TV pool duties, but the White House press office left the network off the list for Donald Trump’s trip to South Carolina, so as a result there will be no pooled TV coverage of the trip,” wrote CNN’s chief media analyst, Brian Stelter, on X.

CNN attorney Ted Boutrous had warned the Justice Department earlier this week that the network would take legal action if the White House continued to exclude CNN from Air Force One.

Boutrous is also representing MS NOW and Politico, which faced the initial wave of Trump’s restrictions alongside CNN last month. He noted in a letter that the White House had until 5 p.m. on Thursday to respond to the developing situation with CNN, or the organization “will be forced to pursue additional judicial relief.”

Semafor’s Maxwell Tani confirmed that Feinberg was also on the outs, sharing on X that “without explanation, the White House told him today that he would no longer be the print pooler on Trump’s Thursday trip.”

The decision came just two days after Trump tore into Feinberg during a White House presser, shushing and demeaning the well-reputed journalist.

“I don’t know who the hell you are, but you better be careful,” Trump said on Tuesday, minutes after Feinberg had introduced himself.

Moments later, Trump called Feinberg a “sick person” and added, “I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”

The president’s official rapid response account on X added fuel to the fire later that day, recirculating the exchange with a new description for Feinberg: “Mongoloid Moron.”

items.title: Trump Tried to Get Google to Rename Atlantic Ocean After Him
items.content_text:
President Trump isn’t done trying to rename things.

The president told a rally audience in South Carolina Wednesday evening that he tried to rename the Atlantic Ocean to “Trump Ocean,” but ultimately decided against it.

“I only like two oceans, the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean, I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two. So, we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean and I called Google Maps who were really great with the lake and really great with …” Trump said, trailing off but referring to the Gulf of Mexico.

Trump said he called Google CEO Sundar Pichai and asked him, “I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean, can you handle it? ‘No no no, this time I’m not doing it,’ he said.”

Trump:

I called Google Maps to change the name of the Atlantic Ocean to Trump Ocean.

Sundar said, “No, no, no. This time I'm not doing it.” He said, “Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don't ask us to do that.”

So we'll probably pass. Let's keep… pic.twitter.com/xnxVplu3fO

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

The audience and Trump laughed.

“He said, he said, he said, ‘Oceans are different, sir. You know, they cover, they cover a lot of, they cover really a lot of countries. Please, don’t ask us to do that.’ So I’ll probably pass. Should I pass it? I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean,” Trump said.

Trump’s ego knows no bounds if he was seriously considering having Google change the name of the Atlantic Ocean. He has signed executive orders changing the names of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to the Gulf of America and Lake America, respectively. He’s proposed renaming the Strait of Hormuz to “Trump Strait,” and earlier this week again mused about renaming New Mexico to “New America.” Meanwhile, the economy is suffering as a result of his failed policies and ill-advised war with Iran, and the Republican Party is facing heavy losses in November’s midterm elections.

items.title: Hegseth’s Staff Destroyed Priceless Artifact From Former President
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s staff badly damaged former President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s globe while moving it into his office.

The globe, which is now housed in the Pentagon, dates back to the 1930s and was reportedly used by Eisenhower during World War II, making it an extremely delicate artifact that needed to be handled with care. But a task that should have been delegated to archivists or museum professionals was instead handled by Hegseth’s own staff, who dropped the globe when they tried to move it to the defense secretary’s office early this year, The Washington Post reported.

That resulted in a gash “several inches wide” in the shell near Antarctica.

An Army spokesperson admitted to the damage, saying the globe was “detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate.”

Hegseth’s office did not respond to the Post’s request for comment.

One anonymous source attributed the gaffe to an “apparent lack of patience.” The mistake has become a source of humor both inside and outside the Pentagon, as the event is a perfect microcosm for the hypermasculine move-fast-break-things mentality that Hegseth has brought to the Defense Department—or the “War Department,” as he insists on calling it.

“Kind of a perfect metaphor for Hegseth’s entire tenure at DOD. Stupid, impulsive, driven by vanity and the result is destruction,” liberal podcaster Tommy Vietor wrote online.

“Hegseth wants an Eisenhower totem to be like Ike, brilliant in war and peace,” retired brigadier general and former West Point military history professor Ty Seidule told the Post. “Hegseth is no Ike. The globe won’t give him Ike’s attributes of humility, intellect and judgment.”

items.title: Transcript: Unraveling Trump Blurts Out Surprise Show of Midterm Panic
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the October 22 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump just unleashed a series of urgent calls to Republican voters, ordering them to vote early in huge numbers and urging them especially to vote by mail. Which is funny, because he previously spent months claiming mail voting is fraudulent to push voter suppression efforts.

In effect, Trump just admitted his attacks on mail voting have been a scam all along, designed to help him rig the election. On top of all that, Trump has badly self-owned here by spending months discouraging Republicans from voting by mail, which he now wants them to do.

So what can we say right now about early voting, both in person and by mail? We’re talking about this with one of the foremost trackers of early voting out there, Professor Michael McDonald, who runs the University of Florida Election Lab. Michael, great to have you on.

Michael McDonald: Great to be with you.

Sargent: So Trump spent many months calling vote by mail “corrupt” and “horrible” and worse. Suddenly he unleashes all these tweets directed at a number of states in which he says this:

“If you have a mail-in ballot, return it immediately and, if not, GO VOTE at the Polls RIGHT NOW. Get everyone you know to VOTE FOR THE REPUBLICAN! Whether you VOTE early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, Republicans must SWAMP the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!

Michael, what do you make of that? It sure seems like Trump kind of screwed himself, doesn’t it?

McDonald: Yeah. And it’s really too late, really, for Republicans to be requesting mail ballots. The Postal Service recommends 10 days to have election mail delivered. And so you’d have to have an election office send you a mail ballot, and you’ve got to return it. And so that may not actually be enough time. So even if, like he’s saying, please do this—it’s just simply not enough time now for Republicans to vote by mail.

Sargent: Well done, Mr. President! I want to clarify for people as well that vote by mail is an essential piece of early voting. In other words, if you want people to vote early, you want them to have the mail option. It’s critical, right?

McDonald: Yeah. And we have states primarily out in the West, but there are others like Vermont and D.C., that have run their elections entirely by mail, in that every active registered voter is sent a mail ballot. So in some places it’s essential that you’re voting by mail. In lots of other places, it’s an option for you to request a mail ballot.

Sargent: OK, so let’s start talking about the current situation. By your count, as of now, more than 16 million people have voted early, and around 10 million of those, more than half, are mail ballots. Is that right? And how does that compare to the previous two midterms?

McDonald: Yes, that’s correct. And while we can’t make really good apples-to-apples comparisons everywhere in the country, where I can make those comparisons, it certainly looks like people are voting at higher rates, maybe even higher than, say, the 2018 election, which was the highest turnout rate election for a midterm election since 1914. So we’re looking at really modern historic rates of voting.

Sargent: So your impression from the early voting data that you’ve collected is that we may be on a pace to actually beat 2018 in turnout in this midterm, right?

McDonald: Yes, it appears, where I can make comparisons to 2018, that turnout is exceeding levels of 2018, which would mean that we are going to have a higher turnout election than 2018.

Sargent: That is really, really striking, because 2018 was a big one.

Let’s start breaking this down by party. What is that 16 million telling you about which party is voting early more and which party is voting by mail more? And what does it mean?

McDonald: Yeah. So in some states that have closed or semi-closed primaries that are restricted to only people who register with the political party, we have data on who’s voting by political party, at least which party they’ve registered with. And when we look at that data, we can see that, well, Democrats, they’re way up from their 2018 and 2020 numbers.

Unaffiliated people, who aren’t affiliated with the party—yeah, they’re up too. You know who’s trailing behind everybody? Republicans. And they’re only up over their previous elections’ turnout in just a couple of states. So it does look like right now that there’s much more enthusiasm on the Democratic side to vote, and even among unaffiliated, than there is among Republicans.

Sargent: Well, let’s just underscore this one more time. Trump told Republican voters not to vote by mail for months and months and months, or even years, right? And so that essentially deprives Republicans of a very critical option to vote early. Isn’t that right?

McDonald: Yeah, absolutely. But it’s not just the mail ballots. We can see it in the in-person early voting that’s going on too. So it’s just like a general malaise among Republicans to participate in this election. And if the polling is correct that we’re going to see a big wave election, this is very consistent with what we would expect to see.

Sargent: OK. Well, as a quick aside here, people, there’s some new polling out. The New York Times national poll has Democrats up by 11 points, 52 to 41, in the generic House ballot matchup. That is a big lead consistent with a wave.

Right now, Democrats are also slightly up in the polling averages in just about all the key Senate races. These are all close, but Democrats do have a small edge. And this includes in a number of red states that Trump won by double digits.

So, Michael, does what we’re seeing in the early voting look consistent with those polls actually being accurate? Can you explain that?

McDonald: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, just a high-level view on it: the Republicans have basically given up on North Carolina, for example. We already know that they withdrew their support, but the early voting numbers there are just abysmal for them. So it looks like, yes, indeed, like the polling, like the political strategists have already determined, North Carolina is off the board for the Republicans—so that means probably, because, you know, it’s kind of a close competitive state.

When we look at where we may be shifting the battleground to places like Nebraska and Kansas and Iowa, places where we do have party registration data, we can see that, yeah, there’s a lot of engagement among Democrats. It’s relatively more than Republicans.

And that’s, again, both by mail and in person. So it looks like, if those states are going to be competitive, at least the data are there, the votes are there so far, that would make those states competitive.

But I do want to say one other thing about this. It’s definitely not a done deal for Democrats in these states. When you start looking at places—include Maine in this group too—when you look at these competitive—really competitive now according to the polling—U.S. Senate elections, you see Republicans voting there too.

Sargent: I just want to flag one more number from the New York Times national poll. Democrats lead in the generic House ballot matchup by 54 to 35 among independent voters, which is an extraordinary lead. It’s a 19-point lead.

Now, you mentioned earlier in this discussion that independent early voting is way up relative to previous midterms as well. So I think that there’s a positive story in that for Democrats, isn’t there? I mean, if Democrats are winning lopsidedly among independents and independent early voting is up, what does that tell us?

McDonald: Yeah, it’s absolutely what the Democrats are going to need to win some of these red states. They can’t just rely on Democrats or Republicans showing up. Democrats have to rely also on the unaffiliated moving their direction.

But I can’t tell that with the data that I have. I don’t know how people voted. I just have party registration. We have to look at polls to see, you know, give some glimmer of how the independents will be breaking.

Sargent: So if we’ve got independents breaking by, like, 19 points in Democrats’ favor, this doesn’t really necessarily confirm this for certain, but you’re looking like Democrats are really doing quite well among independents, and independents are voting very energetically early, right?

McDonald: Yeah, and it’s really unusual behavior, because usually independents, unaffiliated voters, they vote later in the early voting season, closer to Election Day. So to see these levels up right now, it’s a very unusual pattern.

Sargent: That’s really striking. Can you talk a little bit more about that? Like, what do you take from it? Does it mean maybe that we’re going to see independent turnout kind of off the charts in an overall sense, like in terms of both early voting and Election Day voting?

McDonald: Well, we don’t know yet, right? Because we still have a week and a half yet to go. So that remains to be seen. But what we can see from today, and if these patterns persist throughout the entire election, then yes, that would be the answer.

Again, these are very unusual patterns that we’re seeing, especially where we see Democrats up, unaffiliated up, but Republicans, like, either flatlined or even down in some states. It’s very unusual to see this behavior.

Sargent: Well, let’s dig a little deeper into some of this early voting. The data out of North Carolina and Georgia is telling us something about Latinos as well, right?

McDonald: Yeah, those are two states where they ask race and Latino or Hispanic ethnicity on their voter registration form, and they report the statistics of who’s voted by race and Hispanic ethnicity. And so we actually have some idea there of what’s happening. And I can see in the data highly engaged Latinos.

Their numbers are more than doubled from the previous election cycles. And that’s, again, highly unusual to see this behavior. Now, because Hispanics, Latinos, they tend to vote at a much lower rate than whites and African Americans in a midterm election—now, their rates are still not above whites or African Americans, so a little ways to go here, but still, it’s very encouraging to see this level of participation.

And there are a couple of corollaries that emerge from that. One is that if that’s going on in North Carolina and Georgia, it’s likely going on in other states too. And while we don’t have the data in the same way in Texas, you might infer there’s something going on in Texas with Latinos.

The other thing is, let’s go back to that unaffiliated. Latinos tend to not be affiliated with a political party more frequently. So part of what we’re seeing with the unaffiliateds is wrapped up with the fact that lots of Latinos are voting as well.

Sargent: Well, back to the New York Times poll. In this House generic ballot matchup, the Democrats are leading the Republicans among Hispanics by 61 to 31 points. That is a 30-point edge among Latinos. I’ve got to think you put that together with the unusual level of early voting energy among Hispanics, and that tells a story as well, doesn’t it?

McDonald: Yeah, absolutely. And it’s probably going to be a big part of the story once we get all the exit polls in and post-election surveys. People are going to definitely be talking about Latinos and how they participated.

Sargent: OK. So what’s the grand takeaway here, Michael? Things look good, but it would be crazy to get overconfident. Is that the size of it?

McDonald: Yeah, I mean, definitely where the battleground is shifted, it’s on Republican territory. And there are signs of Republican engagement in those states. And even when you drill down into some of the congressional districts that aren’t in those states but are still toss-ups.

So we still have a long ways to go. We have yet to get to Election Day, and it’s going to basically be determined then. Can the Democrats build up enough of a lead in the early vote, which is what they typically do, to withstand what will likely be a very big red day for Republicans on that Tuesday of the election?

Sargent: So what are you looking for at the end of the early voting here? To conclude that Democrats have built up something of a firewall, how will we know that that has happened?

McDonald: Yeah, once we get through it all—I mean, we’re seeing these same-day comparisons now, and you can see that Democrats and unaffiliated are much more engaged than Republicans. Is that going to persist? Is it going to go all the way through to, like, the weekend before Election Day?

And if it does, in the past, that’s been a fairly good predictor of how things turn out on Election Day as well. Because we’re measuring relative enthusiasm to vote when we look at these early vote numbers. And if there’s enthusiasm, you know, the Saturday or Sunday before the election, it’s enthusiasm that tends to carry over to Election Day as well.

Sargent: It seems like there’s another positive civic story here unfolding as well, which is that Trump has been threatening to rig the election and steal the election in all kinds of ways. He tried to pass his voter suppression thing to essentially end vote by mail and make it really, really hard to vote.

And he spent months telling Republicans that they had to do this, otherwise Democrats might actually be able to win the election. He basically spent months saying, we’ve got to close down voting, otherwise we’re screwed. Which is an interesting message, right?

But now, all of a sudden, here we are. Trump’s Save America Act didn’t happen. His effort to hijack the Postal Service to try and steal the election fell apart, and people are voting, right? I mean, that’s where we are. Like, we’re actually seeing the election start to unfold.

People are participating. ICE isn’t showing up at the polls, at least yet, I don’t know. Like, I feel like that might be good. I would certainly not urge people to stop being vigilant, but it’s kind of a positive story that’s emerging here.

McDonald: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, the good news story here is people are voting, and they’re voting, in some cases for a midterm election, at record numbers. So the system seems to be working as normal as we expect it to work.

But I’ll tell you, the way in which people are protecting themselves are probably going to help the Democrats, because we’re seeing mail ballots getting returned sooner, for people who have them.

And because they’re returning them sooner, if there are any problems with those mail ballots, there’ll be a chance for them to—in the election administration world—cure those deficiencies, and have those ballots counted. But we’re also seeing fewer people request and use mail ballots as well. So they’re shifting into in-person early voting.

And it really is like, these deficiencies with mail ballots—people, if you’re going to vote by mail, follow the instructions very carefully. Because every election cycle, hundreds of thousands of people have their mail ballots rejected by election officials because they don’t follow the instructions.

But if they’re voting in person, well any of those problems are going to be resolved at the polling place. So those votes are going to be counted more readily than they are by mail.

Sargent: So again, it looks like Trump may have shot himself in the foot again. I just want to underscore this, because it’s pretty fun. So basically, by threatening vote by mail, by talking about rigging the election, by talking about how our elections are fraudulent, Donald Trump essentially encouraged Democrats and probably a lot of independents as well to, A, vote by mail earlier and be damn sure that you’re getting it right so the vote can’t be taken away from you, and B, more people are voting in person early and not risking Trump stealing their ballot from the mailbox, right? So he really screwed himself in this way too.

McDonald: Yeah, it’s probably a net thousands of Democratic votes that are going to show up because of Trump’s rhetoric.

Sargent: Folks, if you enjoyed this, make sure to follow Michael’s stuff, and you can track what he’s doing on the early vote day in and day out. Go to michaelmcdonald.substack.com, or visit the early vote dashboard at the UF Election Lab. That’s the University of Florida Election Lab. Michael McDonald, awesome to talk to you. Thanks so much for coming on.

McDonald: Great to be with you.

items.title: Sonogram: Grandchild at Eleven Weeks
items.content_text:
The tail has disappeared and this shiver
of life

swallows. Without
hunger. Without thought.

A translucent stub. A heartbeat.
Elbows, knees, fingers sculpted

from warm honeycomb.
It is an ember

with its own fire. Blueprint
of ear, eyebrow, soon

nipples, minuscule
liver. It will

squint, frown, yawn
and keep on.

When my son was born
he opened his eyes and looked all around,

no cry, so calm he could have been
a plant slowly turning

to the sun. Love!
sharp as a defib. The kick of a horse.

Now, someone the size of two olives
in a martini, tiny, skinny limbs

sticking out, is going to
put on shoes and rush

into this treacherous world, dragging my heart.

items.title: A Philosopher Makes the Case to Call Trump Evil
items.content_text:
On the evening of March 15, 2025, while government lawyers haggled in a D.C. courtroom, three airplanes delivered 238 chained prisoners to the Terrorism Confinement Center in El Salvador. Better known as CECOT, the center is little more than a twenty-first-century concentration camp, where conditions are tantamount to “torture,” in the words of a Salvadoran jurist. According to Kilmar Ábrego García, a U.S. resident who was sent there for three months in early 2025 as the result of an “administrative error,” inmates are subjected to “severe beatings, severe sleep deprivation, inadequate nutrition, and psychological torture.”

A grotesque abuse of human rights, the administration’s illegal deportations to CECOT caused a furor across the country. Despite the outrage, however, most elected officials remained silent. Republican lawmakers, perhaps unsurprisingly, either demurred or supported the president. Then–Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem visited the facility, posing in front of a cage brimming with prisoners while sporting a $50,000 watch.

More surprisingly, Democratic congressmen and senators largely stayed mum in the face of administrative evil. “Democrats cannot say a word, apparently,” ex-Republican Bill Kristol seethed on March 31, “without going through some filter of what pollsters have been telling you.” Of the 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus, only a handful criticized the deportations (and in April, Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen visited Ábrego García in El Salvador). In May, a group of centrist senators introduced a milquetoast fact-finding bill—while deportees languished in the prison.

Their fecklessness was, unfortunately, not an anomaly. Despite Democrats’ eagerness to point out the economic missteps of Trump’s second term, the party’s leaders and most prominent figures rarely denounce its worst human rights violations (which have primarily targeted immigrants and trans people, two groups that most Democratic politicians avoid talking about like the plague). And while the party has spent over a decade warning American voters about the threat Trump poses to democracy, it has done little to actually defend it: Senate Democrats routinely vote to confirm Trump nominees (every one of the party’s senators voted to confirm Marco Rubio as secretary of state), favor arming the executive branch with authoritarian powers such as warrantless wiretapping, and have approved slates of Trump-nominated judges.

In her new book, the philosopher Susan Neiman, recently retired director of the Einstein Forum in Berlin, takes Americans to task for failing to call Trump and his administration what they are: evil. Declining to do so, in her view, is not merely a moral failing but has real-world ramifications. “Our culture’s reluctance to trade in moral ideas,” she writes, “has left them to right-wing demagogues and brought us to this pass.” A demand for moral clarity in an amoral world, Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era urges us to face “the moral ideas that Donald Trump embodies and reinforces, ideas that are destructive enough to warrant the word evil.”

In making a case to think about the Trump administration in these terms, Neiman offers a potent rebuke to those who would rather talk about “kitchen table issues” than torture. Yet her peculiar definition of evil makes it difficult to actually face the worst cruelties of this administration and to pin down who, precisely, she is talking about when she suggests that “we’ve lost confidence in moral conviction.”


“Make America moral again,” Joe Biden stated on April 30, 2019, when asked if he had a motto to contrast with Trump’s, “Make America great again.” It is not controversial to state, however, that after four years in power, numerous legislative accomplishments, and every effort to restore a measure of comity to American politics, Biden failed in his goal.

Some would undoubtedly point to the genocide in Gaza, mass slaughter that Biden’s administration did nothing to halt, besides throwing off a few tepid rebukes. Others might point to economic insecurity. As the celebrated economist Isabella Weber took to saying in those years, “Inflation kills governments.” While Neiman is unlikely to disagree with these assessments—a chapter of the book is devoted to Gaza, naming it “the moral watershed of our time”—she argues that the true culprit of our present malaise is the neoliberal ideology of self-interest; that, in the words of Gordon Gekko, “Greed is good.”

Neoliberalism is a word thrown around so freely that it has lost much of its meaning. But it did once refer to a specific political agenda that sought not only to unshackle the “free” market, but also to apply market logic to all spheres of life, hence the all-too-common refrain that governments or universities or other public goods should be “run like a business.” In Neiman’s view, this ideology arose from a bastardized reading of Adam Smith: a free market regulated only by the self-interest of its actors. This belief in a “rational” market was, Neiman adds, complemented by similar misreadings of Charles Darwin, which developed “increasingly baroque explanations of human behavior” to show that this self-interest is evolutionary in its origins. The terminus of this ideology is nihilistic: In a world where everyone is out to maximize profit, “moral concepts are for suckers.”

The more we are convinced that people are “rational” actors motivated only by greed, in short, the more likely we are to act that way. We live in a country where we’re told to look out for ourselves alone, to get ahead whatever the cost. In the process, Neiman contends, “the very idea of social rights,” by which she means everything from housing to education to health care, has become “anathema,” precisely because it infringes on the sovereign self-interest of the individual. But depriving citizens of these rights—or passing them off as “a safety net”—has real consequences. “The undercurrent of anger,” which Neiman contends characterizes American society, arises from the subconscious knowledge that it’s nigh impossible to get by this way, that the American dream is little more than a “mirage.” Trump is an expression of that rage, a symptom of a broken system and a bankrupt ideology, rather than its cause.   

Neiman is certainly not the first to make this diagnosis. The book departs from other recent works on neoliberalism and twenty-first-century fascism in its focus on evil, which Neiman movingly defines as the “idea that arises whenever the gap between the way the world is and the way the world ought to be becomes too big to bear alone.” Pointing to Hannah Arendt’s formulation of the “banality of evil,” she insists that in order to recognize evil in our own time, we must get away from the assumption that it only appears “as demons in jackboots.” Anyone can do evil. Thus, “the worst kind of evil” is not any particular expression of it, but rather “the refusal to recognize morality at all.”


It’s a beautifully simple formulation. Evil isn’t what you think it is, but rather the inability to recognize evil. It echoes Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s stirring dictum that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.” And yet, if prompted, most of us would likely come up with rather a different definition. We might arrive at a definition closer to that offered by Judith Shklar, a Harvard philosopher who was intrigued by the role of emotions in rational government. “Human cruelty,” she wrote, is not only “a distinct and unmitigated evil,” but is the “most evil of all the evils.” In Shklar’s view, the hallmark of a civilized society was its intolerance of cruelty.

Disdain for cruelty is precisely what has gone missing in the Trump era and what sits behind the fanaticism of the president’s most ardent supporters. What, after all, is “owning the libs” if not an indulgence in cruelty for cruelty’s sake? The protesters at No Kings marches and anti–Immigration and Customs Enforcement demonstrations know this. Adam Serwer knew it when he wrote in 2018, “The cruelty is the point.”

Neiman certainly gestures to the everyday atrocities of the last two years, acknowledging that Trump “reflects a culture that sells cruelty as entertainment.” Still, in her view, “faith in the tyranny of self-interest” is “far more significant than vicious or malicious cruelty” because it has allowed “cruelty to become ordinary.” Yet, that logic, as much as we might wish to believe it, doesn’t sustain the barest interrogation. There are plenty of neoliberal societies in which cruelty has not become normalized in the way that it has in the United States. There have been plenty of cruel societies that were not neoliberal in nature. And history is littered with examples of evil committed in the name of morality.

Neiman’s account of actual evil is thus strangely bloodless, the many atrocities of the last two years glossed over. “Counting crimes,” in her view, “is pointless.”

Neiman’s account of actual evil is thus strangely bloodless, the many atrocities of the last two years glossed over. “Counting crimes,” in her view, “is pointless.” A reader will search in vain for descriptions of the CECOT deportations, mentions of Alligator Alcatraz, or the number of innocents who have died in ICE custody. The so-called “Department of Government Efficiency,” which wrecked swathes of the government, putting thousands of dedicated public servants out of work and leading to the deaths of at least seven hundred thousand recipients of U.S. aid, is likewise nowhere to be found. And if you’re looking for sympathy with trans people, whose rights are being systematically shredded, forget it. Neiman tiptoes up to the line of blaming them for their own predicament, writing that a 2019 ACLU questionnaire, which asked if candidates would “ensure that transgender and nonbinary people who rely on the state for medical care—including those in prison and immigration detention—will have access to comprehensive treatment,” was “a thumb in voters’ eyes.”

That kind of slippage is, unfortunately, more a feature than a bug in Neiman’s writing. With a fondness for dramatic claims, she often invokes straw men. “Why aren’t more of us in the streets?” she asks, apparently unaware that more Americans are protesting now than in Trump’s first term. Likewise, she suggests that the word fascist “fell into disuse after Trump began his second term.” Really? Perhaps most egregiously, she contends that the famous gender theorist Judith Butler recently said, “Of course there has been progress in my lifetime; now people can change their pronouns.” In Neiman’s view, “A clearer statement of woke bankruptcy has yet to be made.” The only problem? I’ve found no evidence that Butler ever said such a thing. 

In fact, “the woke” (a term that Neiman does not define, instead arguing that “woke eludes definition because it’s an incoherent concept”) feature prominently in the book’s concluding section. In her view, “the woke” embraced an identity politics that, much like the reactionaries they claimed to oppose, abandoned morality in favor of tribalism. Because of their insistence on a radical kind of social justice that equated progress with “oppression” and reason with “domination,” this amorphous group of figures (Biden, Neiman assures us, “was woke but not left”) “clearly played a role in the second election of Donald Trump.”

Neiman’s fascination with wokeness (three years ago, she published a book titled Left Is Not Woke) means that although she has indeed identified real flaws in American politics and diagnosed a real inability to speak about them in moral terms, the book is criticizing the wrong people. Why, one might reasonably ask, does it not take aim at the centrists, at the politicians, journalists, and intellectuals who for years stoked fears of cancel culture and wokeness, who compared leftist efforts at social justice to fascism? Where is Bari Weiss, who in a few short years has evolved from “a self-styled free speech martyr” to propagandist-in-chief at CBS News? It is these same figures who breathlessly warned about the danger from the left but have gone silent in the face of state efforts to censor the media, shred academic freedom, intimidate political opponents, punish those who have protested Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and strip migrants of even a vestige of rights or dignity. Senator Chuck Schumer, whose main objection to the administration’s deportation regime seems to be its lawlessness rather than its cruelty, is never mentioned. Nor is John Fetterman, who has become Israel’s greatest cheerleader on Capitol Hill throughout its atrocities in Gaza. Why are these figures—rather than “the woke”—not the ones whom Neiman chastises?

Neiman’s definition of evil as an absence of moral reasoning also makes it difficult for her to recommend solutions. While contending we could all learn “impatience with clichés,” she resorts to her own clutch of them, arguing that we ought to start “defending truth” and “renewing the moral concepts the right has trampled.” I’m not sure moral handwringing is worth much to the hundreds of babies and toddlers who have been disappeared into ICE custody since the administration took office. 

Instead, we could start by acknowledging the truth that a great many ordinary Americans have been moved to action by the moral atrocities they are witnessing each and every day. Communities from Minneapolis, Minnesota, and Portland, Oregon, to Austin, Texas, and Cambridge, Massachusetts, have banded together against federal overreach and to protect their neighbors from ICE. State governments have passed measures protecting access to abortion and gender-affirming care. More and more progressives are winning elections, speaking not only about economic justice but also with equal fervor about the moral stain that this administration has visited upon the American people and in which the American people are, to our everlasting shame, complicit.

items.title: Listening to Incense
Vivek Ramaswamy’s Vile Attack Ad Is Trumpism in a Nutshell
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024. Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP’s candidate for governor in the Buckeye State, was trailing his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, by seven points in a Marist poll released yesterday. Ramaswamy now hopes to revive his campaign in the most morally depraved way imaginable: by siding with the man who raped his opponent when she was 12 years old.

Ramaswamy’s campaign admitted this week that it was behind a grotesque attack ad targeting Acton that featured Donna Arthur, her mother. In the ad, Arthur calls her daughter a liar and tells voters not to vote for her in the upcoming election. “Don’t let her become your governor,” Arthur says. “If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse.”

What the ad does not mention is that Acton is estranged from her mother and has not spoken to her since Arthur lost custody of her children in the late 1970s. Acton accused her mother’s husband, Cledith Arthur, of abusing her as a child, in 1978. Acton’s father reported it to the police, who found it credible—the man had faced prior allegations before—and a local prosecutor brought criminal charges against him.

Before he could be brought to trial, Cledith fled town. Donna Arthur sided with Cledith over her own daughter. She lost custody of her children and remained married to him until his death in 2004. Acton told the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019 that she had last seen her mother in the courthouse after he was charged. “I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away,” Acton said. “That was the last time I ever saw her.”

A copy of the Ramaswamy ad circulated without the usual disclaimer language from a candidate, raising initial questions about who was responsible for it. The ad drew a furious response from Phillip Stearns, Acton’s brother, who denounced Ramaswamy and his mother in a statement. “After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died,” he said. “This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core—a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

Ramaswamy has previously mocked the abuse that Acton experienced. At one rally, he told voters that as Ohio’s governor, he would “lay out a positive vision for our state, versus a governor who has none at all other than to complain about what someone else did to her.” His campaign initially demurred on whether it was connected to the Donna Arthur ad, out of cowardice, only to admit it was responsible and double down by committing $4 million to broadcast it.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor,” Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson Connie Luck told reporters before the campaign acknowledged it was behind the ad.

Ramaswamy’s ad is morally reprehensible and electorally disqualifying. It demonstrates utter contempt for survivors of sexual abuse and domestic violence. It is also unsurprising. Protecting abusers is an organizing principle of Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

Ten years ago this month, The Washington Post released a 2005 video of then-candidate Donald Trump bragging to an Access Hollywood host about his penchant for trying to have sex with married women and sexually assaulting them.

“I better use some Tic Tacs just in case I start kissing her,” Trump said in the clip. “You know I’m automatically attracted to beautiful—I just start kissing them. It’s like a magnet. Just kiss. I don’t even wait. And when you’re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab ’em by the pussy. You can do anything.” The footage led to widespread condemnation and multiple calls for him to drop out of the race. Trump instead defended the comments as “locker room talk,” then, a few days later, brought women who had previously accused Bill Clinton of sexual misconduct to his second presidential debate with Hillary Clinton.

To support Trump’s political career is to be comfortable with his abuses. Roughly two dozen women have alleged that Trump harassed or assaulted them over the last four decades. He has never been charged with a crime for these allegations, and he has disputed or denied all of the allegations over the years. E. Jean Carroll, who said in 2019 that Trump had raped her in the mid-1990s in a Manhattan department store, was awarded $5 million by a New York jury after she sued Trump for defamation after he said she was “totally lying.”

Two members of Trump’s second-term Cabinet have faced allegations of domestic abuse and/or sexual assault. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth reportedly paid a woman $50,000 after she accused him of sexual assault in 2017. Republican senators threatened to vote against his confirmation over the allegations, only to bow to pressure from the White House and, in particular, Vice President JD Vance.

When a former nanny said Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had groped her in the 1990s, during his 2024 presidential campaign, he simply replied, “I am not a church boy.” The allegations barely factored into his confirmation process as secretary of health and human services last year; every Republican senator voted to confirm him except Mitch McConnell, who rejected Kennedy’s views on vaccines.

Trump even tried to install a third Cabinet member with a history of sexual misconduct allegations when he nominated former Florida Representative Matt Gaetz for attorney general. That nomination only failed because so many congressional Republicans found Gaetz to be personally loathsome. A wave of leaks followed about a then-impending House Ethics Committee report that, among other things, said Gaetz had paid a 17-year-old girl for sex when he was 35 years old. Gaetz withdrew his name from consideration the following week.

Then there’s Jeffrey Epstein. Trump had a long-standing friendship with the billionaire sex trafficker that persisted well after Epstein’s first encounter with federal prosecutors in the 2000s. (He died in federal custody in 2018 while awaiting trial on a second bout of charges.) Trump allies hoped to crack open the Epstein files in the Justice Department’s possession to implicate Democrats in a wide-ranging scheme of child sex trafficking. What they revealed instead was strong evidence that Trump was personally aware of Epstein’s activities, as well as some unverified allegations that he partook in them.

Among the material was a signed birthday note from Trump to Epstein where the two men have an imagined conversation about their friendship. “We have certain things in common, Jeffrey,” Trump’s character says in the note. “Yes, we do, come to think of it,” Epstein’s character replied. “Enigmas never age, have you noticed that?” Trump’s character said. The note ends with “Donald” wishing “Jeffrey” a “happy birthday—and may every day be another wonderful secret.” The entire conversation takes place in a female silhouette depicted with underdeveloped breasts.

Republicans have stood by Trump and supported him through all of this. Any GOP officials who could not stomach his personal depravity or his public misconduct have long since left the party or politics altogether. Those without moral compasses, who were willing to do or say nearly anything for the blind pursuit of power, were happy and willing to replace them. The Republican electorate has not punished them for their sins; if anything, a great many Americans seem eager to indulge in them.

For Ramaswamy, who has faced no such allegations himself, the ad provides a chance to express his sympathy with this malignant fraternity. Ramaswamy has faced no shortage of racist vitriol from his right flank during this campaign. In April, rival GOP candidate Casey Putsch released a video where he said, “Hey Vivek, want to play Cowboys versus Indians?” then turned to fire a rifle three times. “Don’t worry, it’s feather, not dot,” Putsch added.

Now a number of right-wing commentators openly talk about the “Indian question” in education and employment. Ramaswamy can’t change his appearance or background to appeal to white Trump supporters in rural Ohio, of course. But he can declare his allegiance with them in other ways. What could be more Trumpian, after all, than using a Democratic woman’s experience with childhood sexual abuse against her? No amount of tariff policy papers or anti-woke rhetoric can compare to the intoxicating thrill that the virulent, violent hatred of women can provide for them.

Nor will Trump’s eventual departure from American politics restore any semblance of moral thinking to the American right. Vance, the president’s heir apparent, did not distance himself from Ramaswamy’s ad. To the contrary, he castigated other conservatives for distancing themselves from it, then blamed the entire thing on the other side.

“And now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because, guess what?” Vance told a rally on Wednesday. “Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.” Only a movement led by Donald Trump could think that embracing a child molester who has been dead for more than 20 years is a winning strategy in the midterms. Ohio voters must now prove that they reject this antinomian depravity, as well.

items.title: What JD Vance and Vivek Ramaswamy Don’t Get About Trump’s Success
items.content_text:
Let’s just get this out of the way: The ad released on Tuesday by a super PAC connected to Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy (and later endorsed by the candidate himself) is the most despicable in American political history. It features the mother of Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar.

The ad’s effectiveness requires knowing nothing about Donna Arthur. She has not seen her daughter since 1978, when Acton and her brother were removed from Arthur’s custody after her husband—Acton’s stepfather—was indicted for raping Acton. Arthur left Ohio and stayed with the stepfather, who has since passed away. Acton’s allegations are credible, horrifying, and a key part of her appeal as a candidate who has known struggle. The ad, in context, is revolting and disqualifying. It not only weaponizes an opponent’s trauma but adds a partisan sheen to her allegations of abuse: Ramaswamy and his backers are implicitly suggesting that Acton’s story isn’t believable because she is a Democrat. It’s vile stuff—yet reveals a deep weakness in the GOP as it slouches toward the post-Trump era.

Although an outlier in its severity, the ad is also part of a trend. Republican candidates are attacking their Democratic opponents in crude, personal ways as they panic over an expected shellacking in the midterm elections. JD Vance blatantly insinuated that Texas Senate candidate James Talarico is gay. A super PAC with ties to Senate Republicans has taken a slightly more roundabout route to the same place, running an AI-generated ad of Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff getting his hair and nails done. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a “jihadist,” according to President Trump and Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent. (To Texas Senator Ted Cruz, “there’s every reason to believe” El-Sayed, if elected, will share information that endangers American troops with the Muslim Brotherhood.) More or less every Democratic candidate, according to more or less every elected Republican official or aspirant, is in favor of giving children gender-reassignment surgery without notifying their parent. Don’t even get them started about what will happen to your daughter’s soccer league.

These are familiar attacks because they’ve been deployed again and again by Trump, the most successful Republican this century. But they’re not quite working as planned. Talarico is leading in a state Trump won by nearly 14 points. El-Sayed is on the verge of becoming the first Muslim senator in U.S. history. Acton is leading—and if she wins, that despicable ad will have cemented her victory. Instead of pointing toward a new Trumpian Republican politics, these desperate and nasty attacks suggest something else: Trump is actually quite hard to imitate.

Personal attacks have always been part of politics, of course. Politics is a tough business, as they say. Actually, that’s exactly what JD Vance said when asked about the Ramaswamy ad on Wednesday.

WOW -- Vance *defends* Ramaswamy's reprehensible ad 👇 Q: Ramaswamy's campaign put out a controversial ad featuring his opponent's mother. Some Republicans are backing away from that. Do you think that ad was appropriate? JD VANCE: Well, I'll be honest with you. Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern. My concern is who is gonna govern. I have to admit I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans who are whining more about that ad than they are about what the Democrats want to do.

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 21, 2026

Vance is defensive because the ad has been criticized across the political spectrum. National Review and The Bulwark have both published excellent pieces about its odiousness and lack of veracity. Ohio Republicans are fretting that the backlash could doom them in races across the state. But Vance is telling them to buck up: “I’m a little disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining” about the ad, he said, because Democrats make personal attacks too. He claimed that an attack ad called Ramaswamy a murderer—though I’ve been unable to locate any such ad—and concluded, angrily, “My message to fellow elected Republicans is ... stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.”

It’s a revealing answer. The ad against Acton was meant to stoke outrage—just not like this. Ramaswamy and his allies wanted a Democratic backlash, which they hoped would engender the magic of negative partisanship: a backlash on the right to the Democratic backlash. That doesn’t quite work when the outrage is coming from everywhere, including your own house. It’s hard not to see many of the attacks against Democrats, particularly the ones about gender and sexuality, as seeking to do something similar. Republicans want these attacks to stoke outrage only from Democrats, but they’re managing to offend everyone.

These Republicans are trying to replicate a maneuver perfected by Trump, who was elected president the first time after (among very many other things) questioning the war service of his own party’s 2008 presidential nominee and attacking a Gold Star family. But Trump has a gift that Vance and Ramaswamy do not. He is a master ironist, perhaps the greatest in this age of politics. His world, as Christopher Hooks wrote in this magazine last year, “is irony.” Trump, he wrote, “maintains plausible deniability until the point when he acts.” And that means that one is always at risk of taking him too seriously or not seriously enough, which is to say it’s rarely clear exactly how seriously to take what he’s saying.

That’s been a useful escape hatch for Trump. It’s undoubtedly true that many of his supporters flock to him because of his wanton cruelty, like his pledges to execute political opponents and cripple migrants. But Trump’s use of irony (and sometimes humor, loosely defined) creates a buffer between him and his audience, keeping us all guessing: Is he really serious about shooting protesters, for instance, or is that just part of the larger political game he’s playing? And the sense that he’s playing a game—one that his supporters are caught up in—is a big part of his appeal to a lot of people.

This is why Trump can say things that no other politician could get away with. This applies not only to his cruel and violent ramblings but to his many other rhetorical idiosyncrasies—like, most recently, his obsession with GOP Senator Jon Husted’s (supposedly muscular) ass. As Helen Lewis details in a sharp new Atlantic column, “Trump is politics’ answer to Joan Rivers, and his persona is influenced by all the flavors of American fakery: the carnival barker, the reality-TV host, the kayfabe world of professional wrestling,” she wrote. He is immune to shame, she added, and his “authenticity and disinhibition mean he can get a crowd of white Christians in Kentucky to listen to his homoerotic ramblings—and applaud.”

It goes without saying that Vance and Ramaswamy could never pull this off, but they would never try anyway. They’ve studied Trump and apparently have concluded that his appeal lies in his shocking meanness; then they imitate it, with straight faces, and wonder why no one finds them entertaining. Trump is really the only one who could get away with an ad like the one Ramaswamy is spending $4 million to show across Ohio right now—but I’m not sure even Trump would have approved it.

items.title: How the Consulting Class Is Eating the Democratic Party
items.content_text:
Your phone buzzes with a frantic text message. “DEMOCRACY IS ON THE LINE.” It’s not the first time you’ve gotten a fundraising text like this from the Democratic Party and its candidates. Nor the first time you’ve rolled your eyes. But the ask makes sense. Democracy really is on the line. You have asked yourself what you would have done if you had lived under the authoritarian regimes of the past, and volunteering some time and money seems like the least you could do. You click the ActBlue link and donate $100. The country must be saved, after all.

You, the ordinary American, are expected to step up. But are the party insiders stepping up as well? At the very same moment your $100 clears, the party leadership and strategists are at a donor retreat you were not invited to, walking a few dozen people who write seven-figure checks through the polling and the proprietary model that will set the party’s priorities for the cycle. You have a general sense that this is how the game is played, that winning elections requires money from big and small donors. You’re skeptical of the House and Senate leadership, who are increasingly unpopular with the base. But overall, you see a party apparatus that wants to win and oust the Republican Party from control of government, and you assume both tracks feed that goal.

We’re here to tell you that this view is wrong. The Democratic Party is being devoured by an ecosystem of consultants. Mostly out of view of the party’s voters and activists, political consultants are paid to raise the money, place the ads, and set the strategy. And they’re paid regardless of whether the party wins or loses.

We’ve been studying money in U.S. politics for many years, from uncovering racial inequality in campaign contributions to showing how money in politics helps explain why there are so many lawyers in Congress to studying the feedback loop between wealth inequality, political donations by the ultra-wealthy, and their influence over economic and regulatory policy. More recently, what started as a research project on the exclusion of younger Americans from campaign finance spawned an investigation of what we call “spam PACs” in the Democratic Party fundraising ecosystem. These spam PACs are the groups that raise the bulk of their money by squeezing elderly donors with those high-pressure text messages. What started as a high-volume spam model by a few fundraising organizations in the 2010s has spread to the point that even the Democratic Party’s official campaign committees like the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee are some of the groups that profit most from this strategy. Fundraising spam is destroying trust and enthusiasm for the Democratic Party, driving away young potential donors, and extracting the bulk of funds from a small set of vulnerable senior citizens.

The spam operations are only one half of the problem. The other half is the increasing domination in this realm of an exceedingly small number of very wealthy donors. In the 2024 election cycle, the top 0.01 percent of donors—roughly one in every 10,000 voters—accounted for more than half of all federal campaign contributions. Now billionaires are bankrolling authoritarian consolidation, and the Democratic consultant class has convinced the party that it cannot survive without its own “good billionaires,” as Ken Martin, now the Democratic National Committee chairman, put it while running for that position in early 2025. But this distinction between “good” and “bad” billionaires is probably lost on the 80 percent of Americans who believe big donors have too much influence in politics.

A political party is a vehicle for groups in society—voters, activists, and politicians—to come together to elect representatives who will change the world through public policy and governance. It’s a collective enterprise in which different groups debate and negotiate the direction of the party in primary elections and then come together to take control of government and implement that negotiated agenda. The problem is that the incentives of the Democratic consultant class are not aligned with these goals.

Just as a private equity firm buys out a corporation and strips it for parts, the consultant class installs friendly operatives, charges fees, raids the party’s long-term assets, and gives strategic advice that ultimately serves itself over the long-term health of the party.

This class—and we use the word “class” intentionally to mean the firms, consultants, and strategists paid millions of dollars by Democratic campaigns to raise money, place ads, and set strategy—is extractive, and this extraction is central to many of the party’s pathologies. Just as a private equity firm buys out a corporation and strips it for parts, the consultant class installs friendly operatives, charges fees, raids the party’s long-term assets, and gives strategic advice that ultimately serves itself over the long-term health of the party.

Our thesis is a simple one: Campaign consultants are businesses that act to maximize profits, and this profit-seeking is often at odds with what’s best to defeat American authoritarianism.

In this piece, we detail how and why the consultant class weakens the Democratic Party. We bring new data analysis showing that there is no meritocracy when it comes to Democratic vendors. They are paid the same whether their candidates overperform or underperform in elections. This same consultant class pushes Democratic campaigns toward short-term money over long-term growth and sells campaign strategies that are lucrative for them but ineffective for the party. In pursuing their financial incentives, the consultant class has reshaped who runs for office, how the party raises and spends money, what it says and claims to stand for, and how it relates to its own supporters. They have made the party older, weaker, less honest, and less capable of fighting the most serious authoritarian threat in American history.

Follow the Money

Let’s begin by following that $100 you donated. We’ve spent the last two years tracing money through Federal Election Commission records, vendor networks, and data on hundreds of millions of transactions. We research money in politics for a living, and we’re used to uncovering troubling realities in the data. But when we traced the Democratic fundraising environment, what we found shocked even us.

If your $100 was in response to a fundraising text or email, the single most expensive way to raise money in American politics, $65 is instantly consumed by the cost of asking you for it. Asking this often, and this aggressively, is expensive.
